blocks.text: A 2020 census tract in north-central Allen County: 28.896 square miles of land, internal point 40.8240378, -84.1599836. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), national tract file. Allen County holds 35 tracts in the 2020 geography. [verified] — same source.

**It is 98.5% of Sugar Creek Township plus a fifth of American Township.** Of its 107 blocks, 90 fall in [Sugar Creek](../place/sugar-creek-township.yml) — 82.1% of the tract's land, 1,192 people — and 17 in [American](../place/american-township.yml) — 17.9%, 408 people. [verified] — [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md), block composition; the block areas sum to the tract's own `AREALAND` exactly, which is the check that they are all of it.

It holds all but 0.372 square miles of Sugar Creek and adds 5.175 of American, so a figure published for this tract and read as Sugar Creek Township's **overstates it by about a quarter** — 408 of 1,600 residents live in the other township. [inference]

nodes.label: Ohio's 4th congressional district (2020 geography)

blocks.text: The United States congressional district covering Allen County at the 2020 census. All 3,552 of the county's census blocks fall in it. [verified] — [2020 Census Block Assignment Files](../../catalog/census-block-assignment-2020.md). It runs to 4,665.374 square miles of land with an internal point at 40.387175, -83.935703. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md).

refusals: `effective_to` is absent because the corpus does not know the date the map was superseded, not because the district still stands as drawn.

nodes.label: Ohio House District 4 (2020 geography)

blocks.text: The Ohio House of Representatives district covering Allen County under the map in force at the 2020 census. All 3,552 of the county's census blocks fall in it. [verified] — [2020 Census Block Assignment Files](../../catalog/census-block-assignment-2020.md).

**It is coterminous with the county.** Its gazetteer record reads `ALAND 1042587389`, `AWATER 11152061`, `ALAND_SQMI 402.545`, `INTPTLAT 40.771627`, `INTPTLONG -84.106103` — every field byte-identical to [Allen County](../place/allen-county.yml)'s own record in the county file. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md). Not approximately the same ground: the same ground.

refusals: The coincidence is also not permanent, and this node's `effective_to` being absent does not assert that it is — see [which congressional district Allen County is in now](../question/allen-county-current-congressional-district.yml) for the same vintage problem on the federal map.

blocks.text: The Ohio House district Allen County votes in under the map now in force, adopted by the Ohio Redistricting Commission on 29 September 2023 to govern the rest of the decade. [verified] — [All About Redistricting — Ohio](../../catalog/all-about-redistricting-ohio.md) for the map's date and [Ohio county elected officials lookup](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md) for the county's district.

**The county's House district was renumbered, not redrawn into pieces.** Under the map in force at the 2020 census this county was [House District 4](ohio-house-district-4-2020.yml), coterminous with the county to the byte. It is now the 78th. [verified] — same two sources.

**The county is not split.** The elections roster names one state representative for Allen County and one only; a split county would list two. [inference] — reasoned here from the roster's shape rather than from any boundary file.

nodes.label: Ohio Senate District 12 (2020 geography)

blocks.text: The Ohio Senate district covering Allen County under the map in force at the 2020 census. All 3,552 of the county's census blocks fall in it, so the county is not split. [verified] — [2020 Census Block Assignment Files](../../catalog/census-block-assignment-2020.md).

Unlike [House District 4](ohio-house-district-4-2020.yml), it is much larger than the county: 2,659.11 square miles of land against the county's 402.545, with an internal point at 40.416995, -84.191133 that lies well south of Allen County's. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md). Allen County is roughly a seventh of it by land area. [inference]

refusals: Whether this node and that one describe the same polygon is exactly what the corpus cannot say.

nodes.label: Ohio Senate District 12 (2023 map)

blocks.text: The Ohio Senate district Allen County votes in under the map now in force, adopted 29 September 2023. [verified] — [All About Redistricting — Ohio](../../catalog/all-about-redistricting-ohio.md) and [Ohio county elected officials lookup](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md).

**Its number did not change and that is not evidence its ground did not.** The county was in [Senate District 12](ohio-senate-district-12-2020.yml) under the map in force at the 2020 census and is in a district of the same number now, across a redistricting that renumbered its House district from the 4th to [the 78th](ohio-house-district-78-2023.yml). A number surviving a new map says the legislature reused it, not that it kept its lines. [inference] This node is separate from the 2020 one for that reason, and either may turn out to describe ground the other does not.
**The county is not split**, on the same reasoning as the House district: the roster names one state senator for Allen County. [inference]

refusals: The 2020 node could say Allen County was about a seventh of the district by land area; this one cannot say even that.

blocks.text: A precinct of 1.548 square miles in northern Lima holding 3,240 people and 756 housing units, internal point 40.778293, -84.105936. [verified] — [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md), layer 58.

**It is where three sources disagree with each other in a way that means something.** Its 908 registered voters are 0.28 per resident, the lowest of the county's 88 precincts against a median of 0.68 and a next-lowest of 0.54. [verified] — [OpenElections](../../catalog/openelections-ohio.md) against TIGERweb block population. One of its 43 blocks holds 1,360 people in **zero** housing units, and set those aside and the ratio is 0.48 — low, and inside the range the rest of the county occupies.

The county's state correctional institutions stand in this precinct. [verified] — [Allen County GIS](../../catalog/allen-county-gis-downloads.md), address points projected and tested against the precinct polygon.

**They are now named, and they are the whole of it.** The block holding 1,360 is [Allen Correctional Institution](../site/allen-correctional-institution.yml) and a second block in this precinct holds 153 at [Oakwood](../site/oakwood-correctional-facility.yml) — 1,513 people between them, every one counted in adult correctional facilities, and every person the 2020 census counted in a correctional facility anywhere in Allen County. [verified] — [the group quarters](../measure/allen-county-group-quarters-2020.yml); see [the question this closed](../question/who-lives-in-the-county-without-housing.yml).

**So the precinct's registration ratio is a prison and not a puzzle.** Take both institutions out and 908 registrations stand against 1,727 residents — a ratio of **0.53**, which is inside the band the rest of the county occupies and above the earlier estimate of 0.48 made with only one of the two blocks known. [inference] — computed here. The lowest registration ratio of eighty-eight precincts turns out to be an artefact of where the state put two institutions, and nothing on the face of the map says so.
It voted 287 to 234 for Trump over Biden on a 58.4 per cent turnout — nearly the county's most balanced precinct in a county that went 69 to 29. [verified] — OpenElections.

The single precinct covering [Sugar Creek Township](../place/sugar-creek-township.yml), holding 1,231 people and 515 housing units over 24.094 square miles, internal point 40.824171, -84.173844. [verified] — [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md), layer 58.

**It is coterminous with the township.** The township's own gazetteer record gives 24.094 square miles of land and an internal point of 40.824171, -84.173843 — the same figures, differing in the last decimal place of the longitude by about four inches. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md). It is the only one of the county's 88 precincts that is a whole civil subdivision; four others are whole villages, and the remaining 83 are pieces.

nodes.label: Allen County is declared for COVID-19, March 2020

properties.location_description: Allen County. `occurred` is the earlier of the two declaration dates and `occurred_through` the end of the incident window both records give. [verified] — the same source.

blocks.text: **The most recent thing this corpus can date**, and the longest incident in the county's federal record by a factor of twenty-nine. Allen County was named in EM-3457-OH on 13 March 2020 and again in DR-4507-OH on 31 March 2020, both carrying an incident window from 20 January 2020 to 11 May 2023 — **1,207 days**, against forty-one for the longest of the county's other declarations. [verified] — [OpenFEMA](../../catalog/fema-disaster-declarations.md); see [the declarations](../measure/allen-county-disaster-declarations-1965-2020.yml).

**Two declarations, one incident.** The emergency declaration came eighteen days before the major disaster declaration, on identical incident dates. That is the same pattern as June 2012, where an emergency was declared on the 30th and a major disaster seven weeks later for one four-day storm. [verified] — same source. Counting rows here counts federal acts, not events in the world. [inference]
**Neither carried Individual Assistance.** Both designated Public Assistance and the major disaster declaration added Hazard Mitigation. [verified] — same source.

**It is the only event in this corpus that overlaps a census.** The 2020 census was taken inside this incident window, and the county's group-quarters counts, its housing occupancy and its population were all enumerated during it. [inference] — see [the group quarters](../measure/allen-county-group-quarters-2020.yml) and [the 2020 count](../measure/allen-county-population-2020-census.yml). The corpus does not assert that the enumeration was affected; it records that the two overlap, which is a thing a reader of those figures should know and could not otherwise learn here.

**And it bought a house out of a floodplain.** The mitigation allocation this declaration generated funded a riverine property acquisition, approved April 2023 and closed 18 August 2026. [verified] — [the mitigation](../measure/allen-county-hazard-mitigation-2003-2026.yml). A declaration generates money for hazards it had nothing to do with. [inference]

refusals: The corpus does not assert that the enumeration was affected; it records that the two overlap, which is a thing a reader of those figures should know and could not otherwise learn here.

nodes.label: Allen County is declared for Hurricane Katrina, September 2005

properties.location_description: Allen County. `occurred` is the declaration date; `occurred_through` is the end of the incident window the file gives, which for this record is a real window rather than a repeated declaration date. [verified] — the same source.

blocks.text: **A county in north-west Ohio has a hurricane declaration.** On 13 September 2005 Allen County was named in EM-3250-OH, "Hurricane Katrina Evacuation", with Public Assistance designated and an incident window running 29 August to 1 October 2005. [verified] — [OpenFEMA](../../catalog/fema-disaster-declarations.md).

**What was declared was the sheltering, not the storm.** An evacuation declaration reimburses a state and its local governments for taking in people from somewhere else; the hazard is nine hundred miles away and the cost is here. [inference] This is the only one of the county's ten declarations whose incident did not happen in Ohio. [verified] — same source; see [the declarations](../measure/allen-county-disaster-declarations-1965-2020.yml).
**It carried no Individual Assistance**, which is the ordinary shape here: eight of the county's ten declarations paid governments and two paid households. [verified] — same source.

nodes.label: The raid on the Allen County jail

properties.location_description: The Allen County jail at Lima, near Main Street.

blocks.text: On the night of 12 October 1933 three armed men walked into the Allen County jail at Lima, shot Sheriff [Jess L. Sarber](../person/jess-l-sarber.yml), freed the prisoner John Dillinger from his cell, locked the sheriff's wife and his deputy in it, stripped the building of its guns and ammunition and drove west out of town. [verified] — [Chronicling America](../../catalog/chronicling-america.md), *The Times-News* (Hendersonville, N.C.), 13 October 1933, page 1, carrying a United Press dispatch datelined Lima.

It is the county's most widely reported hour and the corpus's first event of the twentieth century. Before this node the county's dated happenings stopped in 1885. [verified] — the corpus's own event nodes.

**Why the man was in this county's jail.** Dillinger was being held on a charge of robbing a bank in Allen County — "the Bluffton, O., Commercial Bank of $2200" — and had been brought up from Dayton about a week before. [verified] — same archive, *The Washington Daily News*, 13 October 1933, page 3.

So the night was not a national story that happened to land in Lima. It began with a bank in [Bluffton](../place/bluffton.yml), forty minutes up the road, and the county was holding the man who was charged with robbing it. [inference]
[verified] — same page.

**The same dispatch contradicts itself about how long the sheriff lived.** In its fourth paragraph he "died 20 minutes later in a hospital"; nine paragraphs on, a pedestrian hears shouting, fetches the chief of police, and the sheriff is taken to the hospital "where he died a few minutes later". [verified] — same page. That a wire story can hold both readings in one column is the plainest evidence this corpus has for how a newspaper differs from the records it was built on, and it is the case that produced [two papers printing one dispatch](../../decisions/two-papers-printing-one-dispatch-are-one-witness.yml).

**Who was named.** Harry Pierpont, Charles Makley and Russell Clark were tried at Lima for the murder, and Pierpont was named the trigger man. Sarber himself, before he died, identified his assailant as "Harry Copeland"; officers said they were convinced the right name was Pierpont. [verified] — same archive, *Evening Star* (Washington, D.C.), 13 October 1933, page 10.

**The county tried all three of them, and it took the National Guard to do it.** Three trials at Lima, each about a week, through February and March 1934, prosecuted by Ernest M. Botkin before Judge E. E. Everett, with Ohio National Guardsmen under Brig. Gen. Harold M. Bush holding the town — machine gun nests at the approaches to the jail, another at the end of the cell corridor, sandbag defenses, and nobody admitted without a written order from the sheriff, the prosecutor or the judge. [verified] — same archive, *Evening Star*, 4 March 1934, page 3, and 25 March 1934, page 2.

**How it ended.** Pierpont was found guilty in the early morning hours of 11 March 1934. [verified] — same archive, *Evening Star*, 12 March 1934, page 3. Pierpont and Makley were sentenced to die and Clark, alone, "drew a verdict of guilty with mercy, obligating the court to pronounce sentence of life imprisonment". [verified] — *Evening Star*, 25 March 1934, page 2, whose Lima dateline has an illegible day.

On 22 September 1934 Pierpont and Makley tried to bluff their way off death row at the Ohio Penitentiary with guns carved from soap; guards shot both, and Makley died within the hour. [verified] — *Evening Star*, 23 September 1934, page 2. Pierpont was electrocuted shortly after midnight on 17 October 1934. [verified] — same archive, *The Daily Alaska Empire*, 17 October 1934, page 1. Twelve months and five days after the raid, all three of the men who came into the jail were dead or serving life, and so was the sheriff.

**What it did to this county's government, which is the reason the corpus went looking.** The sheriff's office passed to his son, [Donald F. Sarber](../person/donald-f-sarber.yml). [verified] — same archive, *Evening Star*, 4 March 1934, which calls the dead man "the elder Sarber, who preceded his son as sheriff". See [the two irregular sheriff transitions](../question/two-irregular-sheriff-transitions.yml), the question this event was retrieved to answer.

refusals: This corpus does not establish what the trials cost the county or how they were paid for.
This node does not establish where the jail stood.

blocks.text: **The organic act of 1820, which divided the cession into fourteen counties and laid out Allen as one of them.** [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md), which gives the act's disposition county by county: Allen was "all of the second townships to the northern limits of the organized counties", and the act further provided that it "be attached to Shelby County for judicial purposes". Allen was afterwards attached to Mercer, and stayed attached until [the organization of 1831](../question/when-allen-county-was-organized.yml).

Laying out a county and organizing its government were separate acts in Ohio practice, often years apart. The corpus had reasoned to that from general practice and put the gap at "about a decade"; the record makes it eleven years, and names both counties Allen was attached to in the meantime. [verified] — same source.

**The date within 1820 is April 1.** "Allen County was formed from the Indian Territory April 1, 1820." [verified] — same source, its chapter on Ohio's counties, both scans identical. That chapter is compiled state-history filler rather than the commissioners' record the rest of this node rests on, so the day is carried at the standard of a gazetteer entry and not of a minute book.

**The act passed on February 12, 1820, and April 1 is when it took effect.** "Allen County was erected by act of February 12, 1820, and was organized by act of February 9, 1831." [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md), both scans identical. That answers the question this node asked in the sentence it replaces: the 1885 volume's "formed... April 1, 1820" is the effective date, the 1906 volume gives the passage date, and the two are consistent rather than in conflict.

nodes.label: The assembly of the Ford Lima engine plant's ground

properties.location_description: The north-west quarter of section 17, township 3 south, range 7 east — Bath Township, about 3.3 miles north-east of Lima's internal point.

blocks.text: Between 24 August 1955 and 17 August 1956, Ford Motor Company took the ground its Lima engine plant stands on, in five conveyances, all of them recorded in the Recorder's tract abstract for the north-west quarter of section 17, township 3 south, range 7 east. [verified] — [Section Ground book list](../../catalog/allen-county-recorder-section-ground.md), volume 0028A pages 163–166; see [the plant](../site/ford-lima-engine-plant.yml).

**It is the corpus's first dated event since 1933.** The history this corpus can put a day on ran 1818, 1820, 1832, 1848, 1885, 1918, 1933 and then stopped, which the site has been saying in those words. This is the first thing to fill that end of it, and it arrived from a land record rather than from a newspaper. [verified] — the corpus's own event nodes.

**Ford did not buy this ground in its own name first.** DTI Enterprises Inc bought from the National Lime & Stone Company on 2 June 1955 and from a private owner on 24 December 1955, and conveyed to Ford four times between August 1955 and August 1956; a fifth parcel came to Ford directly from two individuals in January 1956. [verified] — same pages.

A company acquiring adjacent parcels over eighteen months and passing them to one manufacturer is the ordinary shape of a site assembly, in which the assembler exists so that the buyer's name does not appear and the price does not move. [inference]

**What it was before.** A quarry. National Quarries Company held it from 1917, conveyed to the National Lime & Stone Company in January 1944, and it was National Lime & Stone that sold to the assembler in 1955. [verified] — same pages.

**What followed, on the same ground.** A mechanic's lien for $91,546.07 was filed against Ford Motor Company by Carlson Manufacturing Inc on 30 September 1957 — a claim for work done, and so the first dated evidence this corpus holds that the plant was being built. [verified] — same pages.

refusals: Whether DTI Enterprises was Ford's agent, and whether it is connected to the Detroit, Toledo & Ironton Railroad that held ground in this same quarter from 1924 to 1943, this corpus does not know.
This node does not establish when the plant opened or when it first made an engine.

blocks.text: **"The commission form of government comes into effect January 1, 1922, at the end of the term of Mayor Burkhardt. Henceforth initiative, referendum and recall enter into the conduct of public service."** [verified] — [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md).

**It replaced an aldermanic government of eighty years.** "For four-score years Lima has been ruled by a mayor", and "the mayor and members of City Council have hitherto served two years". [verified] — same source. Four-score is exact: the town organized in March 1842 and the charter took effect in January 1922, seventy-nine years and nine months. [inference] — computed here.

**The movement began in 1919 and the charter was drafted to order.** "A movement to replace the aldermanic form of government with the commission-manager charter plan was begun early in 1919, and a commission was named and instructed to draft a charter." [verified] — same source. The 1912 revision of the Ohio Constitution is what made it available. [verified] — same source.

**What the charter secures and what it does not.** "It secures home rule for Lima except that the charter shall in no way interfere with the tax limit laws of the state governing municipalities; city officials are not granted any greater debt-incurring power than they now possess. Public hearings are required upon appropriations of public money." [verified] — same source. That answers, from a source and with a date, what [the office node](../office/mayor-of-lima.yml) had only inferred from three term calendars: Lima is a home-rule city under a charter of its own, and this is when.

**The reason given is that the county had changed under the law.** "When many laws on the statutes of Allen County were enacted it was purely an agricultural county, but Lima is now an industrial center with manufacturing and commercial interests." [verified] — same source. The book is arguing, not reporting, and the argument is the same one [the oil boom](../period/lima-oil-boom.yml) makes about everything else in the county. [inference]

**The first half of that question is answered and the answer is yes.** By November 1939 Lima had a mayor who took office, cut twelve men from the street department within forty-eight hours, and four months later called a civil service examination "under provisions of the City Charter and Ohio civil service laws". [verified] — [The Bluffton News](../../catalog/chronicling-america.md); see [the mayors named inside the gap](../measure/lima-mayors-1939-1956.yml). A charter was in force and so was a mayor, seventeen years after this book said the office ended. Whether the charter of 1922 always kept one, or the city changed its government again in between, is not established. [inference]

nodes.label: The 1885 Lima oil strike

blocks.text: The well at Lima that struck oil in 1885 and opened the Lima–Indiana field. [inference] The drilling was after natural gas, following the Findlay boom to the north; oil is what came up. [inference]

The Lima crude was sour — high in sulphur, and difficult to refine into a saleable illuminant by the methods of the day. That property is why the field's development depended on a desulphurization process and hence on the capital and patents of [Standard Oil](../organization/standard-oil.yml) rather than on local operators. [inference]

The strike `affected` the county and not only the city: the Lima–Indiana field extended well beyond the corporate boundary. [inference] That is why this node carries an `affected` edge to the county alongside its `occurred-in` edge to Lima — the two say different things, and only the first is true of the ground outside the city.

**What the strike did to the county was add, not replace.** This node used to say the county's economy "was reoriented from agriculture to petroleum and the manufacturing that followed it", which was written before the corpus had measured any agriculture at all. It has now. Twenty-five years after the strike, Allen County had 2,939 farms against 2,858 in 1900, 92.5 per cent of its land area in farms, and improved acreage higher than before the boom began. [verified] — [Abstract of the Thirteenth Census, Supplement for Ohio](../../catalog/census-1910-abstract-supplement-ohio.md); see [the county's farms](../measure/allen-county-farms-1900-1910.yml). The farms did not go anywhere. A city grew beside them. [inference]

**The one farm figure that moved sharply is price.** An acre of Allen County farmland went from $38.39 in 1900 to $76.28 in 1910, and all farm property rose 89.0 per cent against 58.7 for Ohio. [verified] — same source, which prints both percentages.

[verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md). A book that catalogues a $12,000 flour mill would not have missed an oil field in the town it is written about. So the strike had not happened, or had not yet registered, when this went to press — which bounds it from below without naming a well, and is the first independent support this corpus has for the year 1885 at all. [inference]

**The conditions the received account requires are all in the book, and the oil is not.** Gas shows across the county; a gas boom at Findlay, whose "two gas wells" the same volume notes; a Lima Gaslight Company with a secretary who married [B. C. Faurot's](../person/benjamin-faurot.yml) daughter in January 1885; and Faurot himself owning the paper mill that needed the fuel. [verified] — same source. The story of a man drilling for gas at his own mill is not verified here, but every one of its preconditions now is.

**The well was completed on May 9, 1885, and it was not looking for oil.** The drill began work in the spring of 1885 on the grounds of the Lima Straw Board Works, on the bank of the [Ottawa River](../natural-feature/ottawa-river.yml), under the direction of [B. C. Faurot](../person/benjamin-faurot.yml); the contractors were Brownyear and Martin. **It was put down for a double purpose** — "they needed a better quality of water and more of it for manufacturing purposes, and they hoped they might possibly get a supply of natural gas", gas having been found shortly before at Bowling Green and Findlay. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md), both scans agreeing on every figure below.

The oil was "dark in color, low in gravity and very offensive in odor", and "to a Pennsylvania oil man, these characteristics seemed to condemn the new supply". [verified] — same source. The water motive is the detail every retelling drops, and it is the one that makes the event legible: a paper mill wanted a better well.

**The famous well failed.** The pioneer well met "a series of misfortunes that left it useless". The Citizens' Gas Company, formed to establish whether there was really oil about Lima, put down a **second** well that autumn, and it is that one "to be credited with yielding the first regular and persistent supply of petroleum from the Trenton limestone in Ohio" — 40 to 45 barrels a day at first, **1,450 barrels in December 1885**, and an average of 26 a day through the first quarter of 1886. Its oil was the first sent to refineries to be tested at scale, and the tests established that Lima crude could be deodorized. [verified] — same source. So the event this corpus named for a single strike is two wells: one that made the discovery and broke, and one that proved the field. [inference]

I. E. Dean, experienced in Canada, was among the first outsiders to arrive and organized the Trenton Rock Oil Company — which within a year held a lease that nearly cost Lima [its refinery](../site/lima-refinery.yml). [verified] — same source and [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md).

**The first primary record of the boom reaching a named piece of ground.** On 29 September 1885, four and a half months after the well, an oil lease over part of the north-west quarter of section 17 in [Bath Township](../place/bath-township.yml) — 3.3 miles north-east of Lima's internal point — was granted to **B. C. Faurot and others**, and recorded the following April. It was later released. [verified] — [Section Ground book list](../../catalog/allen-county-recorder-section-ground.md), volume 0028A page 164, lease volume L-3 page 121.

Until now the claim that the field extended beyond the city was an inference from the field's name. This is a dated instrument, on ground the corpus can point at, taken by the man who financed the well, in the September after it came in. [inference] A second oil lease over the same quarter followed on 2 November 1898, also released. [verified] — same pages.

**And there is an earlier one, twenty days after the well.** An oil lease over part of the north-west quarter of section 14 in [Shawnee Township](../place/shawnee-township.yml) — the ground the tank plant stands on now — ran to "B C Faurot Et al" dated **29 May 1885**, recorded 20 July 1886, and was afterwards cancelled. [verified] — same source, volume 0034A page 89, lease volume 3 page 410. The well came in on 9 May. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md).

So within three weeks of the strike its financier was taking oil rights four miles south of the city, and by that September four miles north-east of it. [inference] The two leases are the only record this corpus holds of what the boom did in its first months, and what it did was move across the county in both directions almost at once. [inference]

**Others followed, and then Standard's operating company.** A second lease over the section 14 quarter went to H M Earnst in February 1886; the **Ohio Oil Company** took four leases over it between September 1895 and September 1897 and three rights of way in April 1907. [verified] — same pages.

Both Faurot leases were released or cancelled, so neither says anything about whether oil was found there. A lease is a record of where people expected oil, which is a different and in some ways more useful fact. [inference]

refusals: **A source printed in 1885 does not know this happened, and that is evidence.** The county history published that year is exhaustive about Lima's industry — it names the paper mills, the machine works, the iron fence company, the egg-carrier patent, the gas works, every bank and the year each was organized.

nodes.label: The organization of the town of Lima

properties.location_description: Lima, then the county seat of a county eleven years old, platted in 1831 on ground the commissioners controlled. [verified]

blocks.text: Lima got a government of its own on **29 March 1842**, eleven years after the county commissioners platted it and told it what to do. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md), whose two scans carry the date identically.

**The corpus has held this date since the settlements phase and never as an event.** [The corporation](../jurisdiction/city-of-lima.yml) records it in prose; nothing put it on the dated record, so the timeline ran from 1848 to 1854 with the county seat's own founding inside the gap. This node is the same fact promoted to the class the corpus counts. [verified]

**The town was platted in 1831 and run by the county until 1842.** "The original town as platted in 1831 was entirely controlled by the county commissioners. In 1841 a movement to organize a system of village government was favorably received; the commissioners were petitioned in the matter, and as a result the village of Lima was established." [verified] — same source, scan B; scan A reads 1881 for 1831, which is impossible on the book's own account of a county organized in 1831 and a book printed in 1885.

**The first officers, as the book prints them.** H. D. V. Williams, mayor; W. McHenry, recorder; John Alexander Jr., Samuel Black, H. Davison, T. K. Jacobs and D. D. Tompkins, trustees. The council then elected John B. Wamsley treasurer and Amos Clutter marshal, and in April appointed Alexander Beatty, Daniel Bowyer and R. E. Thomas street commissioners and Daniel Musser supervisor. [verified] — same source. See [Henry D. V. Williams](../person/henry-d-v-williams.yml).

**Five officers and five trustees is not the government the city has now.** Lima today elects a mayor, an auditor, a director of law, a president of council and seven council members by ward, and its marshal, recorder and street commissioners are gone. [verified] — [the city's government](../measure/lima-city-government-2026.yml).

refusals: The book uses village, town and city interchangeably in the same paragraph and this corpus cannot say which was the legal event.

nodes.label: Removal of the Ottawa from the Auglaize and Ottawa river reserves

blocks.text: The removal of the Ottawa from their reserved lands in and near this county to territory west of the Mississippi, following further cession in the early 1830s. [inference]

nodes.label: The renaming of German Township

properties.location_description: German Township, Allen County, by order of the county commissioners.

blocks.text: On 16 August 1918 the Allen County commissioners, acting on a citizens' petition, changed the name of German Township to [American Township](../place/american-township.yml). [verified] — [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md).

The petition's stated ground was formal: Article II says only "that good cause is shown why the name of said township should be changed", and stipulates that the change "shall in no wise affect the right of property, or the internal concerns of said township". The historian who prints it reads the language for what it is — "'good cause' means patriotism" — and records that school books were being reset and businesses were dropping the word. [verified] — same source.

**This node exists because the corpus had the date and no place to put it.** The renaming was established two phases before this one and recorded as prose on a place and a question, which is where an answer goes and not where a happening goes. It was therefore absent from every view built on the event class, including the site's timeline, and its absence made the county's eighteen-eighty-five-to-nineteen-thirty-three gap look wider than the corpus's own knowledge. [verified] — the corpus's own history; see [what became of German and Ottawa townships](../question/what-became-of-german-and-ottawa-townships.yml).

It is one of two Allen County township name changes this corpus knows of, and the only one whose day it has. [inference] The instrument is the same one that erected every township in the county and incorporated every village here: a petition and an order of the county commissioners. [verified] — same source.

refusals: This node does not establish how the vote went or who signed the petition.

properties.location_description: In session at Lima. The act text names no place; the commissioners had met in the court house since 1842. [inference]

blocks.text: The sitting at which the Allen County commissioners redrew every township line in the county at once, "consequent on the formation of Auglaize County". [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md), which resumes the commissioners' record. Both scans carry the act's text identically.

**The county lost its southern half and gained a northern one.** In March 1846 Allen County assessed sixteen townships in four districts, eight of which — Deuchoquette, Moulton, Washington, Pusheta, Clay, Union, Wayne and Goshen — are in Auglaize County today. [verified] — same source, the 1846 assessors' districts. In exchange the act took ground from Putnam and Van Wert Counties: Riley Township's south tier to [Richland](../place/richland-township.yml), the south half of Jennings to [Marion](../place/marion-township.yml), and Salem's north-east quarter with Jennings' east half set off as [Spencer](../place/spencer-township.yml).

**The transfer was settled in cash.** In May 1853 the commissioners of Allen and Putnam met and agreed that Allen owed Putnam **$3,848.76** arising from the changes. [verified] — same source. Two counties reconciling an account five years later is the strongest internal evidence that the 1885 compiler was reading a real record rather than composing one.

**Allen County's population before and after this date is not a series.** The 1885 statistics chapter gives county totals of 578 in 1830 and 9,079, 12,116, 19,185, 23,623 and 31,314 for 1840 to 1880, and footnotes that the marked townships "form a portion of the adjoining county of Auglaize" since the change. [verified] — same source. The 1840 figure therefore counts ground that has not been in this county since 1848, and does not count Sugar Creek, Monroe or Richland, which were Putnam's. Any trend drawn across 1848 is a trend about two different counties — see [the pre-1970 series](../question/pre-1970-population-series.yml).

**The two accounts of what went name different townships.** The 1846 assessors' districts above give eight — Deuchoquette, Moulton, Washington, Pusheta, Clay, Union, Wayne and Goshen. The 1921 history gives four: "In 1848 Allen lost Logan, Deuchoquette, Union and Wayne townships to Auglaize County." [verified] — [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md). Logan is in the second list and not the first, and Logan is the township that holds [Fort Amanda](../site/fort-amanda.yml). The act transcribed here explains why it can be in one and not the other: it establishes a new Amanda from "the south half of Marion and the north half of Amanda", so old Amanda's south half — with the fort — left under a name it did not have in 1846. [inference]

**The same historian grieves over it and then argues with himself.** "It was a rude fate that removed Fort Amanda with its historic traditions from the bounds of Allen County. However, it is used as an Allen County asset today because the military post located there was in Allen County ... and in its traditions Fort Amanda belongs to Allen County." [verified] — same source. He also reads the act as a trade: "Since 1848, Delphos has been in Allen County, offsetting the loss of Fort Amanda when Auglaize County was securing recognition from the Ohio Assembly." [verified] — same source.

**And he puts a number on the whole exchange, and adds a county.** "When Auglaize County was formed Allen lost on the south and gained on the west and north, annexing something from Mercer, Van Wert and Putnam counties. Through the juggling process **it lost 138 square miles of territory**." [verified] — same source, a single witness read once for the figure. Mercer is a third donor the 1885 act transcript does not name, and 138 square miles is about a fifth of the county's present 404.

nodes.label: Settlers occupy the blockhouses at Fort Amanda, 1817

properties.location_description: Inside the stockade at Fort Amanda, on the west bank of the Auglaize — in Allen County at the time and in Auglaize County now. [verified]

blocks.text: **The first American settlement in Allen County was three men moving into an abandoned army post.** "In 1817 a few settlers arrived, who occupied the block-houses within the stockade around this fort." [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md), both scans, and reprinted word for word in [the 1906 history](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md).

They were **Andrew Russell**, who died five years later and was buried in the military cemetery; **Peter Diltz**, who went back to Montgomery County in August 1818 and returned in 1821; and **William Van Ausdall**, who died in 1824 and was laid next to Russell. [verified] — same source, both scans. Two of the county's first three settlers are buried inside the fort's cemetery, which makes the graves there a mixed burial ground of soldiers and civilians and not the national cemetery the same page calls it. [inference]

**The 1885 history is emphatic about the precedence and puts it twice.** "The initial point in the history of the settlement of Allen County must be known as Fort Amanda," and, opening the township chapter, "This division of the county was the first to fall into the possession of the American pioneer, and one of the first divisions of the entire Northwest to be occupied by United States troops." [verified] — same source, both scans.

**And the ground it happened on has not been in Allen County since 1848.** [verified] — [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md); see [the fort](../site/fort-amanda.yml) and [of here is not located here](../../decisions/of-here-is-not-located-here.yml). The settlement that follows is inside the present county: Henry Hartel in 1820, Dye Sunderland and family in 1821, and a roll of some thirty names to 1829. [verified] — [the 1885 history](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md).

**What made the fort habitable is what made it a place to die in.** The storehouse at the centre of the quadrangle had a second storey added in 1813 to serve as an army hospital, and most of those in the cemetery died in that room. Four years later three men moved their families into the same enclosure. [verified] — [the 1921 history](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md), which calls it "rather an uncanny introduction to the place as a home for the settlers a few years later".

nodes.label: The building of Fort Amanda, September 1812

properties.location_description: The west bank of the Auglaize River, in what was then unorganized territory attached to Mercer County and became Allen County in 1820. The ground is in Auglaize County today. [verified]

blocks.text: Col. Thomas Poague's command built a stockaded post on the west bank of the Auglaize in September 1812, and Poague named it for his wife. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md), both scans, whose wording is that it "is, therefore, conceded" — the compiler is inferring the date from Harrison's correspondence rather than reading it off an order.

**What Harrison was doing.** Appointed commander-in-chief of the Northwestern Army on 17 September 1812, he massed troops at Wooster, Urbana, St. Marys and Defiance and made the southern line of the Black Swamp, from Upper Sandusky to St. Marys, his base. The posts on the Auglaize appear first in the report of military affairs that followed the appointment, alongside the Ohio cavalry under Col. Finley, the Kentucky cavalry under R. M. Johnson, and the infantry under Cols. Poague, Barbee and Jennings — "the former of whom erected Fort Amanda and the latter Fort Jennings". [verified] — same source, both scans.

**The 1921 history tells it as a road first and a fort second.** Poague "cleared the way through the wilderness from St. Marys, where General Harrison had his headquarters, to Fort Defiance at the junction of the Auglaize and the Maumee", and built the fort on the return journey. [verified] — [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md), single witness. It also has the road following ground already cut: Wayne had ordered a military road from the present St. Marys to a point on the Auglaize near where the fort was built, after Fort Recovery was retaken, and that stretch is part of Wayne's Trace. [verified] — [the 1885 history](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md), both scans.

**The month is not agreed.** The 1885 history says September 1812; the bronze tablet the State of Ohio put on the monument in 1915 says the fort was erected by Harrison's order "in October, 1812". [verified] — the 1885 history and [the 1921 history](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md) quoting the tablet. The corpus records both and dates this node September, because that is the reading a book gives with its reasoning shown against a tablet that gives none. [inference]

nodes.label: The first electric car in Lima, July 4, 1886

properties.location_description: The Lima public square, where the crowd stood. [verified] — the 1921 history. The route is not stated; the street railway's 1878 lines ran from the Fort Wayne depot along Wayne, Main and Market.

blocks.text: **"It is said the mule was emancipated in Lima in 1886 — July 4th, when the first electric car in use west of the Allegheny Mountains, was seen in Lima. The town was full of people, although it rained all day; some would take a ride were there horses or mules to draw them. The Lima public square was full of people who 'took the rain,' watching the first electric car in the city. It was a curiosity — no horse or mule to draw it."** [verified] — [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md).

**The 1906 history makes a different superlative about the same thing.** Under a photograph captioned "First electric car in Lima" it prints: "(Lima had the second electric street railway line in the United States)". [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md). First west of the mountains and second in the country are compatible statements, and neither book cites the other or anything else. Two boasts that do not contradict are still one piece of evidence apiece. [inference]

**What is on firmer ground is the local sequence.** [Benjamin Faurot](../person/benjamin-faurot.yml) installed Lima's first electric light plant in 1883 beside his opera house; the street railway organized in 1878 ran horse cars; and this is the year the two met. [verified] — the 1921 history for the light plant, and [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md) for the horse cars; see [the street railway under four names](../measure/lima-street-railway-1878-1921.yml).
**It happened one year into the oil.** The strike was May 1885 and the electric car July 1886, so the city electrified its streetcars in the first full year of the field. [inference]

nodes.label: The raising of the first Lima company

properties.location_description: Lima, at the second Allen County courthouse and on the square before it.

blocks.text: Eight days between the news of Fort Sumter reaching Lima and the county's first company being inducted into United States service — ninety-two men, rank and file. [verified] — [the 1921 history](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md).

The officers were M. H. Nichols captain, C. M. Hughes lieutenant, T. J. Hustler second lieutenant, J. A. Anderson sergeant, J. N. Cunningham second sergeant, William Bradley third, W. H. Ward fourth, and C. C. Oldfield, Milton Titus, J. B. Davison and Samuel McClure corporals. [verified] — same source.

**The book dates the first day April 12 and calls it a Sunday, and it cannot be both.** April 12, 1861 was a Friday; the Sunday of that week was the 14th, the day the garrison marched out of Fort Sumter and the day the wires would have carried it into northwestern Ohio. The corpus takes the weekday over the date, because the scene the book describes — congregations in church, a flag raised, a crowd on the way out — is a Sunday scene and the rest of the sequence is dated consistently around it. [inference] — computed here.

**It happened at the second courthouse, not the one that stands.** The flag was strung between Ashton Hall and the courthouse, "in the days of the second Allen County courthouse on the site of the Cincinnati Block". [verified] — same source. The building on Main Street today is the third and opened in 1884; see [the courthouse](../site/allen-county-courthouse.yml).

**This is the sixty hours, corrected.** Two of the three county histories say the county had men on the road to Washington within sixty hours; the phrase belongs to the First Ohio Volunteer Infantry, not to Allen County, and this sequence — from the same book that repeats it — is what actually happened. [inference] — see [what the county sent](../measure/allen-county-civil-war-service.yml).

nodes.label: The first railroad reaches Allen County

properties.location_description: The line ran east and west across the county through Lima and Delphos, on the route now held by the Chicago, Fort Wayne & Eastern. No source here gives a route in survey terms. [verified]

blocks.text: The opening of the Ohio & Indiana Railroad from Crestline to Fort Wayne, through Lima and Delphos, under authority the Legislature granted on 20 March 1850. It was consolidated into the Pittsburgh, Fort Wayne & Chicago in 1856 and is now part of no trunk line at all. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md), whose two scans agree word for word, and [History of Allen County, 1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md), which calls it "Lima's first railway".

**Three county histories name the same road and three different years.** 1853 in Miller, 1854 in Leeson, 1856 in Rusler. [verified] — the three sources named here and [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md). None of the three is a company record and none cites one, so what the corpus holds is a spread of three years in which its own sources disagree, not a date three of them confirm.

**1854 is the reading that survives both checks the corpus can run.** It is Leeson's, the nearest witness in time, carried identically by both scans of that book; and Rusler, who dates the opening latest, also reports that the first steam locomotive in the county arrived in **1854**, brought by canal from Toledo as freight to Delphos, named the *Lima*, and used for construction work on this same road. [verified] — [the 1921 history](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md). A construction engine delivered in 1854 is not consistent with a line already open in 1853. [inference]
**The county paid for it and got the money back.** Allen County subscribed $50,000 in stock, and the stock was later sold at par, "so the railroad cost the county nothing". [verified] — same source.

**The second road came four years later and was the one that built the shops.** The Dayton & Michigan was chartered in 1856–57 and completed through Allen County in 1858; its passenger trains began running to Dayton on **5 April 1858** and the line was finished to Toledo in August 1859. [verified] — [1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md) and [1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md), which agree on the year. Rusler puts it in 1857, one year after his own date for the first road, so his pair is internally consistent and two years earlier than everyone else's. [inference]

**What it did to the county is the thing that is not in dispute.** Within a decade Lima stood at the crossing of the two roads and Delphos, the canal town, did not. [inference] — see [Lima](../place/lima.yml), [the canal](../site/miami-and-erie-canal.yml) and [the network the two roads became](../measure/allen-county-railroads-1883-1921.yml).

properties.location_description: Delphos, then wholly described within [Marion Township](../place/marion-township.yml) by the 1885 book's chapter that carries it, and today a city standing in Allen and Van Wert counties. [verified] — the same source.

blocks.text: **Delphos became a municipal corporation on 7 February 1851.** "The first election for Delphos Village under the Act of Incorporation February 7, 1851, took place March 8 of that year." [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md).

**The two scans of that book disagree about the day of the first election and not about the incorporation.** Scan A reads "March 8" and scan B reads "March 3"; both read February 7, 1851 for the act. The corpus records the act's date and prints the election as the 3rd or the 8th. [verified] — same source, both scans.

**Lester Bliss was elected mayor**, Smith Talbott recorder, and N. White, E. N. Martin, J. P. Cowan, J. P. Murphy and T. Wrocklage councilmen; F. J. Lye treasurer and E. N. Talbott marshal followed on 21 March. **The corporation's expenses for its first year were $80.67**, a figure scan A renders as "180.67" with the dollar sign read as a digit. [verified] — same source, scan B; the roll of town officials from 1852 to 1884 follows it.

**It is the second-oldest municipal corporation in the county** and the only one the sources attribute to an act of incorporation rather than to a county commissioners' order or a ballot. [verified] — see [the incorporations](../measure/allen-county-municipal-incorporations-1842-1904.yml).

**The corporation's date was in this book the whole time.** The corpus has cited the 1885 history in dozens of nodes and had never asked it this question; the field on [the city](../jurisdiction/city-of-delphos.yml) stood empty for sixty-eight phases. [inference] — see [a count of absences is not an agenda](../../decisions/a-count-of-absences-is-not-an-agenda.yml).

nodes.label: The naming and incorporation of Bluffton, 1861

properties.location_description: Bluffton, on Sections 1 and 12 of [Richland Township](../place/richland-township.yml), platted in 1837 as Shannon and today a village standing in Allen and Hancock counties. [verified] — the 1885 history.

blocks.text: **On 17 August 1861 the town voted, in one ballot, both to incorporate and to stop being called Shannon.** "Ballot, on August 17, 1861, to incorporate the place and call it 'Bluffton.' J. S. Powell was elected first mayor, and E. H. Edsal, the first clerk." [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md). The 1921 history gives the same date: "The matter of changing the name was voted on August 17, 1861, and the town was duly incorporated as Bluffton." [verified] — [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md).

**It is the only incorporation in this county the sources put to a vote of the people.** The other seven were granted by the county commissioners on a petition or passed as an act. [verified] — see [the incorporations](../measure/allen-county-municipal-incorporations-1842-1904.yml).

**This closes a dangling qualifier the corpus has carried since the settlements phase.** The 1885 history says the name "was changed to Bluffton in 1872-73, although long prior to this the latter name was bestowed upon it", and the corpus quoted that phrase without being able to say what "long prior" meant. It meant a ballot eleven years earlier. [inference] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md); see [the place](../place/bluffton.yml).

**The two dates are reconcilable and describe different things.** The 1861 vote named the *corporation*; the 1885 book's 1872–73 is the *post office*, which had been Croghan and then Shannon and which the same book says was "again in 1873 named Bluffton". A town and its post office changed names twelve years apart. [inference] — the 1885 book, both scans.

**Why the name existed to be voted on.** The post office could not be called Shannon because of another Shannon in Ohio, and Jacob Mosier, who had come from Bluffton, Indiana, proposed the name so that the town and the post office might match. [verified] — the 1921 history.

properties.location_description: Cairo, on Sections 29, 30, 31 and 32 of [Monroe Township](../place/monroe-township.yml), west of the Perrysburg Road at its crossing with the Bucyrus Road. [verified] — the 1885 history.

blocks.text: **Cairo Village was organized on 12 April 1875, on the authority of the county commissioners and the petition of forty-one named citizens.** [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md) and [History of Allen County, 1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md), which print the same date and the same petition.

**Dr. J. S. Clippinger was its first mayor**, in 1875; Thomas H. Waltz followed in 1877 and David Hartzog in 1879, who was re-elected in 1881 and resigned in October of that year to remove to Kansas. Robert E. Davis filled the unexpired term, was re-elected in April 1883, and was mayor when the 1885 book went to press. [verified] — the 1885 history.

**The petition is the largest list of a founding act's participants this corpus holds.** Forty-one men signed for it, against one petitioner named for Lafayette in 1867. [verified] — same source, counted here; see [the village of Lafayette](../jurisdiction/village-of-lafayette.yml).

**It corporated twenty-seven years after it was platted, and under a different name from the ground.** [West Cairo](../place/cairo.yml) was laid out in 1848 by Jacob Miller; the corporation of 1875 is *Cairo Village*, and the 1921 history was still calling the incorporated place West Cairo in 1920, with 380 people. [verified] — the 1885 and 1921 histories. **A place and the corporation over it can carry different names for seventy years.** [inference]

**It gives the corpus a third witness for a date it held on one.** The date was already recorded from the 1921 history, which the corpus noted as "a single witness read once". It is now three, from three books, with a mechanism and a first mayor. [verified] — the three histories.

nodes.label: The Ottawa River flood of January 22, 1959

properties.location_description: Measured at the Ottawa River gauge at Allentown, downstream of Lima, draining 160 square miles. The measurement is of one point on the river; the extent of the event is not established here, which is why the edge below points at the county and not at [the river](../natural-feature/ottawa-river.yml). [verified] — the same source.

blocks.text: **The largest flow ever measured on the Ottawa River: 7,740 cubic feet a second at Allentown on 22 January 1959, at a gauge height of 10.88 feet.** [verified] — [USGS peak streamflow](../../catalog/usgs-nwis.md), site 04187500.

**It is more than twice the median annual peak** of 3,240 cubic feet a second across that gauge's fifty-two water years, and it stands nineteen per cent above the next largest, 6,160 in March 1939. [verified] — same source, computed here; see [the peak flows](../measure/ottawa-river-peak-flows-1924-2025.yml).

**It sits in one of the corpus's two remaining holes in the record of what happened here.** The spine had nothing between 1955 and 1965 until this phase, and this is a dated thing in the middle of it — established by an instrument rather than by anybody's account. [inference] — see [a dataset can make an event](../../decisions/a-dataset-can-make-an-event.yml).

**It is a flow and not a flood, and the corpus is careful about the difference.** A discharge figure says how much water passed the gauge and nothing about what the water reached. Whether this one left the banks, what it covered, and whether anyone was harmed are not in this source and are not in any source held here — there was no federal disaster declaration for Allen County that year, and the county's first is six years later. [verified] — [the declarations](../measure/allen-county-disaster-declarations-1965-2020.yml).

properties.location_description: A 17.8-mile track from 40.80, −84.20 to 40.87, −83.87, 400 yards at its widest, running west-north-west to east across the northern half of the county from Elida to Bluffton. [verified] — the same source.

blocks.text: **The deadliest thing that has happened in Allen County in the corpus's whole weather record, and the only thing in it that has killed anybody.** An F4 tornado, 17.8 miles of track, 400 yards at its widest, **eleven dead and a hundred injured**, $2.5 million of property damage. [verified] — [the Storm Events Database](../../catalog/noaa-storm-events.md), event 10083979.

**It crossed the north of the county diagonally, from Elida to Bluffton.** The file starts it at 40.80, −84.20, nine-tenths of a mile from [Elida](../place/elida.yml), and ends it at 40.87, −83.87, 1.8 miles from [Bluffton](../place/bluffton.yml). Those endpoints are 17.92 miles apart against a stated track of 17.8, so the track and the coordinates are the same tornado. [inference] — computed here from the same source. It passed north of [Lima](../place/lima.yml).

**This is the storm the corpus said it did not hold.** [The declaration of April 1965](the-tornadoes-of-april-1965.yml) asked four questions — the storm's date, its track, whether it touched ground in this county at all, and what it destroyed — and answered none. The first three are answered above. **The declaration came three days after the tornado**, on 14 April, and the declaration file recorded the incident as beginning and ending on the day it was signed. [verified] — same source and [OpenFEMA](../../catalog/fema-disaster-declarations.md).

**The corpus looked for it in the wrong instrument.** That node named a newspaper of that week as the source that would answer, and observed that this catalog holds none reaching 1965. The answer was in a federal weather database that had been publishing it since before the corpus existed. [inference]

**Eleven people were killed and the file holds nothing else about them.** The companion fatality file, which carries an age, a sex and a location for each death, has seventeen rows for the whole United States in 1965 and not one of them belongs to this event. [verified] — same source. **A count of eleven is the entire record.**

**Its clock is stamped Central for a county on Eastern time.** The row reads 20:30 with `CZ_TIMEZONE` = CST, as does every row here from 1950 to 1991. If the stamp means what it says, the local clock read 21:30. [inference] — same source.

properties.location_description: A 9.7-mile track from 40.72, −84.08 to 40.83, −83.97, 300 yards at its widest, crossing the county from the south-east side of Lima to Beaverdam. [verified] — the same source.

blocks.text: **The first thing in the county's weather record, and it injured thirty people.** An F3 tornado tracked 9.7 miles across a path 300 yards wide, killed nobody and did an estimated $2.5 million of property damage. [verified] — [the Storm Events Database](../../catalog/noaa-storm-events.md), event 10086810.

**It ran from the south-east edge of Lima to Beaverdam.** The file gives a start at 40.72, −84.08 — 2.2 miles from [Lima](../place/lima.yml)'s centre — and an end at 40.83, −83.97, two-tenths of a mile from [Beaverdam](../place/beaverdam.yml). Those endpoints are 9.53 miles apart against a stated track of 9.7. [inference] — computed here from the same source.

**Its clock is stamped in a timezone this county has never kept.** The row reads 15:15 with `CZ_TIMEZONE` = CST, and so does every other row here from 1950 to 1991; Allen County is on Eastern time. If the stamp means what it says, the local clock read 16:15. [inference] — same source. See [a file has more than one date](../../decisions/a-file-has-more-than-one-date.yml).

**It is the corpus's first dated happening between the jail raid of 1933 and the government's purchase of the tank plant ground in 1951.** [verified] — [the jail raid](allen-county-jail-raid-1933.yml) and [the tank plant purchase](the-united-states-buys-the-tank-plant-ground-1951.yml).

**Its damage figure and the 2006 windstorm's cannot be compared.** $2.5 million in 1950 dollars and $1,970,000 in 2006 dollars are in different currencies, and this file carries no deflator. [inference] — see [the storm record](../measure/allen-county-storm-events-1950-2026.yml).

properties.location_description: Allen County, as the declaration's `designatedArea` names it. The declaration is county-wide and says nothing about where within the county anything happened. [verified] — the same source.

blocks.text: **The first thing this corpus can date in Allen County after 1955**, and it arrived in a table rather than in a book. On 14 April 1965 the county was named in federal disaster declaration DR-191-OH, "Tornadoes & Severe Storms", with both Individual and Public Assistance designated. [verified] — [OpenFEMA](../../catalog/fema-disaster-declarations.md).

**It is one of only two declarations in fifty-five years that brought money to households here.** The other is 2007. [verified] — same source; see [the declarations](../measure/allen-county-disaster-declarations-1965-2020.yml).

**The date is the declaration's, and the storm's is not in this file.** The record gives an incident beginning and ending on 14 April 1965, which is also the day the declaration was signed and the day the request was made. A tornado outbreak severe enough to bring federal aid to households did not last zero days; the field was filled with the declaration date, as it was for the 1978 blizzard. [inference] — see [a file has more than one date](../../decisions/a-file-has-more-than-one-date.yml).

**So the corpus dates the declaration and not the weather.** `occurred` below is 14 April 1965 because that is what the source establishes: a presidential act naming this county. What the sky did, and when, is not held here. [inference]

**Three of those four questions are now answered, and not by a newspaper.** The storm was an F4 tornado on **11 April 1965**, three days before this declaration; it ran 17.8 miles from Elida to Bluffton; it killed eleven people and injured a hundred. [verified] — [the Storm Events Database](../../catalog/noaa-storm-events.md); see [the tornado](the-tornado-of-11-april-1965.yml). **It touched ground in this county and it is the only weather that has ever killed anybody here.** [verified] — same source.

**That confirms what this node inferred about its own dates.** The tornado is three days outside an incident window one day long, and that one day is the declaration date. The field was filled with the declaration date, as this node said it was. [inference]

**This node named the wrong instrument.** It said a newspaper of that week would answer all four questions and that this catalog held none reaching 1965. The answer was in a federal weather database, published continuously since before this corpus existed and never asked. [inference]

nodes.label: The United States buys the tank plant's ground

properties.location_description: The north-west quarter of section 14, township 4 south, range 6 east — Shawnee Township, about 2.8 miles south of Lima's internal point.

blocks.text: Between 20 and 28 June 1951 the United States of America took the north-west quarter of section 14, township 4 south, range 6 east, from five private owners in five warranty deeds — 60.24 acres, 5 acres, 40 acres of the west half of the east half, and two parcels described only as "Pt". Each was recorded on the day it was signed or the day after. [verified] — [Section Ground book list](../../catalog/allen-county-recorder-section-ground.md), volume 0034A pages 89–92, at volumes 320 pages 573, 574 and 577 and 321 pages 245 and 246.

It is the ground the [Joint Systems Manufacturing Center](../site/lima-army-tank-plant.yml) stands on, and this is the corpus's answer to a question that node has carried since genesis. [verified] — same pages and [the survey sections](../measure/allen-county-survey-sections.yml).

**The date is the finding.** The received account of tank building at Lima is a wartime one, and this corpus had assembled its own version of it: the Lima Locomotive Works taking a medium tank contract in 1941, [the Lima Tank Depot](../site/lima-tank-depot.yml) under construction in January 1943. None of that is this ground. Through the whole of that war it was a mortgaged farm — borrowed against in 1940, 1941 and 1944, leased to a fishing and game club in April 1940, and crossed by pipeline rights of way its private owners granted in 1939, 1940 and 1949. [verified] — same pages.
The Army arrived here six years after that war ended, in the second year of the Korean one. [inference]

**Nine days, five sellers, same-day recording.** That is what a government buying to a deadline looks like rather than a farm changing hands, and it is the only thing the record says about how the acquisition was conducted. [inference]

refusals: This node does not establish when anything was built on the ground it describes.

properties.location_description: County-wide. Reports run from Delphos and Spencerville in the west through Lima to Beaverdam and Bluffton in the east, between 14:05 and 14:25 Eastern. [verified] — the same source.

blocks.text: **A line of wind crossed the whole county in twenty minutes and left two-thirds of it without power.** Nine Allen County rows share one episode: Delphos and Spencerville at 14:05, Lima from 14:15, a tornado at Beaverdam at 14:18, Bluffton at 14:25. Gusts were estimated at 70 knots over Lima, 60 at Delphos and Spencerville, 52 at Bluffton. [verified] — [the Storm Events Database](../../catalog/noaa-storm-events.md), episode 1213131.

**$1,970,000 of damage, which is more than any weather here but the tornadoes of 1950 and 1965.** Those two and this one are $6,970,000 of the $9,408,250 the file records for seventy-six years. [verified] — same source, summed here; see [the storm record](../measure/allen-county-storm-events-1950-2026.yml).

**Most of that was aircraft.** "Three aircraft hangars destroyed. About 17 airplanes and the Allen County Sheriff's Office helicopter were significantly damaged or destroyed" — $1.6 million on one row, reported by the county's emergency manager. [verified] — same source. It is the only mention of an aircraft, an airfield or an air unit anywhere in this corpus, and see [the sheriff](../office/allen-county-sheriff.yml).

**In Lima the wind took the street furniture.** "Along a strech of Shawnee Rd. from Fort Amanda Rd. to Reed Rd., every power pole and traffic signal was blown over, completely blocking the road." A motel roof collapsed on Harding Highway, an automotive shop's roof came down at Jackson Street and Findlay Road, three tractor-trailers were blown over on Interstate 75, and about two-thirds of the county lost power. [verified] — same source, quoting the event narratives.

**It moved at about seventy miles an hour.** Delphos and Bluffton are 23.7 miles apart and the file's first and last reports are twenty minutes apart, which is 71 miles an hour across the ground. [inference] — computed here from [the two villages' centroids](../place/bluffton.yml).

**Five of its nine reports came from a newspaper, two from amateur radio operators, one from the emergency manager and one from a storm survey.** [verified] — same source. **This is what the county's weather record is made of.** [inference]

**The file's injury count and the file's own prose disagree.** `INJURIES_DIRECT` totals two across the episode and `INJURIES_INDIRECT` reads zero on all nine rows, while the narrative on one of them says "there were also up to 15 indirect injuries from automobile accidents during the storm". [verified] — same source. The corpus records two, which is what the countable field says, and records that the field is not the whole of what the forecaster wrote down. [inference]

nodes.label: The winter storms of December 2004 and January 2005

properties.location_description: County-wide. The incident window is the declaration's; the two dated weather events inside it are a winter storm and an ice storm, both recorded for the county as a whole. [verified] — the same sources.

blocks.text: **The broadest disaster in the county's federal record: twenty-two separate governments and bodies were paid for it, more than any other event before or since.** [verified] — [OpenFEMA assistance programs](../../catalog/openfema-assistance-programs.md), DR-1580; see [who was paid](../measure/allen-county-disaster-aid-applicants-2005-2025.yml).

**It ran from 22 December 2004 to 1 February 2005** — forty-one days, and the forty-one days [the declarations](../measure/allen-county-disaster-declarations-1965-2020.yml) already named as the longest non-pandemic incident window this county has — and was declared on 15 February 2005 as "Severe Winter Storms, Flooding, and Mudslides". [verified] — [OpenFEMA](../../catalog/fema-disaster-declarations.md); see [the declarations](../measure/allen-county-disaster-declarations-1965-2020.yml).

**The weather record holds two events inside that window and no more.** A winter storm on 22 December 2004, the first day of the incident, and an ice storm on 5 January 2005. [verified] — [the storm record](../measure/allen-county-storm-events-1950-2026.yml).

**What it cost was mostly branches.** Forty-one projects, $1,243,330 of federal money, and twenty of the forty-one are Debris Removal at $964,518 — seventy-eight cents in the dollar for clearing what the ice brought down. One project in the whole declaration is Roads and Bridges. [verified] — [the assistance](../measure/allen-county-disaster-assistance-2005-2025.yml).

**It is why the corpus can name the county's local governments from a federal grant file.** Nine of the county's ten municipal corporations, eight of its twelve townships, the county, its commissioners, its engineer, a village fire department and a township of Auglaize County all filed for this one storm. [verified] — same source.

**And it is the corpus's only dated event that is established by an accounting record rather than by an observation or a book.** The storm file records two days of weather; the grant file records forty-two days of consequence and twenty-two bodies clearing it. [inference] — see [a dataset can make an event](../../decisions/a-dataset-can-make-an-event.yml).

properties.location_description: St. Marys, in present-day Auglaize County, Ohio. [inference]

blocks.text: The 1818 treaty negotiations at St. Marys, Ohio, by which Native nations ceded the remaining lands in northwest Ohio — the cession that made the ground Allen County was later laid out on available for survey and sale. [inference]

The cession also established reservations, including Ottawa reserves on the Auglaize and Ottawa rivers, which were themselves ceded and their occupants removed within about fifteen years — see [the Ottawa removal](ottawa-removal.yml). [inference]

nodes.label: Allen County Court of Common Pleas

blocks.text: **It is divided five ways by its own rules and staffed four.** The court's local rules, adopted under Article IV, Section V(B) of the Ohio Constitution and effective 1 February 2023, govern practice "in the General Trial Division, Criminal Division, Domestic Relations Division, and where applicable, the Juvenile Division and Probate Division". [verified] — [the court's local rules](../../catalog/allen-county-common-pleas-local-rules.md). Four judges are elected, to the [General](../office/judge-of-the-common-pleas-general-division.yml) (two seats), [Domestic Relations](../office/judge-of-the-common-pleas-domestic-relations-division.yml) and [Probate](../office/judge-of-the-common-pleas-probate-division.yml) divisions. [verified] — [Ohio county elected officials lookup](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md). The Criminal Division has no separately elected judge. [inference]

**Three sources divide this court three ways and none of them is wrong.** The rules divide practice into five, the county's site divides it into three offices with their own sites, and the ballot divides it into four seats. They are answers to different questions and the corpus keeps all three rather than picking one. [inference]

Its judges serve six years where every other elected officer of this county serves four. [verified] — same roster; the length is arithmetic on the term dates. [inference] Three of the four terms begin in February and one in January.

Its records are kept by [the clerk of courts](../office/allen-county-clerk-of-courts.yml), an elected county officer who is not part of the court. [verified] — [the clerk's site](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md).

properties.authority_source: Ohio Revised Code 3311.05, which constitutes an educational service center out of a county's territory less its city and exempted village school districts. [verified]

blocks.text: The county's school jurisdiction that is not a school district. Its office is at 1920 Slabtown Road, Lima, and its governing board has five elected members on four-year terms. [verified] — [the elected officials roster](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md).

**Who governs it now.** Brooke L. Hedges, David Earnest Mayer and Lori M. Ringwald to 31 December 2029, and Ann B. Best and Walter W. Paxson to 31 December 2027; Hedges and Paxson were appointed. [verified] — same source. Two of five is the heaviest use of appointment on any school board in the county. [verified] — [the seat count](../measure/allen-county-elected-seats-2026.yml).

**The statute defines it by subtraction, which is why it has no boundary of its own.** An educational service center is *"the territory within the territorial limits of a county ... exclusive of the territory embraced in any city school district or exempted village school district"*, with territory detached for school purposes excluded and territory attached for them included. [verified] — [Ohio Revised Code 3311.05](../../catalog/ohio-revised-code.md). So this jurisdiction is Allen County minus [Lima City](lima-city-school-district.yml), minus the Allen part of [Delphos City](delphos-city-school-district.yml), and minus the Allen part of [Bluffton](bluffton-exempted-village-school-district.yml)'s — the three districts here that are not *local* districts.

properties.authority_source: An act of the Ohio General Assembly laying out the county from lands ceded at the Treaty of St. Marys. [inference] — the act itself has not been retrieved.

blocks.text: The county government: the unit of general-purpose government whose territory is [Allen County](../place/allen-county.yml). Ohio counties are administrative subdivisions of the state rather than home-rule corporations. [inference]

**Nine separately elected offices govern Allen County, and eleven people hold them, because the board of commissioners seats three.** [verified] — [Ohio county elected officials lookup](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md).
