Sugar Street, and the two are staffed in opposite ways: [Jackson Township](jackson-township.yml) elected all four of its officers and four of this council's six were appointed. [verified] — [the elected officials roster](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md) and [the seat count](../measure/allen-county-elected-seats-2026.yml).

properties.authority_source: An act of incorporation passed in 1867; the first village election followed the same year. [verified]

blocks.text: The municipal corporation governing [Spencerville](../place/spencerville.yml), 2,198 people over 0.965 square miles inside [Spencer Township](../place/spencer-township.yml) — the largest of the six villages lying wholly inside the county, though smaller than [Bluffton](../place/bluffton.yml), which does not. [verified] — [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md) and [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md).

**It was founded on the canal.** The county records the settlement as founded in 1844 on the banks of the [Miami and Erie Canal](../site/miami-and-erie-canal.yml). [verified] — [Allen County](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md), cities and villages page. That is the first thing in this corpus to connect the canal to a settlement that still exists: the canal node and [the canal era](../period/canal-era.yml) had until now no consequence anywhere else in the graph, and a village dated to the canal's own decade is one.

**The act of incorporation was passed in 1867 and the first village election held that year**, returning J. C. Campbell mayor, Merritt Harvey recorder, Jacob Dehart treasurer and W. H. Orcutt marshal, with five councilmen. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md), which then carries the roll of officers year by year to 1885. Twenty-three years separate the settlement from the corporation.

**Who governs it now, and the roll resumes after a hundred and forty-one years.** Darrell Edward Pugin is mayor to 31 December 2027. Its six council members are Anthony Joseph Lammers and Courtney Danielle Brown to 31 December 2027, and James E. Penix Jr. (R), Katie Ruth Cotterman (D), Nicholas Richard Goergens (R) and Nicole L. Lotz to 31 December 2029; all four of the 2029 seats were filled by appointment. [verified] — [the elected officials roster](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md). This corpus held the officers of this village for every year from 1867 to 1885 and for no year after; it now holds 1885 and 2026, and nothing between.

**Three of the four appointees carry a party letter**, which almost nothing else at this level of government in the county does — seven of the 145 seated township, village and school officers, and six of those seven are appointees. [verified] — [the seat count](../measure/allen-county-elected-seats-2026.yml).

An Auglaize County district with the thinnest reach into Allen of any of the twelve — 2,698 people over 62.864 square miles, internal point 40.591434, -83.964064, serving PK–12. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), unified school district file, and [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md) block population.

It is three counties wide and almost entirely in one: 2,629 people in Auglaize, 52 in Logan and **17 in Allen**, on two blocks at the south-east corner of [Auglaize Township](../place/auglaize-township.yml). [verified] — [2020 Census Block Assignment Files](../../catalog/census-block-assignment-2020.md) crossed with TIGERweb block geography, block by block.

**Its board is not on Allen County's roster.** A school board is elected by its own district's voters, and this district's centre is in Auglaize County. [verified] — [the elected officials roster](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md).

**Its board is Thomas B Brookhart, Michelle Steinke and Brad Vorhes to 31 December 2027, and Kevin Ewing and David Pepple to 31 December 2029.** [verified] — [the elected officials roster](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md), queried by district type; the Auglaize County view carries the same five people and spells four of them differently. See [the school boards](../measure/allen-county-school-boards-2026.yml). **No Allen County precinct ballots this board**, verified across all eighty-eight. [verified] — same source.

**It is the smallest district holding ground in this county and the second-highest spender per pupil.** 472 pupils in 2023 against 590 in 2010 — a fall of 20.0 per cent, one of the three steepest here — at $17,896 a pupil on 10.2 per cent child poverty. [verified] — [enrolment](../measure/allen-county-school-enrolment-2010-2023.yml), [the finance survey](../measure/allen-county-school-finance-2023.yml) and [child poverty](../measure/allen-county-school-district-poverty-2023.yml).

nodes.label: Allen County age structure, 2023

properties.method: 2023 five-year estimates. Under-18 sums B01001 male 3-6 and female 27-30; 65-and-over sums male 20-25 and female 44-49. The twelve townships and Lima sum to the county's 101,685. [verified]
properties.parameter: median age (B01002) and population by age (B01001)

blocks.text: Median age and the shares under 18 and 65 or older, for the county, its thirteen civil subdivisions, the state and the nation. [verified] — [American Community Survey](../../catalog/census-acs-summary-file.md), 2023 five-year estimates.

**Lima is the young end of this county, not the old one.** Its median age is 35.4 against the county's 39.7, its 65-and-over share is 15.6 per cent against 18.7, and its under-18 share is higher than the county's. [verified] — same source. Eleven of the twelve townships are older than the city by the 65-and-over measure.

The corpus does not establish that. The city is younger than every part of the county except Sugar Creek and Spencer townships, so whatever natural decrease the county has is not principally Lima's, and the two findings do not compose into that story. [verified] — see [natural change](allen-county-natural-change-2021-2024.yml) and [the depopulation period](../period/depopulation.yml).
Sugar Creek Township's median age of 29.9 in 1,398 people is the shape a college makes in a small denominator, and this node does not read it as a finding about that township. [inference]

refusals: The corpus does not establish that.

properties.method: Every row of Ohio's BAS boundary-change files whose entity FIPS place code is one of the ten Allen County places — Beaverdam 04752, Bluffton 07426, Cairo 10884, Delphos 21602, Elida 24808, Fort Shawnee 27944, Harrod 34118, Lafayette 41118, Lima 43554, Spencerville 74034. Sixteen tab-delimited files, two record layouts, joined on the fields the readme names. Delphos and Bluffton cross county lines and the pre-2018 layout carries no county column, so their totals include ground on the Van Wert and Hancock sides. [verified]
properties.parameter: annexations reported to the Boundary and Annexation Survey

blocks.text: **Fifty-seven annexations, all of them dated, none of them held by this corpus until now.** Seven Allen County municipalities reported a boundary change to the Census Bureau between 12 April 1990 and 12 November 2024, each with the legal instrument that authorised it, the day it took effect and an acreage. [verified] — [the Boundary and Annexation Survey](../../catalog/census-bas-boundary-changes-ohio.md), Ohio files for 1991–2000, 2001–2010, 2011 and each survey year from 2012 to 2025.

Written out: **Delphos reported twenty-six annexations totalling 784.4 acres, Lima eleven totalling 622.0, Bluffton nine totalling 477.5, Elida five totalling 912.9, Spencerville four totalling 209.7, and Cairo and Harrod one each of 10.4 and 12.9 — fifty-seven records and 3,029.8 acres in thirty-five years.** [verified] — same files. Five of the fifty-seven state no acreage, so every total here is a floor.

**Every one is an annexation.** No detachment, merger, incorporation or dissolution appears in thirty-five years of Ohio's file for this county, and the corpus reads that as a property of the survey rather than of the county: a government that gives ground up has less occasion to file than one that takes it. [inference] — the reasoning is this corpus's; the absence is [the survey's](../../catalog/census-bas-boundary-changes-ohio.md).

**Four villages that annexed nothing.** Beaverdam, Lafayette, Fort Shawnee and Westminster have no record in the series at all. For [Fort Shawnee](../place/fort-shawnee.yml) that is a fact worth having beside the rest: the largest of the county's villages by population never once moved its own line. [verified] — same files, searched on all ten Allen County place codes.

**The shape is a decade of nothing, then a burst, then nothing again.** Lima annexed 21.0 acres in 1990 and 1991, then reported no boundary change for ten and a half years; then took 601.0 acres in eight annexations between June 2002 and December 2009; then one more in June 2017 and nothing since. [verified] — same source. Twenty-nine of the county's fifty-seven records fall in the 2000s and only eleven in the fifteen years after.
**The largest single annexation in the county's record is Lima's ordinance 90-02**, 215.9 acres effective 24 June 2002, and it is the act that ends the ten-year pause. [verified] — same source.

**The last one is the odd one.** Resolution 408-17 of 29 June 2017 is the only Lima record in thirty-five years authorised by resolution rather than by ordinance, and the only one with no acreage on it — an Ohio annexation begins with a resolution of the county commissioners and ends with an ordinance of the city, so a resolution reported alone is the first half of the act. [inference] — the two-instrument procedure is [the survey readme's](../../catalog/census-bas-boundary-changes-ohio.md) and the reading is this corpus's.

**Lima reported 601.0 acres of annexation effective inside the 2000s, and the Census Bureau's own measurement of Lima grew by 582.4 acres over the same decade.** The city's total area was 12.88 square miles in the 2000 geography and 13.79 in the 2010 geography, a rise of 0.91 square miles. [verified] — [the 2000 volume](../../catalog/census-phc-3-37-ohio.md) and [the 2010 volume](../../catalog/census-cph-2-37-ohio-2010.md), county-subdivision tables.

The two figures agree to 3.1 per cent, and they have nothing in common: one is the sum of numbers a city clerk wrote on eight forms across eight years, the other is a polygon the Census Bureau measured twice ten years apart. [inference] — the comparison is this corpus's. Against Lima's **land** area rather than its total the same reported acreage covers only 83 per cent, and the gap is the water inside annexed ground plus a remeasurement that touched every entity in Ohio; see [the control is the figure that cannot move](../../decisions/the-control-is-the-figure-that-cannot-move.yml).

**Elida reports more annexation than Elida is.** The village's five records total 912.9 acres, and the village occupied 703.6 acres in the 2012 geography and 745.6 in the 2024 one. [verified] — the survey files against [the gazetteer series](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), Ohio place files for 2012 and 2024. A single record, ordinance 622-92 of 11 March 1992, claims 640.0 acres — one square mile, to the acre, which is the size of a survey section and not the size of a parcel.
Two of the five are the same acreage four months apart: resolutions 344-2009 and 348-2009, both 61.6 acres, effective 7 April and 7 August 2009. [verified] — same files.

**What the total is not.** 3,029.8 acres is 4.73 square miles, and the seven municipalities did not grow by that. It is the sum of what was reported, on a form, by the party that benefited, with no adjustment for double-reporting, for water, or for the difference between a legal description and a measured polygon. [inference] — computed here. The figure it should be read against is not the county's area but the county's other annexation record, which for the 2000s is Lima's 601 reported against 582 measured.

nodes.label: The Allen County roll of Ohio attorneys, 1925–2026

properties.method: One POST to the directory's `Ajax.ashx` with `county=Allen` and every other field empty. The response carried `TooManyResults: false`, so the 334 rows are the whole answer at the 1,000-row cap rather than a truncation. The county filter is a substring match and is not scoped to a state; the same query with `state=IN` returns zero rows, which is how these were confirmed to be Ohio addresses and not Fort Wayne's. Counts by status, by decade and by admitted-by are tallies of those rows and nothing is estimated. [verified]
properties.parameter: persons admitted in Ohio with an Allen County address of record

blocks.text: **Three hundred and thirty-four people have given the Supreme Court of Ohio an address of record in Allen County, and one hundred and forty-four of them may practice law.** [verified] — [the attorney directory](../../catalog/ohio-attorney-directory.md), queried by county on 1 September 2026 and returned complete rather than capped.

**This is a roll and not a bar.** It is cumulative, never purged, and its admissions run from 6 January 1925 to 17 November 2025 — a hundred years and eleven months. [verified] — same source. Nothing in it marks a person as dead, and it is not a list of the lawyers now working in this county: it is a list of the addresses on file.

**The century shows in the statuses, and every registrant admitted before 1940 is in the same one.** All sixty-three of them are `Not Required`, and no `Active` registrant here was admitted before 1966. [verified] — same source, counted here.
**The eleven decade totals are 20, 23, 24, 23, 26, 44, 46, 42, 23, 41 and 21, and the active column beside them is 0, 0, 0, 0, 2, 10, 26, 28, 21, 36 and 21.** [verified] — same source, counted here.

**The eight Retired are a closed class with a date on it.** Every one was admitted between 1943 and 1962, and the Court stopped offering the status on 1 September 2007, so no ninth can ever be added. [inference] — the admission years are the source's; the closure is the source's; that no ninth can join follows from the two.

**`Not Required` is the second-largest category and the Court will not say what it is.** Its definition in the source is "for a variety of reasons ... please contact the Office of Attorney Services". It cannot be read as "deceased": four of the 138 dated ones were admitted since 2000, and one is a 2017 admission. [verified] — same source. The corpus records the count and declines to name the reasons.

**Three hundred and twenty-five of the 334 were admitted by examination.** Seven came in by motion, one by transfer of a Uniform Bar Examination score, and one carries `Not Admitted` with no admission date at all. [verified] — same source.

**Admission is a ceremony, so the dates repeat.** The 333 dated admissions fall on 166 distinct days, and three days carry six of these registrants each — 3 November 1973, 4 November 1985 and 6 November 1989. [verified] — same source, counted here. A shared admission date is therefore no evidence at all that two people are connected.

**The registration number is an identifier and not a sequence.** They run from 774 to 106164, and sorting the 333 dated registrants by admission date leaves 133 of the 332 adjacent pairs with a higher number before a lower one. [inference] — computed from the same rows.

**A rate, stated as a rate and not as a workforce.** 144 active registrations against [100,866 residents](allen-county-population-2024.yml) is one for every 700 people. [inference] — the two figures are three years apart and the numerator is addresses, not persons at work.

**Thirteen of the 334 are officers this corpus already names.** Six judges of the county's own courts, four of [the Third District](../office/judge-of-the-third-district-court-of-appeals.yml), the prosecuting attorney, Lima's director of law and the county's member of the Ohio House. Every one of the thirteen was admitted by examination, the earliest on 7 May 1979 and the most recent on 17 November 2008, and all thirteen are active. [verified] — same source, read against [the elections roster](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md). The join is a match on a name and a county; neither source carries an identifier for a person. [inference]

**Five of the thirteen were admitted on two days.** Three of the officers now sitting — an appellate judge, a second appellate judge and the county's member of the Ohio House — were admitted together on 4 November 1985, and two more on 1 November 1983. [verified] — same source. That is the ceremony and not a connection between them.

**The county in this register is the county of a business address.** Its own disclaimer reads: "The directory lists an attorney's business address. An attorney's residence address is displayed only if the attorney has not provided a valid business address." A result does not say which of the two it returned. This corpus cannot say from it where any of the thirteen lives. [verified] — same source, its definitions panel.

**The count is a floor, and the county's own geography is what shows it.** Of 305 registrants with a Lima, Ohio address, 298 name Allen County and seven name no county at all — and Lima lies wholly in Allen County. [verified] — same source. Against that, [Delphos](../place/delphos.yml) divides thirteen Allen to seven Van Wert with none left over and [Bluffton](../place/bluffton.yml) six Allen to two Hancock with none left over. The field is complete for the two cities a county line runs through and incomplete for the one it does not, so the true number of Ohio attorneys with an Allen County address is at least 341. [inference]

refusals: This corpus cannot say from it where any of the thirteen lives.

properties.method: Counted here from the 2025 Ohio file, selecting Allen County and matching `FEATURES_DESC_006A` and `FACILITY_CARRIED_007` by substring. Those fields are free text entered by the state and are inconsistently abbreviated, so a bridge described as "AUGLAIZE RIVER FAULKNER" is counted to the Auglaize and one described as "STREAM SLABTOWN RD" is counted to nothing. The counts are therefore floors, and the residue is structures over unnamed water. [inference]
properties.parameter: bridges crossing the Ottawa River in Allen County

blocks.text: **Forty-one of the county's bridges cross the Ottawa River** — nearly twice as many as cross the Auglaize, which is the larger river. [verified] — [the National Bridge Inventory](../../catalog/national-bridge-inventory.md), 2025 Ohio file, matched on the free-text description of what each structure spans.

**The Ottawa's lead is Lima's.** The Auglaize is the county's principal river and it runs through farmland; the Ottawa runs through the county seat, and a city is a place where every street has to get across the water. [inference] — computed here against [the city](../place/lima.yml).

**Twenty-one structures carry Interstate 75 and twenty-four carry U.S. Route 30**, and a further twenty-nine cross over one or the other. Forty-five of the county's 364 bridges — one in eight — exist because of two roads built in the middle of the last century. [verified] — same source, counted here.

**The busiest structure in the county carries Interstate 75 over Lost Creek**, at 39,060 vehicles a day. [verified] — same source. That figure is a 2015 count in a 2025 file, as are the counts on 293 of the county's 364 bridges; see [a file has more than one date](../../decisions/a-file-has-more-than-one-date.yml).

**This is the third transport network the corpus holds for this county and the first that is current.** The canal is a ditch, the interurban stops in 1921, and the railroads' last measured mileage is 1883. [verified] — see [the canal](../site/miami-and-erie-canal.yml), [the interurban](allen-county-interurban-1901-1921.yml) and [the railroads](allen-county-railroads-1883-1921.yml). Every one of them crossed the same water in the same places, and this is the only one of the four for which the corpus can say how many times.

nodes.label: Allen County's bridges, 2025

properties.method: Selected from the 2025 Ohio delimited file on `COUNTY_CODE_003` = 3 and counted here. "Poor" is the minimum of items 58, 59, 60 and 62 being 4 or less, which is the Federal Highway Administration's own rule; structures with no rating in any of the four are not counted either way, and there were none. The count is of structures in the county whatever the owner, which is not the same as the count of bridges the county maintains. [verified]
properties.parameter: highway bridges in Allen County

blocks.text: **364 highway bridges stand in Allen County**, and not one of the hundred and three the state owns is in poor condition. [verified] — [the National Bridge Inventory](../../catalog/national-bridge-inventory.md), 2025 Ohio file, county code 3.

[verified] — same source, counted here. Written out: **not one of the state's 103 bridges here is in poor condition, 29 of the county's 242 are, and 4 of the municipalities' 19 — 0.0, 12.0 and 21.1 per cent.** **A bridge in this county is in poor condition or not according to who owns it**, and the ladder runs from the government furthest away to the one nearest. [inference] — computed here. The corpus does not know why, and the two obvious readings — that the state maintains better, or that the state owns newer and larger structures on the interstate — are not separated by anything in this file.

**No township owns a bridge, and that is the law rather than an accident.** The county engineer "shall have general charge of the ... maintenance, and repair of all bridges and highways within the engineer's county, under the jurisdiction of the board of county commissioners"; townships build and improve roads. [verified] — [Ohio Revised Code §5543.01](../../catalog/ohio-revised-code.md). Three hundred and sixty-four rows of a federal file agree with one sentence of state law; see [the county engineer](../office/allen-county-engineer.yml).

**The county's own count is 371 and this one is 364, and neither is wrong.** The engineer's office reports 371 bridges and over 1,400 culverts. This inventory admits a structure only if it spans more than twenty feet, and the rule holds in the data: the shortest of the 364 is 6.4 metres against a threshold of 6.1, with no exception. So the seven are not missing — they are short. [inference] — computed here; see [a farm count is a definition](../../decisions/a-farm-count-is-a-definition.yml).

**Half of them predate 1980.** 179 of 364 were built before that year, with the peak in the interstate decades — 69 in the 1960s and 72 in the 1970s, 39 per cent of the county's bridges in twenty years. [verified] — same source, counted here. The median structure is 19.2 metres long; the longest is 241.2 metres, a 1964 state structure carrying County Road 185 over Interstate 75, a Norfolk Southern line and another county road at once.
**The oldest was built in 1909 and it is still a county bridge.** [verified] — same source; see [the Hay Road bridge](../site/hay-road-bridge.yml).

refusals: The corpus does not know why, and the two obvious readings — that the state maintains better, or that the state owns newer and larger structures on the interstate — are not separated by anything in this file.

nodes.label: Allen County's Civil War dead, counted from the roster

properties.method: Both archive.org digitizations of the 1885 county history were parsed into roster records — a capitalised surname after a sentence break, followed by a given name — over the five sections of Chapter IX's roster, filtered against a stop list of place names, months, unit words and running heads. Scan B yields 1,877 records and scan A 1,745, against a printed 1,920. A record counts as a death if it carries any of: `died`, an abbreviated `d.` followed by a date or a place, `killed`, `k'd`, `k'l'd`, `k.` before a place, `mortally`, `drowned`, or `lost on`. The published value is the **lower** of the two scans, because every failure mode here — an unrecognised entry, an OCR-mangled abbreviation, a roster silent about a man's fate — pushes the count down, and none pushes it up. [inference] Place of death is counted only where the place name falls within one clause of the word recording the death, so that a man who enlisted at one place and died at another is not counted twice. The two scans agree exactly at Corinth and Atlanta and differ by one at Nashville. Regiment counts are **not** published: the two scans differ on those by up to a factor of two, because one of them reads "81st" as "8l8t". [inference]
properties.parameter: Allen County men recorded as dying in United States service, Civil War

blocks.text: The 1885 roster records the fate of each of its 1,920 men and never totals them. This is that total, computed. [inference] — counted from both digitizations of [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md), Chapter IX; method in the properties below and in [a printed list is a dataset](../../decisions/a-printed-list-is-a-dataset.yml).

**At least 164 of the 1,920 did not come home** — 8.5 per cent of the men of record — and the figure is a floor, not a total. The lower of two independent readings of the same page is taken, and neither reading recovers every entry. [inference] — computed here.

**About one death in five was in action.** By cause, taking the lower reading of each so that every figure is a floor: **35** killed or mortally wounded, **5** dead of wounds, **3** drowned or lost at sea, and **121** whom the roster gives a place and a date and no cause at all. [inference] — computed here. Those places are hospitals and camps, and this is the ordinary arithmetic of that war seen from one county.

**More Allen County men died at Corinth, Mississippi, than anywhere else.** Taking the lower of the two readings at each place: Corinth **11**, Atlanta **9**, Nashville **9**, Chattanooga **4**, Rome **3**, Andersonville **2**, Resaca **2**, Knoxville **2**. [inference] — computed here, counting only a place named within a clause of the word recording the death, so that a man who enlisted at one place and died at another is counted once.

Corinth is where the 81st Ohio — the regiment this county filled most — fought on October 3 and 4, 1862 and then wintered, and the eleven are a mixture of both: some killed on those two days, some dead of disease in the camp the following spring. [inference] — the roster's own entries.

**Three deaths in the list are not military at all, and both scans carry them word for word.** Abraham Baumgardner of the 81st drowned at Hamburgh, Tennessee, on August 25, 1862; B. F. Burget of the 180th drowned near Fort Monroe on April 23, 1865, a fortnight after Appomattox; and Joseph Harter of McLaughlin's Squad was "lost on Str. Sultana", the steamer that burned and sank above Memphis on April 27, 1865 carrying released prisoners home. [verified] — the 1885 history, both scans.

The *Sultana* entry is where the two-scan rule earns its keep: the cleaner scan reads the year as **1805** and the other reads **1865**. [inference] — computed here; see [two scans of one book](../../decisions/two-scans-of-one-book.yml). The same eight-for-nought substitution runs through that scan's whole military chapter, which is why no date in it is taken from one reading alone.

**Three men died in Confederate prisons**, two at Andersonville and one at Belle Isle, and the roster names them the way it names everything else — in the field where a discharge date would go. [verified] — the 1885 history.

nodes.label: Allen County in United States service, 1861-1865

properties.method: Read from the military chapter of the 1885 county history, whose roster covers 1861-1865 and was compiled twenty years after the close. The 1,920 is the compiler's own total of his own list, stated twice. The check is a parse of the roster text from both archive.org digitizations of the book: entries are detected as a capitalised surname following a sentence break and followed by a given name, filtered against a stop list of place names, months, unit words and running heads, and validated against the alphabetical order the roster is printed in. Scan B yields 1,877 records and scan A 1,745, against 1,920 printed. [inference] The regiment ranking is computed from the same records and is reported as a ranking rather than as counts, because the two scans disagree on the counts by up to a factor of two — scan A renders "81st" variously as "8l8t" and "Slst" — and agree on the order of the first six. [inference]
properties.parameter: Allen County men in United States service, Civil War

blocks.text: Every figure the county's own histories print for its Civil War service, with what each one actually counts. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md), Chapter IX, Military History, pages 318-378.

**The 1,920 is a roster total and the roster is printed**, forty-nine pages of it: field officers by rank, then captains, first and second lieutenants, then the non-commissioned officers and privates, alphabetically, each with regiment, date of enlistment and date of death, resignation, transfer or discharge. The book states the total twice, in the same paragraph, and gives the same number both times. [verified] — same source.

**An independent parse of the roster recovers 1,877 of the 1,920 — 97.8 per cent.** The other digitization of the same book recovers 1,745, or 90.9 per cent. Neither reaches the printed total and both are the same order; the count is a check on the number, not a replacement for it. [inference] — computed here; see [a printed list is a dataset](../../decisions/a-printed-list-is-a-dataset.yml).

**The enrollment is the county's own and not the district's.** The 3,792 is stated in a sentence about the Eighth Military District, which was more than one county. Against the county's 19,185 people in 1860 it is 19.8 per cent, which is what a militia enrollment of men eighteen to forty-five comes to; against a district of eight counties it would be a twelfth of that. [inference] — computed here against [the 1860 count](allen-county-population-1830-1900.yml).

**The regiments the county filled are not the regiments Camp Lima raised.** Sorted by how often each appears in the roster, the order is the same in both digitizations: the **81st** Ohio Volunteer Infantry first by a wide margin, then the **118th**, the **151st** Ohio National Guard, the **180th**, the **99th** and the **54th**. [inference] — computed here. The 99th and the 118th were the two ordered mustered at [Camp Lima](../site/camp-lima.yml); the 81st, which the county filled most, was not.

**The 776 was corrupted in transmission, and the corruption is datable.** The 1885 book says the 776 are the Allen County men "whose names occur in the roster of the 100,224 men, contributed by Ohio, **in 1861**". [verified] — the 1885 history. Twenty-one years later the year is gone: "Of the 100,224 common soldiers which Ohio sent to the war, Allen County furnished 776." [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md). Fifteen years after that the figure is a whole-war total in conflict with another: "one account says Allen County had 776 soldiers in the Civil war, while another says the official report, October 1, 1863, accredits 1,200 men to the army and navy from Allen County". [verified] — [the 1921 history](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md).

There is no conflict. A first-year cohort and a two-and-a-half-year credit are different measurements, and the 1921 book is setting them against each other because the 1906 book dropped four words. [inference] — the three passages above, read together.

**The same three books do it a second time with the sixty hours.** The 1885 book says of the *First Ohio Volunteer Infantry* that "within sixty hours after Lincoln's call for men, the First was en route to Washington" — a fact about a state regiment, in a list of state regiments. [verified] — the 1885 history. The 1906 book: "in just 60 hours thereafter soldiers from this county were en route for Washington." [verified] — the 1906 history. The 1921 book moves the clock's start from Lincoln's call to the attack on Fort Sumter: "within sixty hours after the attack on Fort Sumter it had a company of soldiers en route." [verified] — the 1921 history.

A statewide fact became a county one, and then acquired three extra days. What actually happened is in the 1921 book, four sentences later, dated: Fort Sumter fired on, the printer Charles N. Moyer to Columbus on April 16, the company ready on April 19 and inducted on April 22 — a week after Lincoln's call, not sixty hours. [inference] — the 1921 history, read against itself. See [the first company](../event/the-first-lima-company-1861.yml).

properties.method: IPEDS twelve-month enrolment, level 1 (all students), summed over the six institutions the directory places in county 39003. The collection year labels the academic year ending in it, so 2023 is 2022-23. [verified] The file's column layout changes across the period and the change is silent: before 2020 the level code is `EFFYLEV` and from 2020 it is `EFFYALEV`, with `EFFYLEV` retained beside it and carrying a different code set. Reading the old name in the new files returns nothing for every institution, which looks exactly like an institution that closed. The values are also space- padded. Both are noted here because the first version of this table read four years as zero. [inference] Twelve-month headcount is used rather than autumn headcount because two of the six institutions are non-degree-granting and enrol in cohorts through the year: Apollo Career Center's autumn headcount is 527 against a twelve-month 1,439, and an autumn series would misstate its size by a factor of three. [inference]
properties.parameter: twelve-month unduplicated headcount at Allen County institutions

blocks.text: **The county's colleges have lost a third of their students in thirteen years, and all six of them have lost students.** [verified] — [IPEDS](../../catalog/ipeds.md), twelve-month unduplicated headcount, all students.

**16,702 to 10,789 is a fall of 35.4 per cent.** [inference] — computed here. Institution by institution: the Ohio State Beauty Academy down 55.6 per cent, Ohio State's Lima campus 47.9, Apollo Career Center 45.7, the University of Northwestern Ohio 36.6, Bluffton University 38.1, and Rhodes State College 23.5 — the smallest fall, at the largest institution.

**The county did not shrink anything like that fast.** Allen County went from 106,331 people in 2010 to 102,206 in 2020, a fall of 3.9 per cent. [verified] — [the 2010 count](allen-county-population-2010.yml) and [the 2020 count](allen-county-population-2020-census.yml). Enrolment fell nine times faster than population over an overlapping period, so whatever is happening here is not the county emptying out. [inference] — computed here.

**It is not a pandemic either, though the pandemic is in the series.** The fall from 2010 to 2019 is 4,017 students, or 24.0 per cent, and it is complete before Covid: every one of the six was below its 2010 figure by 2019, and the largest fall between consecutive observations here is Apollo Career Center's 2,648 to 1,275 between 2010 and 2013 — 1,373 students, before the decade was half over. [inference] — computed here. The years after 2019 continue a line that was already drawn.

**The two largest held up longest and then did not.** Rhodes State and the University of Northwestern Ohio were both marginally above their 2010 figures as late as 2016, while the four smaller institutions had already fallen; between 2016 and 2023 Rhodes lost 1,348 students and Northwestern Ohio 1,892. [inference] — computed here.

nodes.label: Who comes and goes to work in Allen County, 2022

properties.method: LODES8 origin-destination files for Ohio, `JT00` — all jobs — for 2022, filtered to origin-destination pairs with a block in Allen County on either end, plus the auxiliary file for workers living outside Ohio. Counties are read from the first five digits of a block identifier and "Lima" from the tract whose internal point falls inside the city's 2020 boundary, which is a statement about where a tract's centre is. Earnings bands are the file's own `SE01`, `SE02` and `SE03`. Every total here is a sum over thousands of cells; no cell is quoted. [verified]
properties.parameter: jobs located in the county, and where their holders live

blocks.text: Half the jobs in this county are held by people who do not live in it. [verified] — [LEHD Origin-Destination Employment Statistics](../../catalog/lehd-lodes.md), LODES8, all jobs, 2022.

**The three flows, in one line.** 24,461 people both live and work in Allen County, 24,269 commute into it, and 18,374 residents leave it for work — on 48,730 jobs located here and 42,835 held by people who live here. [verified] — same source.
**The county draws 5,895 more workers than it sends**, and 42,643 people cross its line in one direction or the other on a working day. [inference] — computed here from the rows above.

**Where they come from and where they go are not the same counties.** The largest sources of in-commuters are Auglaize with 3,298, Putnam 2,986, Van Wert 2,016, Hardin 1,453 and Hancock 1,007 — the ring of rural counties around this one. The largest destinations for residents who leave are Auglaize 1,988, **Franklin 1,723**, Hancock 1,458, Putnam 1,371 and Shelby 1,118. [verified] — same source.

**Franklin County is a hundred miles away and this corpus does not read it as a commute.** The 1,723 are spread across many Columbus tracts, the largest holding 79, so it is not one employer's administrative address; it is what a file that has passed disclosure avoidance looks like at small grain. [inference] See [the flow is real and the cell is not](../../decisions/the-flow-is-real-and-the-cell-is-not.yml).

**Lima holds 46.1 per cent of the county's jobs and 37.2 per cent of its employed residents.** 22,460 jobs in the sixteen tracts whose internal point falls inside the city, against 15,950 residents with jobs. [inference] — computed here, on the same sixteen tracts used for [life expectancy](allen-county-life-expectancy-2010-2015.yml). The city is a net importer of workers inside a county that is a net importer of workers.

**The three flows are alike in what they pay.** Of jobs held by residents working in the county, 47.1 per cent are in the file's top earnings band, above $3,333 a month; of in-commuters' jobs, 50.8 per cent; of out-commuters', 49.4. [verified] — same source. The corpus expected the in-commuters to hold the better-paid work and they do not measurably.

**Two independent counts of the county's jobs agree within two per cent.** 48,730 here for 2022 against 49,690 covered jobs in 2024. [inference] — [the wage file](allen-county-wages-2024.yml). They are different years, different programmes and different definitions of a job, and they land 960 apart.

properties.method: Census of Agriculture, harvested acreage and production for the 2022 calendar year, read from NASS's Quick Stats bulk county file. The 1909 column is the Thirteenth Census, enumerated April 15 1910 for the 1909 crop year. Yields are computed here by dividing production by harvested acres, which is not how either census reports yield and is comparable only because both report both terms. [inference] `(D)` is a suppressed cell, not a zero; a dash is a crop the source does not name for this county in that year, which for 1909 soybeans is a statement about the volume's crop list and not a count of zero acres. [verified]
properties.parameter: crop acreage and production, Allen County

blocks.text: What the county grows, beside what it grew in the year this corpus already measures. [verified] — [USDA Census of Agriculture](../../catalog/usda-census-of-agriculture.md), county file, and [Abstract of the Thirteenth Census](../../catalog/census-1910-abstract-supplement-ohio.md).

**The county's largest crop did not exist here in 1909.** Soybeans took 76,200 acres in 2022, more than corn, and the 1910 census names no soybean acreage in Allen County at all. [verified] — [the Census of Agriculture](../../catalog/usda-census-of-agriculture.md) and [the Thirteenth Census](../../catalog/census-1910-abstract-supplement-ohio.md).

**An acre of Allen County corn yields five times what it did**, 192.7 bushels against 38.7, and an acre of wheat six times, 81.8 against 13.4. [inference] — computed here by division. The county grew a quarter more corn acres in 2022 than in 1909 and took six and a quarter times the grain off them.

**The oats went with the horses.** 30,156 acres of oats in 1909, 11 acres on three operations in 2022; 3,107 acres of rye then, and now one operation in the county, whose acreage the census withholds because one operation is all there is. [verified] — same sources. Hay fell from 39,664 acres to 2,431. Together those three crops were 72,927 acres in 1909 — twenty-eight per cent of the county — and they were what fed the 14,676 horses and 21,336 cattle counted in [the same volume](allen-county-domestic-animals-1910.yml).

**Two crops are now 84.9 per cent of the harvest.** Soybeans and corn take 140,976 of the county's 165,982 cropland acres. [inference] — computed here. What is left is wheat, 2,686 acres of hay and haylage, 793 acres of popcorn on fourteen operations, and $1,663,000 of vegetables, fruit, nursery stock and everything else together. [verified] — [the 2022 county profile](../../catalog/usda-census-of-agriculture.md).

nodes.label: Who was paid federal disaster aid in Allen County, 2005–2025

properties.method: Distinct `applicantId` across the county's 95 project rows, resolved to names through the applicant register with the filter scoped to Ohio. Scoping is required: `003-99003-00`, the identifier the county government itself files under, returns more than a hundred and eighty county governments across the United States and an unscoped join names a Delaware one. Dollars are the federal share obligated, nominal, summed per applicant and rounded to the dollar; the table's rounded rows do not sum exactly to the total published in [the assistance measure](allen-county-disaster-assistance-2005-2025.yml). Parenthesised county names are the file's own. [inference]
properties.parameter: applicants paid federal public assistance for work in Allen County

blocks.text: **Twenty-eight applicants, and one hospital took 82.74 per cent of the money.** [verified] — [OpenFEMA assistance programs](../../catalog/openfema-assistance-programs.md), the public assistance projects joined to the applicant register on `applicantId`, scoped to Ohio.

**A disaster is the one occasion on which nearly every government in this county files the same form.** Nine of the county's ten municipal corporations appear — Lima, Delphos and the villages of Bluffton, Elida, Fort Shawnee, Harrod, Lafayette, Spencerville and Beaverdam — and eight of its twelve townships. [verified] — same source. **The only municipality absent is [Cairo](../place/cairo.yml)**, and the four townships absent are Auglaize, Marion, Monroe and Spencer. [inference] — computed against the corpus's own roster.

**The county files as four separate applicants.** Allen County, the Allen County Commissioners, the Allen County Engineer and the Allen County Health Department each hold their own `applicantId`, and each was paid separately. [verified] — same source; see [the engineer](../office/allen-county-engineer.yml).

**Delphos files twice because it stands in two counties.** "Delphos, City of (Allen County)" and "Delphos, City of (Van Wert County)" are two registrations of one municipal corporation, and both were paid — $41,075 and $7,710. [verified] — same source; see [the city](../jurisdiction/city-of-delphos.yml). A township of Auglaize County is here too, for work counted in this one.

nodes.label: Federal disaster assistance to Allen County, 2005–2025

properties.method: Fetched from the OpenFEMA public assistance funded projects endpoint filtered to `stateAbbreviation` OH and `county` "Allen County" — the longer spelling, which this dataset requires and the declarations dataset does not — and summed here. The `as_of` is the last obligation date in the file and not the query date: this file grows. Dollars are nominal and span twenty years, so the four declaration rows above are not comparable to one another as amounts of purchasing power. The applicant count is of distinct `applicantId`s and treats the two Delphos registrations as two, because the file does. [inference]
properties.parameter: federal share obligated for public assistance projects in Allen County

blocks.text: **$10,608,108 of federal money on 95 projects, and eighty-four cents of every dollar is the pandemic.** [verified] — [OpenFEMA assistance programs](../../catalog/openfema-assistance-programs.md), public assistance funded projects, Ohio, Allen County. This closes the cost question [the declarations](allen-county-disaster-declarations-1965-2020.yml) opened.

**Four of the county's ten declarations produced funded projects.** [verified] — same source. The 1965 and 1978 declarations predate the file; the 2004 declaration was designated for hazard mitigation only; the three emergency declarations of 2005, 2012 and 2020 are each paired with a major disaster declaration that carries the projects. [inference] — computed from [the declarations](allen-county-disaster-declarations-1965-2020.yml).

**The pandemic is 84.28 per cent of the money on 7.4 per cent of the projects.** Eighty-eight weather projects across fifteen years came to $1,667,603, against $8,940,505 for seven pandemic projects. [inference] — computed here.

**What a federal disaster buys in this county is cleanup.** Fifty-four of the 95 projects are Debris Removal or Emergency Protective Measures, and among the 88 weather projects it is 49 of 88 and $1,321,835 of $1,667,603 — seventy-nine cents in the dollar for picking things up and keeping people safe while it happened. Nine projects in twenty years are Roads and Bridges and one is a Water Control Facility. [verified] — same source, counted here. **Nothing here rebuilds anything.** [inference]

**The pandemic projects are the same category and not the same thing.** Five of the seven are Emergency Protective Measures and two are Management Costs; the largest, at $4,645,416 federal, covers March to June 2020 at one hospital, and the county health department's is titled "ACPH Super POD Project #1". [verified] — same source.

**The money arrives years after the weather.** Obligations run from 20 April 2005 to 28 May 2025, and the 2020 declaration's largest project was still being obligated in February 2025 — four years and eleven months after the incident began. All 95 projects are closed out. [verified] — same source.

properties.method: Fetched from the OpenFEMA v2 API filtered to `fipsStateCode` 39 and `fipsCountyCode` 003, and counted here. The `as_of` is the last declaration and not the query date: this file grows, and the figure is a count of what had happened by then. Distinct incidents are counted by grouping rows on the incident window, which merges 2012's pair and 2020's and separates the two of 2004 and 2005. Incident dates before 2004 are not usable — the 1965 and 1978 rows give an incident beginning and ending on the day the declaration was signed. [inference]
properties.parameter: federal disaster and emergency declarations naming Allen County

blocks.text: **Ten declarations in fifty-five years, for eight distinct incidents.** [verified] — [OpenFEMA](../../catalog/fema-disaster-declarations.md), disaster declarations summaries, Ohio county 003.

**Counting declarations is not counting disasters.** The June 2012 storm produced an emergency declaration on 30 June and a major disaster declaration on 20 August, seven weeks apart, for the same four-day incident window; COVID-19 produced two in eighteen days. Ten rows, eight incidents. [inference] — computed here from the incident windows.

**Nine of the ten carried Public Assistance**, which is aid to governments for debris and public works — every declaration but the hazard-mitigation-only one of September 2004. [verified] — same source. **What a federal disaster usually means in this county is a bill to the county, not a cheque to a family.** [inference]

**Three of the ten brought money to households, and this node said two.** Individual Assistance, the flag `iaProgramDeclared`, was designated in 1965 and 2007 and in no other year — that part stands. But the file carries a fourth flag this node had not read, `ihProgramDeclared`, the Individuals and Households Program, and it is true for 2007 **and for the COVID-19 major disaster declaration of 31 March 2020**, under which $3,595,938 reached 507 households here. [verified] — same source; see [the household aid](allen-county-household-disaster-aid-2007-2020.yml). The earlier count was of three flags where the file prints four.

**A county nine hundred miles from the Gulf has a hurricane declaration.** EM-3250-OH, 13 September 2005, "Hurricane Katrina evacuation" — Public Assistance for a county that took in people. [verified] — same source; see [the Katrina declaration](../event/allen-county-declared-for-hurricane-katrina-2005.yml).

**The rate looks like it rose tenfold and almost certainly did not.** Two declarations in the thirty-nine years to 2004 and eight in the sixteen after. A programme that changed its coverage, its designation threshold and its politics is a likelier cause than weather changing by a factor of ten, and nothing in this file separates them. [inference] The corpus records the count and refuses the trend.

**The longest incident in the file is 1,207 days.** COVID-19 ran from 20 January 2020 to 11 May 2023 on both its rows; the longest of the other eight is forty-one days. [verified] — same source, computed here.

**Six of these ten are for weather, and five of the six now have a storm with a date.** Matched against the county's severe weather record: the 2004 declaration has a flash flood inside its window, the 2005 pair of winter declarations has a winter storm on the first day of the window and an ice storm inside it, 2007 has a flash flood, and the June 2012 storm has four thunderstorm-wind reports on the exact day the incident window opens. 1965 has a tornado three days before a window one day long. [verified] — [the storm record](allen-county-storm-events-1950-2026.yml) and [the Storm Events Database](../../catalog/noaa-storm-events.md).

**The sixth is the blizzard of January 1978 and the weather file does not contain it.** There is no Allen County row for 1978 at all, and no row of any kind within thirty days of that declaration, because the first blizzard this county's weather record admits is in 2007. **The administrative file holds the storm the observational file cannot see.** [verified] — same source; see [a category has a birthday](../../decisions/a-category-has-a-birthday.yml).

**What they cost is now held, and four of the ten account for all of it.** $10,608,108 of federal public assistance on 95 projects, of which $8,940,505 — eighty-four per cent — is the 2020 pandemic declaration and $1,667,603 is fifteen years of weather. [verified] — [the assistance](allen-county-disaster-assistance-2005-2025.yml). Three hazard mitigation projects and $4,237,572 to households sit beside it. [verified] — [the mitigation](allen-county-hazard-mitigation-2003-2026.yml) and [the household aid](allen-county-household-disaster-aid-2007-2020.yml).

**These cannot be crossed with the river's flow record, and finding that out was the point.** The Ottawa River gauge at Lima is missing water years 2000 to 2009 exactly, and the declarations for storms and flooding fall in 2004, 2005 and 2007. Exactly one non-pandemic declaration here lies inside the gauge's record — June 2012, titled for straight-line winds, in a water year whose peak ranked sixteenth of twenty-seven. [verified] — [the peak flows](ottawa-river-peak-flows-1924-2025.yml); see [the intersection, not the union](../../decisions/the-intersection-not-the-union.yml).

nodes.label: Allen County domestic animals, on farms and off, 1910

properties.method: Thirteenth Census of Agriculture, enumerated April 15, 1910. Read from rendered images of a 400-dpi scan. Checked by arithmetic self-closure: on the farms the seven animal values sum to the printed $2,501,226 exactly, and cattle, horses, mules, swine and sheep each sum from their own age and sex classes; off the farms the five values sum to $350,736 exactly. The colonies-of- bees value is damaged on this scan and was recovered as $2,561 from the property total, an identity that closes exactly in the neighbouring county column. County totals are added here. [inference]
properties.parameter: domestic animals on and off farms, Allen County

blocks.text: The county's animals counted twice over — once on the farms and once inside the town lots. [verified] — [Abstract of the Thirteenth Census, Supplement for Ohio](../../catalog/census-1910-abstract-supplement-ohio.md), statistics of agriculture, Table 1 (farms and ranges) and Table 6 (not on farms).

**There were 14,676 horses in Allen County in 1910 — one for every 3.9 people.** [inference] — computed from the two tables, against the county's 56,580. The horses were worth $1,391,032 on the farms and $304,989 off them, together more than half the value of every animal in the county.

**1,788 inclosures that were not farms kept animals**, holding 2,766 horses, 887 cattle and 664 swine. [verified] — same source, Table 6. This is the town half of the county: a place that was half city by population and nine-tenths farm by ground still moved itself on horses, and 713 of its dairy cows stood in yards rather than fields. See [Lima](../place/lima.yml) and [the farms](allen-county-farms-1900-1910.yml).
**The swine outnumbered the people.** [inference] — 59,695 against 56,580, computed here. Sheep and goats came to 41,240 and cattle to 21,336.

**There is a later count now, and it does not say when the horses went.** In 2022 the county held 316 horses and ponies, 8,576 cattle, 877 sheep and 622 goats, and a dairy herd the census will not print. [verified] — [the Census of Agriculture](../../catalog/usda-census-of-agriculture.md); see [the modern livestock](allen-county-livestock-2002-2022.yml). Every animal in the 1910 table is down by nine-tenths or more except the swine, which nearly quadrupled to 235,800.

refusals: So the fall from 14,676 happened somewhere in the ninety-two years between, and this corpus still cannot say when.

nodes.label: Allen County elective seats and how their holders arrived, 2026

properties.method: Union of the eighty-eight precinct pages of the boards of elections roster, deduplicated on the office name and the page's own `hid_office` code. Vacancies are counted from its `N Vacant Seat(s)` rows and appointments from its `*Appointed*` marker; the class column is this corpus's grouping and the roster totals nothing. [verified] **It is a county's roster, so a ward seat of a city that crosses the county line does not appear.** Delphos contributes ten seats here and 3,182 of its people live in Van Wert County, so its council is undercounted by an unknown number of ward seats. [inference] No other government here is affected: Bluffton also crosses a line and elects its council at large.
properties.parameter: seated holders of elective office, and seats vacant, by class of government

blocks.text: Every elective seat whose constituency lies inside Allen County, with the seat filled or vacant and — where filled — whether the roster marks its holder as appointed to it. [verified] — [the elected officials lookup](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md), read across all eighty-eight precincts.

**This counts the ballot and not the register, and the roster answers both ways.** The same lookup queried by district type returns twelve boards of education for this county, not nine: the three districts centred in Putnam and Auglaize counties have boards here and no Allen precinct votes on them. Their fifteen seats are outside the table above because the table is of seats an Allen County elector fills. [verified] — same source, both views; see [the school boards](allen-county-school-boards-2026.yml).

**Twenty-three per cent of this county's local government arrived by appointment.** Of the 166 seated township, village, city and school officers, 39 hold seats they were appointed to fill. [verified] — same source. Every one of the twenty-two county offices and judgeships is filled, and every one of them by election. [verified]

**The village form is where it concentrates, and size is not what separates it from the township form.** Twenty-five of the forty-seven seated village officers were appointed and five village seats stand empty, against one appointment and no vacancy across all forty-eight township seats. [verified] — same source. [Spencer Township](../jurisdiction/spencer-township.yml) holds 3,024 people and [Spencerville](../jurisdiction/village-of-spencerville.yml) inside it holds 2,164, so most of the township's people are the village's people and both govern them. [verified] — [the race table](allen-county-race-2023.yml) and [the estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md), a year apart in vintage. The township fills four seats and elected all four; the village fills seven and appointed four of them. [verified]

**Two villages cannot fill their governments at all.** [Cairo](../jurisdiction/village-of-cairo.yml)'s six-member council is five appointees and one vacant seat: no elected member sits on it. [Harrod](../jurisdiction/village-of-harrod.yml)'s board of public affairs is three seats and all three are empty; of its ten village seats, four are vacant, five are held by appointees and one — a single council member — was elected. [verified] — same source.

refusals: This does not establish that these seats go unfilled because nobody stands for them.

nodes.label: Allen County employment by sector, 1986 and 2022

properties.method: County Business Patterns county files for 1986 and 2022, with sector 62 traced across 2000, 2005, 2010, 2015 and 2020. Both endpoint years close exactly: the ten 1986 SIC divisions sum to 45,917 and the twenty 2022 NAICS sectors to 42,814, each equal to its file's own total row. Government, the self-employed and farms are excluded. [verified]
properties.parameter: private employment by industry sector, Allen County

blocks.text: What the county's private workforce did, at the two ends of the only span this corpus can measure it over. [verified] — [County Business Patterns](../../catalog/census-county-business-patterns.md).

**Health care is the county's largest private employer sector, and manufacturing is second.** [verified] — same source. In 1986 manufacturing employed more people than the next two divisions together.

**The two schemes are not comparable line by line and the top line is the point.** SIC "services" in 1986 is a division that NAICS breaks across health care, accommodation, professional services and more, so the 1986 column cannot be subtracted from the 2022 one sector by sector. [verified] — the break is a change of definition. What survives the break is the rank of manufacturing: first in 1986, second in 2022. [inference]

**Health care did not simply rise past manufacturing, and this node had the shape of its fall wrong.** Sector 62 peaked at **12,431 in 2013** — not at the 11,744 of 2010 this node used to call its high — and stood above 11,744 again in 2016, before falling to 9,151 in 2022. [verified] — same source, read every year rather than every fifth; see [the annual series](allen-county-health-care-employment-2010-2022.yml) and [a sample is not a series](../../decisions/a-sample-is-not-a-series.yml). Against 2010 the county's largest sector still lost 2,593 while [manufacturing gained 1,446](allen-county-manufacturing-employment-1986-2022.yml). [inference]

**What contracted is now established, even though why is not.** Of the 2,593 lost since 2010, hospitals are 1,866, nursing and residential care 549, social assistance 170, and ambulatory care 8. [verified] — same source, read annually. The county's five hospitals are named, and their own reported full-time equivalents fell across the same span. See [hospital employment](allen-county-hospital-employment-2011-2023.yml).

nodes.label: Allen County farm output and farm expenses, 1909

properties.method: Thirteenth Census of Agriculture, for the calendar year 1909. Read from rendered images of a 400-dpi scan. Checked by arithmetic self-closure: the six crop-value classes sum to $2,425,973 exactly; the six cereals sum to the printed cereal acreage and to the printed bushel total; the six tame grasses sum to the tame-grass acreage and tonnage, and those plus three minor forages sum to the hay total — eight closures with no residual. The orchard and small-fruit itemisations leave residuals, as they do in the state column, because both omit minor kinds. [verified]
properties.parameter: value of crops, live stock products and farm expenses, Allen County

blocks.text: What the county's farms grew, sold and spent in the same year the corpus measures Lima's factories. [verified] — [Abstract of the Thirteenth Census, Supplement for Ohio](../../catalog/census-1910-abstract-supplement-ohio.md), statistics of agriculture, Tables 3, 4 and 5.

**Corn was half the county's cropland and two-thirds of its grain.** [verified] — same source. Cereals took 100,285 acres and yielded 3,146,354 bushels; corn alone was 51,293 of those acres. Wheat was a minor crop here, on a seventh of the cereal acreage. The county grew no tobacco and no sugar beets at all.

**Farms spent $184,390 in cash on labour in 1909**, with 1,571 of the 2,939 farms reporting any, plus $47,888 in rent and board furnished. [verified] — same source, Table 5. Fertilizer took $12,957 across 428 farms and feed $63,780 across 708. Receipts from the sale of feedable crops were $423,118.

**Against this, Lima's factories made $7,753,877 of products in the same year.** [verified] — [Lima manufactures](lima-manufactures-1899-1909.yml), from the manufactures chapter of this same volume. [inference] Both are gross output and neither nets out what was bought to make it, so the ratio of about three to one is a comparison of two gross figures and not of two incomes.

nodes.label: Allen County farms and farm property, 1900–1910

properties.method: Thirteenth Census of Agriculture, enumerated April 15, 1910, with 1900 comparatives printed in italics. Read from rendered images of a 400-dpi scan. Checked by arithmetic self-closure: the three tenure classes of Table 2 sum to Table 1's farm count, acreage, improved acreage and land-and-buildings value independently; the ten size classes sum to 2,939; improved plus woodland plus other unimproved sums to land in farms; the four property components sum to the total in both years; and all six printed averages and percentages recompute. [verified]
properties.parameter: farms, farm acreage and value of farm property, Allen County

blocks.text: What the county was made of, on the ground, at the height of the oil boom. [verified] — [Abstract of the Thirteenth Census, Supplement for Ohio](../../catalog/census-1910-abstract-supplement-ohio.md), statistics of agriculture, Tables 1 and 2.

**Nine-tenths of Allen County was farmland in 1910 — 240,472 acres of 259,840, or 92.5 per cent.** [verified] — same source, which prints the percentage and the land area beside it. Of that, 203,222 acres were improved, 32,316 were woodland in farms and 4,934 were otherwise unimproved. The average farm was 81.8 acres; the commonest was between 50 and 99 acres, and 1,138 of the 2,939 were that size. One farm in the county exceeded 500 acres and none reached 1,000.

**The county had 2,939 farms in 1910 and 2,858 in 1900, on 240,472 acres against 245,283.** [verified] — same source. Farms rose by 81 and farmland fell by 4,811 acres, about 2 per cent, while improved acreage *rose* by 6,757. Twenty-five years after [the strike](../event/lima-oil-strike.yml), whatever the boom did to this county, it had not taken the farms out of it. See [Lima manufactures](lima-manufactures-1899-1909.yml) for the other side of the same volume, and [what the county was](../period/lima-oil-boom.yml).

**The farms that multiplied were rented ones.** Owner-operated farms fell from 2,089 to 2,046 while tenanted farms rose from 730 to 871, and tenancy went from 25.5 to 29.6 per cent of all farms. [verified] — same source, Table 2. Of the 871 tenants, 509 paid shares and 275 paid cash. Of 2,046 owners, 655 carried mortgage debt and 1,378 were free of it.

**The other end of the century is measured now.** 178,921 acres in 2022, 69.4 per cent of the county, with 94,325 of those acres rented from somebody else. [verified] — [the Census of Agriculture](../../catalog/usda-census-of-agriculture.md); see [the modern series](allen-county-farms-2002-2022.yml). The 2,939 farms of 1910 and the 897 of 2022 are not subtracted here: the two censuses use different definitions of a farm, and the difference between the thresholds is not a quantity anything in this corpus can supply. See [a farm count is a definition](../../decisions/a-farm-count-is-a-definition.yml).

nodes.label: Allen County farms, farmland and farm income, 2002–2022

properties.method: Census of Agriculture, taken for the 2022 calendar year, read from NASS's Quick Stats bulk county file and checked against the published county profile, which agrees on every headline figure. The four tenure rows sum to land in farms exactly and the two sales components sum to the total exactly. NASS defines a farm as "any place from which $1,000 or more of agricultural products were produced and sold, or normally would have been sold, during the census year", which is not the definition the 1910 census used. [verified] See [a farm count is a definition](../../decisions/a-farm-count-is-a-definition.yml).
properties.parameter: farms, land in farms and value of products sold, Allen County

blocks.text: Five agricultural censuses of the county's largest land use, and the first this corpus has read since 1910. [verified] — [USDA Census of Agriculture](../../catalog/usda-census-of-agriculture.md), county files.

**Allen County was 92.5 per cent farmland in 1910 and is 69.4 per cent farmland now** — 178,921 acres of the 257,629 in its 402.545 square miles. [inference] — computed here from [the 1910 farms](allen-county-farms-1900-1910.yml) and [the county's land area](allen-county-land-area-2020.yml). The two censuses measure land area on different geographies, so the shares are firmer than the difference between them.

**Nine-tenths of the fall happened before this series begins.** Land in farms was 240,472 acres in 1910 and 188,150 in 2002 — 52,322 acres gone — against 9,229 more across the twenty years since. [inference] — same two sources. There is no agricultural census between them in this catalog, so this corpus knows that the farmland went and cannot say when. See [when the farmland went](../question/when-the-farmland-went.yml).

**Land in farms, five censuses in one line.** 188,150 acres in 2002, 187,238 in 2007, 183,186 in 2012, 186,623 in 2017 and 178,921 in 2022, against 240,472 in 1910. [verified] — same source, and [the 1910 farms](allen-county-farms-1900-1910.yml).

**More than half the county's farmland is worked by someone who does not own it.** 94,325 of 178,921 acres are rented — 90,661 by 268 part-owner operations and 3,664 by 38 tenants — and the 591 operations that own everything they farm hold 34,912 acres between them, a fifth of the total. [verified] — same source, tenure domain, whose four figures close on the county acreage exactly.

**So 268 operations farm 78.4 per cent of the ground.** [inference] — computed here. In 1910 the same county held 2,939 farms, of which 2,046 were owner-operated. [verified] — [the 1910 farms](allen-county-farms-1900-1910.yml).

**The census cannot resolve its own headline.** The county profile prints farms up 5 per cent and land in farms down 4 per cent since 2017; the figures are 897 ± 69 farms and 178,921 ± 16,171 acres, so the first change is inside one standard error and the second is inside half of one. [verified] — same source, Appendix A Table C. **39.0 per cent of the county's farm count is adjustment for coverage, nonresponse and misclassification rather than a returned form**, and 28.6 per cent of its acreage is. The corpus does not read the sales row of that table, whose standard error is printed in a unit the table does not name.

**Federal money reached 344 of the 897.** $1,898,000 in 2022, of which $698,000 went to 283 operations for conservation and wetlands and $1,200,000 to 86 for everything else. [verified] — same source. Expenses were $168,593,000 against $240,849,000 of sales; feed alone was $34,822,000, a fifth of all spending, in a county whose animals are described [next door](allen-county-livestock-2002-2022.yml).

refusals: There is no agricultural census between them in this catalog, so this corpus knows that the farmland went and cannot say when.

properties.method: Summed by candidate over the county's 88 precincts, from a volunteer transcription of the certified returns. [verified]
properties.parameter: votes cast for governor

blocks.text: Of 35,961 votes for governor, **24,200 for DeWine and 10,825 for Cordray** — 67.3 per cent against 30.1, with 605 for Irvine and 331 for Gadell-Newton. [verified] — [OpenElections](../../catalog/openelections-ohio.md), summed over the county's 88 precincts.

It sits between the two presidential elections in this corpus at 66.5 and 69.0 per cent Republican, which is the useful thing about it: the county's partisan balance barely moved between a presidential year and a midterm, while **the number of people voting fell by a fifth** — 45,815 in 2016 to 35,961 here, and back to 47,993 in 2020. [verified] — same source, and [2016](allen-county-presidential-vote-2016.yml) and [2020](allen-county-presidential-vote-2020.yml).
Who turns out changes far more here than how they vote. [inference] — from three elections, which is enough to see the pattern and not enough to date it.

properties.method: Table P5, Group Quarters Population by Major Group Quarters Type, from the Ohio file of the 2020 Census Redistricting Data Summary File (P.L. 94-171). Summed from the 3,552 block records for county 39003, joined to the geographic header on LOGRECNO. The block sums close on the file's own county record exactly, in every one of the ten cells. [verified] The Census Bureau's API serves the same table from the Demographic and Housing Characteristics file and refuses the request without a key, which is why the flat file was taken instead — the same reason this corpus reads the ACS from its summary file rather than its API. Institution identification is by geometry, not by address: a block is identified with a landmark only where the two carry the same land area and the same internal point. Two do. [inference] — see [a block can be a fence](../../decisions/a-block-can-be-a-fence.yml). The 2020 census applied disclosure avoidance to every published block figure, so a single small cell is noisy; the county totals are not, and the two large correctional cells are corroborated by the geometry they sit on.
properties.parameter: population in group quarters, Allen County

blocks.text: The 3,522 people the 2020 census counted in Allen County who were not living in a household — 3.4 per cent of its 102,206, in 43 of its 3,552 blocks. [verified] — [the 2020 redistricting file](../../catalog/census-2020-redistricting-file.md), Table P5, summed from block records.

**Two of the county's blocks are its two state prisons, and the census drew the block on the fence.** Block `390030112001004` holds 1,360 people, all of them in adult correctional facilities; the Census Bureau's own landmark file gives *Allen Correctional Instn* the same land area to the square metre — 364,210 — and the same internal point to seven decimal places, `+40.7751673 -084.0996846`. Block `390030112001001` holds 153 and matches *Oakwood Corr Faclty* the same way, at 1,383,460 square metres and `+40.7812913 -084.1012253`. [verified] — [TIGER/Line landmarks](../../catalog/census-tiger-landmarks.md) against the redistricting file's geographic header. See [a block can be a fence](../../decisions/a-block-can-be-a-fence.yml).

**Lima holds nearly two thirds of the county's group quarters on a third of its people.** 2,210 of the 3,522, including every one of the 1,513 in correctional facilities. [inference] — computed here from the same file.

**The nursing homes are the county's most distributed institution.** 966 people in fifteen blocks across the city and seven townships, the largest holding 132 — from Bluffton in the north-east to Delphos in the north-west to Shawnee in the south. [inference] — computed here. Nothing else in this table is spread at all: the prisons are two blocks, and 494 of the 788 in student housing are on one campus.

**"Other noninstitutional facilities" is the census's name for shelter.** The category covers emergency and transitional shelters for people experiencing homelessness, group homes intended for adults, residential treatment centres, workers' quarters and Job Corps centres. [verified] — [the technical documentation](../../catalog/census-2020-redistricting-file.md), Appendix B. The county has 255 such residents, and 124 of them are in six blocks of one downtown Lima tract.

**The county records no juvenile facility, no psychiatric-hospital population and no military quarters at all.** [verified] — same source. The zero for other institutional facilities is worth reading carefully rather than as an absence: that category is where psychiatric hospitals are counted, and this county's psychiatric hospital is [Oakwood](../site/oakwood-correctional-facility.yml), whose residents are inmates and are therefore counted as correctional. [inference]

**The county's student housing does not sit where its students are.** Only two of the six post-secondary institutions in Allen County provide institutionally controlled housing, and they reported 2,228 beds between them in 2020 — Bluffton University 692 and the University of Northwestern Ohio 1,536. Against that the census counted 788 people in college student housing, 35 per cent of the beds. [verified] — [IPEDS](../../catalog/ipeds.md), institutional characteristics, against the redistricting file. Census day 2020 fell some weeks after American campuses sent their students home, and this corpus cannot separate that from ordinary vacancy. [inference]

properties.method: Fetched from the OpenFEMA hazard mitigation assistance projects endpoint filtered to state Ohio and county "Allen" — the short spelling, where the public assistance endpoint requires "Allen County". `as_of` is the last close-out date in the file. The federal share for the denied project is null rather than zero and is printed as absent, because a project that was never obligated is not a project obligated at nothing. Dollars are nominal across twenty-two years and are not summed. [inference]
properties.parameter: federal hazard mitigation projects recorded for Allen County

blocks.text: **Three projects in twenty-three years: a plan, a house bought, and a house refused.** [verified] — [OpenFEMA assistance programs](../../catalog/openfema-assistance-programs.md), hazard mitigation assistance projects, Ohio, county Allen.

**The county's flood buyout was paid for with pandemic money.** DR-4507 is the COVID-19 major disaster declaration, and the project it funded is "Acquisition of Private Real Property (Structures and Land) – Riverine" — one property, bought out, at a ninety per cent federal share. [verified] — same source. **A mitigation allocation is generated by a declaration and is not confined to the hazard that caused it**, which is why a biological incident bought a house out of a floodplain. [inference]

**The mitigation plan was bought with another county's disaster.** DR-1484 is an Ohio declaration of 2003 that never named Allen County; the recipient is "Statewide" and the subrecipient is Allen County, which used $34,500 of federal money to write a Local Multihazard Mitigation Plan. [verified] — same source, checked against [the declarations](allen-county-disaster-declarations-1965-2020.yml), which has no 2003 row.

**The refused project passed its own benefit-cost test.** FMA-PJ-05-OH-2016-009, a Flood Mitigation Assistance acquisition of one riverine property, carries a benefit-cost ratio of 1.63 and net benefits of $221,479 against a project cost of $135,540 — and its status is "Not Approved / Denied", with no approval date, no obligation and no federal share. [verified] — same source. **It is the only Allen County record in this file that names a benefit-cost ratio at all**; both HMGP rows carry zero. [inference]

**So the county's whole federal flood-buyout record is two houses, one bought and one not.** [inference] — computed here. Neither is located: `projectCounties` reads ALLEN and there is no coordinate, address or watershed in the file. [verified] — same source.
**The buyout took three years and four months for one house.** Initially approved 5 April 2023, obligated on the 7th, closed 18 August 2026. [verified] — same source.

nodes.label: CDC's health estimates for Allen County and Lima, 2022–2023

properties.method: Crude prevalence only, because the tract file publishes nothing else and a crude figure must not be set against an age-adjusted one. Thirty-five of the forty measures rest on BRFSS 2023 and five — all teeth lost, dental visits, mammograms, colorectal screening, short sleep — on BRFSS 2022. "Differs by more than the confidence limits allow" means the city's published interval and the county's do not overlap, which is a weaker test than a significance test and is the only one these published fields support. [verified]
properties.parameter: modelled prevalence of health measures, county and city
properties.unit: per cent of Lima adults food insecure, as estimated

blocks.text: The corpus's first health source, and it is a model rather than a measurement. [verified] — [CDC PLACES](../../catalog/cdc-places.md), which publishes forty measures for the county, for the City of Lima and for all thirty-five of the county's 2020 census tracts. Every figure below is what CDC estimates, not what anyone counted here; see [a modelled estimate is not an observation](../../decisions/a-modelled-estimate-is-not-an-observation.yml).

**Thirteen of the forty differ between Lima and its county by more than their confidence limits allow**, and eleven of the thirteen are Lima the worse. [verified] — same source, crude prevalence throughout, comparing the city's interval with the county's.

**Five of the top eight are not diseases.** Food stamps, food insecurity, housing insecurity, utility shut-off threat and lack of reliable transportation are the measures CDC groups as health-related social needs, and they are where the city and the county separate most. [verified] — same source.
