**No chronic-disease gap clears the intervals at all.** Diabetes, high blood pressure, coronary heart disease, stroke, asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, depression and obesity all estimate higher in Lima and every one of those differences sits inside its own confidence limits. [verified] — same source. So on this model the city and the county differ in what people are short of and in what has happened to their teeth, and not measurably in what they have been diagnosed with.

**The dental pair is the one place two measures corroborate each other.** A quarter of Lima residents over sixty-five have lost all their teeth against a sixth countywide, and half the city's adults saw a dentist in the year against 58 per cent of the county's. [verified] — same source. Both gaps clear their intervals and they point the same way.

**The tracts spread much further than the city and the county do.** Across the thirty-five, CDC's estimate of adults receiving food stamps runs from 4.9 to 46.1 per cent, food insecurity from 7.2 to 41.3, fair or poor health from 13.9 to 40.5, and total tooth loss among the over-65s from 7.6 to 42.7. [verified] — same source. One tract, `39003014100`, holds the county's highest estimate on nine of those ten measures on a population of 1,695.

**Part of what is in that tract is now on record.** `39003014100` is downtown Lima: it holds [the courthouse](../site/allen-county-courthouse.yml) and [the county jail](../site/allen-county-justice-center.yml), and **124 of the county's 255 residents of shelters, group homes and residential treatment centres** — the census's "other noninstitutional facilities" — across six of its blocks. [verified] — [the group quarters](allen-county-group-quarters-2020.yml) and [TIGER/Line landmarks](../../catalog/census-tiger-landmarks.md).

That is 48.6 per cent of the county's such population on 1.7 per cent of its people, and 7.3 per cent of the tract's own 1,695. [inference] — computed here. A tract that holds the county's highest modelled estimate on nine of ten health measures is also the tract that holds its shelters, which is a coincidence worth naming and not an explanation: the estimates are modelled from a survey of households and this population is not in households at all.

**The file closes on the corpus's own count.** The thirty-five tract populations sum to 102,206, which is the county's 2020 census total and the closure this corpus has used since its block composition phase. [verified] — same source and [the 2020 count](allen-county-population-2020-census.yml).

nodes.label: Allen County health care employment by subsector, 2010–2022

properties.method: County files, fipstate 39 fipscty 003. The four subsectors sum to the sector total exactly in all thirteen years, so no line is suppressed. [verified]
properties.parameter: paid employees for pay period including March 12, NAICS 62 and its four subsectors

blocks.text: The county's largest private sector, every year rather than every fifth. [verified] — [County Business Patterns](../../catalog/census-county-business-patterns.md).

**The sector peaked at 12,431 in 2013, in a year nobody had looked at**, and hospitals are where the fall since went: 1,866 of the 2,593 lost from 2010, 1,049 of the 3,280 lost from the 2013 peak. [verified] — same source. Which share depends on the baseline, and all three are in [a sample is not a series](../../decisions/a-sample-is-not-a-series.yml).

refusals: This does not establish why any of it fell.

properties.method: Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System, 2023-24 collection. Institutions selected by the directory file's `COUNTYCD` equal to 39003, which returns six, all of them active. Autumn headcount and full-time equivalent from the derived enrolment file; twelve-month unduplicated headcount from the twelve-month enrolment file at level 1, all students; awards from the completions file, first majors only, with the institution-total rows excluded; housing capacity and price from the institutional characteristics files. [verified] Award levels are the file's own eight categories rather than a simplification, because two of them — certificates under twelve weeks and certificates of twelve weeks to a year — are together 38 per cent of everything this county awards, and a table that collapses them into "certificates" hides the shape of what two of the six institutions do. [inference] Both totals close: the six institutions' awards sum to 2,918 by institution and by level, and to the same figure across the field families. [inference]
properties.parameter: post-secondary students enrolled, Allen County

blocks.text: Six post-secondary institutions, 8,615 students in the autumn and 10,789 over the twelve months, and 2,918 credentials awarded in the academic year. [verified] — [IPEDS](../../catalog/ipeds.md), 2023-24 directory and the enrolment, completions and characteristics surveys for the same cycle.

**The county's largest college is a two-year one and its students are mostly part-time.** [Rhodes State](../organization/james-a-rhodes-state-college.yml) enrols 3,968 in the autumn, of whom 615 are full-time and 3,353 are not; its full-time equivalent is 1,968, half its headcount. [verified] — same source. Every other institution in the county is majority full-time.

**Two of the six share an address.** Rhodes State and [Ohio State's Lima campus](../organization/ohio-state-university-at-lima.yml) are both at 4240 Campus Drive, in [Bath Township](../place/bath-township.yml) outside the city whose name they carry, and the Census Bureau puts both in the same block. [verified] — same source and [the Census geocoder](../../catalog/census-tiger-landmarks.md). A third pair share a block too: the Ohio State Beauty Academy is at 1760 North Eastown Road, in the block that holds [the University of Northwestern Ohio](../organization/university-of-northwestern-ohio.yml)'s own address, and IPEDS records it as a member of that university's system. [verified] — same source.
[verified] — same source, first majors. 2,482 of the 2,918 are below the baccalaureate, which is 85.1 per cent. [inference] — computed here.

[verified] — same source, completions by two-digit CIP family, first majors, all award levels. Health care is also the county's largest employer, at 9,767 jobs; see [what work pays](allen-county-wages-2024.yml). Those two facts agree, and the second-largest field does not agree with anything in the county's labour market. [inference]

**Every one of the 706 awards in vehicle repair is from one institution, and two thirds of its entering students come from outside Ohio.** Of 877 first-time students at the University of Northwestern Ohio in autumn 2023, 295 were Ohio residents and 582 were not — 101 from Michigan, 83 from Indiana, 48 from Pennsylvania, 31 from New York. At Rhodes State 432 of 436 were Ohio residents, and at Ohio State's Lima campus 255 of 263. [verified] — same source, residence of first-time students.

So the county's second-largest field of study is not a local labour supply and should not be read as one; see [located here is not of here](../../decisions/located-here-is-not-of-here.yml). [inference]

**In-state tuition and fees run from $4,560 to $35,498, an eightfold spread.** Rhodes State $4,560, Ohio State-Lima $8,937, Northwestern Ohio $11,352, Bluffton $35,498. Out of state the two public institutions charge $9,120 and $34,443; the two private ones charge the same to everyone. [verified] — same source, 2023-24 academic year charges. Apollo Career Center and the Beauty Academy price by programme rather than by year and are not in that table.

nodes.label: Allen County mortgage lending, 2018-2024

properties.method: Rates use actions 1, 2 and 3 and exclude withdrawn, purchased and incomplete files, as in [the single year](allen-county-home-lending-2023.yml). [verified] "Lima tracts" is the same sixteen of thirty-five used there. Dollar totals are sums of published loan amounts, each rounded to a $10,000 midpoint, so a total of this size carries a rounding band of its own and is quoted to the nearest hundred thousand. [inference]
properties.parameter: mortgage applications acted on, originations, denials and dollars originated
properties.unit: applications acted on across seven years

blocks.text: Seven years of every mortgage application acted on in this county. [verified] — [the HMDA register](../../catalog/hmda-loan-application-register.md), 2018 through 2024.

**Half a billion dollars in 2020 and 2021, and half of that in 2023.** Lending doubled and fell back inside four years while the number of institutions barely moved. [verified] — same source. The denial rate ran the other way, from 14.0 per cent in 2020 to 23.7 in 2024, which is the highest of the seven. [verified]

**The corpus published "you can buy a house in Lima as easily as anywhere in this county" from the one year in seven where that was true.** Over 2018–2024 the purchase denial rate in Lima's tracts is 13.3 per cent against 10.8 elsewhere — 363 denials of 2,737 against 645 of 5,996 — and Lima's rate is the higher one in six of the seven years. [verified] — same source. The claim is withdrawn and replaced by the figures above; see [a rule is not a habit](../../decisions/a-rule-is-not-a-habit.yml).

**What survives the correction is the size of the difference, which was the real finding.** On everything but purchase, Lima's rate is 37.7 per cent against 21.5 — 1,104 denials of 2,926 against 2,000 of 9,289. The purchase gap is 2.5 percentage points and the other gap is 16.2, so the shape of the 2023 reading holds and its sharper half does not. [verified] — same source.

refusals: This does not establish why either gap is there.

nodes.label: Allen County mortgage applications and denials, 2023

properties.method: Rates use actions 1, 2 and 3 — originated, approved and declined, denied — and exclude the 388 withdrawn, 197 purchased and 93 closed for incompleteness, none of which is a decision about a borrower. [verified] "Lima tracts" is the sixteen of the county's thirty-five whose 2020 population is majority Lima; they hold 32,575 of the city's 35,579 people and 3,093 who live outside it. [verified] — [block assignment](../../catalog/census-block-assignment-2020.md). Nine rows carry no tract, seven of them decisions; those seven are in the county's totals and in neither column, which is why the columns sum to 2,599 and not 2,606. [verified]
properties.parameter: mortgage applications acted on, originations and denials

blocks.text: Every mortgage application acted on in Allen County in 2023, by purpose, by census tract and by the race the file records for the applicant. [verified] — [the HMDA register](../../catalog/hmda-loan-application-register.md). Of 3,294 rows, 2,606 are decisions about a borrower: 1,932 originated, 611 denied, 63 approved and declined. The county's denial rate is 23.4 per cent and $270.3 million was lent.
**In 2023 the purchase denial rate inside the city's tracts was 13.9 per cent and outside them 14.4, and every other purpose taken together was 42.9 against 27.6.** [verified] — same source.

**The sentence this node used to open that paragraph with is withdrawn.** It read *you can buy a house in Lima as easily as anywhere in this county*, with no year in it, and 2023 is the only one of seven in which Lima's purchase rate is the lower one. Over 2018–2024 it is 13.3 per cent against 10.8. [verified] — [seven years](allen-county-home-lending-2018-2024.yml). The figures above are unchanged and were never wrong; what was wrong was reading a year as a county. See [a rule is not a habit](../../decisions/a-rule-is-not-a-habit.yml).

**The reason the register gives is the house.** Twenty-one per cent of denials in Lima tracts cite collateral against 13 per cent elsewhere — 43 of 201 against 53 of 404 — where credit history leads in both at 43 and 45. [verified] Collateral is the property, and Lima's median house is worth $95,900 and was built in 1953. [verified] — [the stock](allen-county-housing-stock-2023.yml) and [its age](allen-county-housing-age-2023.yml). The median purchase loan originated in a Lima tract was $115,000 against $175,000 elsewhere, both medians of $10,000 bands. [verified]

**Applications from Black applicants were denied at 37.9 per cent and from white applicants at 22.6** — 66 of 174 against 458 of 2,023 — and the gap holds inside every income band the corpus cut. Under $50,000: 45.3 against 33.4. From $50,000 to $99,000: 38.0 against 20.5. At $100,000 and over: 25.6 against 15.8. [verified] — same source. Black applicants earning $50,000 to $99,000 were denied more often than white applicants earning under $50,000. [verified]

refusals: This does not establish that those applicants were treated differently.

properties.method: `Number of Beds` for CCNs 360009, 360066, 360263, 361322 and 362020. The total takes one row per hospital per year, which in FY2014 means Kindred's first row only — it filed twice that year across a change of fiscal year. [verified]
properties.parameter: Number of Beds

blocks.text: Beds reported by each of the county's five hospitals, every fiscal year from 2011 to 2023. [verified] — [CMS hospital cost reports](../../catalog/cms-hospital-cost-reports.md).

**The county's bed count fell 13 per cent and one hospital's fell 44.** [Lima Memorial](../organization/lima-memorial-health-system.yml) went from 195 beds to 110, with a low of 95 in 2019, while [St. Rita's](../organization/mercy-health-st-ritas-medical-center.yml) ended seven beds higher than it began. The three small hospitals never moved: twelve, twenty-five and twenty-six in all thirteen years. [verified]

**Beds and staff moved in opposite directions at the same hospital.** Lima Memorial lost 44 per cent of its beds and gained 28 per cent of its [full-time equivalents](allen-county-hospital-employment-2011-2023.yml) across the same thirteen years. [verified] — same source.

properties.method: CCNs 360009, 360066, 360263, 361322 and 362020 across the thirteen annual files — 66 rows. County totals sum the four calendar-year filers; [Kindred](../organization/kindred-hospital-lima.yml) left the calendar year after FY2013, so FY2014 holds two of its rows. [verified]
properties.parameter: FTE - Employees on Payroll

blocks.text: Full-time equivalents on payroll at each of the county's five hospitals. Thirteen fiscal years were read, 2011 to 2023; four are shown and every figure below is computed from all thirteen. [verified] — [CMS hospital cost reports](../../catalog/cms-hospital-cost-reports.md).

**The county's hospital employment fell 19 per cent, and one hospital fell by more than the whole.** The four calendar-year filers went from 3,598.20 to 2,913.00, a fall of 685.20; [St. Rita's](../organization/mercy-health-st-ritas-medical-center.yml) alone fell 1,019.08 while [Lima Memorial](../organization/lima-memorial-health-system.yml) rose 278.89 and [the Institute](../organization/institute-for-orthopaedic-surgery.yml) rose 74.05. [verified] Most of St. Rita's drop — 625 — is on the FY2013/FY2014 boundary, where it began filing as an LLC, and is not only employment. [inference]

A full-time equivalent is not an employee, so no figure here may be subtracted from [County Business Patterns](allen-county-health-care-employment-2010-2022.yml), which counts people on a payroll: 3,677 FTE against 4,848 employees in 2011, 2,990 against 3,211 in 2022. [verified]

nodes.label: Federal aid to Allen County households, 2007 and 2020

properties.method: Two endpoints, owners and renters, filtered to state OH and county "Allen (County)" — a third spelling of the county on the same API — and summed here. `value` is the two disasters' approved IHP amounts added: $641,634 for 2007 and $3,595,938 for 2020, in nominal dollars thirteen years apart, which is a total and not a comparable one. Registrations are `validRegistrations` and are not households: a household that registers and is found ineligible is counted here. The two endpoints carry different fields — owners have an inspected-damage dollar figure and renters have damage bands — so no damage total is computed across both. [inference]
properties.parameter: federal individual and household assistance approved in Allen County

blocks.text: **Two disasters have put federal money into households here, and the pandemic put in five and a half times what the flood did.** [verified] — [OpenFEMA assistance programs](../../catalog/openfema-assistance-programs.md), housing assistance to owners and to renters, Ohio, county "Allen (County)".

**The 2007 flood was inspected and the pandemic was not.** Two hundred and seventy-two properties were visited in 2007 and $663,302 of damage was written down; $486,239 of the money that followed was for repair or replacement. Under the 2020 declaration nobody was inspected, nothing was recorded as damaged, and every dollar of the $3,595,938 is classed Other Needs — not repair, not rent. [verified] — same source.

**The corpus's declaration table said two of ten brought money to households. It is three.** The flag the corpus read is `iaProgramDeclared`, true for 1965 and 2007 only. There is a fourth flag, `ihProgramDeclared` — the Individuals and Households Program — true for 2007 and for the 2020 major disaster declaration, and it is the one under which the $3,595,938 was paid. [verified] — [OpenFEMA](../../catalog/fema-disaster-declarations.md); see [the declarations](allen-county-disaster-declarations-1965-2020.yml), which now says so.

**Three-quarters of the 2007 flood damage in this county was in Bluffton.** ZIP 45817 holds 109 of the 227 owner registrations, 91 of the 195 owner inspections and $481,404 of the $663,302 written down — 72.6 per cent — and the average inspected damage there was $4,416.55. [verified] — same source, computed here. The Blanchard River crested near a record at Ottawa that week; see [the storm record](allen-county-storm-events-1950-2026.yml).

**The 2007 rows are coherent and the 2020 rows are not.** The flood's sixteen ZIP codes are Allen County's and its neighbours'. The pandemic's twenty-one include Pittsburgh, Richmond Heights outside Cleveland, Sherwood in Defiance County and Union City on the Indiana line, all filed under Allen County. [verified] — same source. **A programme that inspects a property knows where it is and a programme that pays a person knows where the person wrote from.** [inference] — see [a grant file counts offices, not ground](../../decisions/a-grant-file-counts-offices-not-ground.yml).

**Five hundred and forty-five of the 568 pandemic registrations are classed as renters.** In a county where 27,960 of 40,928 occupied units are owner-occupied — over two-thirds — that is a classification produced by a programme with no inspection rather than a fact about tenure. [inference] — [the housing stock](allen-county-housing-stock-2023.yml). The corpus reports the split and reads nothing into it.

nodes.label: When Allen County's housing was built, 2023

properties.method: Shares are computed here from published counts; the medians are published. [verified] The bands describe *surviving* housing, so a low count for an early decade is demolition and construction together and cannot be read as construction alone. [inference]
properties.parameter: housing units by year structure built (B25034) and median year built (B25035)

blocks.text: The year the county's standing housing was built, by band, for the county and for each of its thirteen civil subdivisions. [verified] — [American Community Survey](../../catalog/census-acs-summary-file.md), 2023 five-year estimates, table B25034. All eleven bands close exactly against the county's own row.

**The county's biggest building decade was the 1970s**, 8,298 units ± 585 against 6,529 ± 563 for the 1950s. Only "1939 or earlier" holds more, and that band is not a decade — it is everything before one. [verified] — same source.

**Six thousand three hundred and thirty-three of those 8,298 were built outside Lima.** The city took 1,965 of the decade in which it reached its own peak of 53,734 and held 48.4 per cent of the county. [verified] — the table and [the city and the rest](allen-county-outside-lima-1890-2020.yml). The ring was built while the city was full, not after it emptied. [inference]

**The median house in Lima was built in 1953 and the median house in Bath Township in 1975.** Shawnee and American are 1973. Lima is 34.9 per cent pre-1940 where the three townships that ring it are between 6.4 and 7.1. [verified] Marion at 37.0 per cent and Richland at 38.0 read higher than Lima and this does not establish that they are older: 1,069 ± 235 of 2,886 ± 242 and 930 ± 195 of 2,449 ± 168 leave all three indistinguishable. [verified]

**11,327 units of this county's standing housing were built in 1980 or later**, a quarter of the whole, and the county fell from 112,241 to 100,866 over the same span. [verified] — the table and [the county](../place/allen-county.yml). The two are not a ratio and nothing here divides them — one counts dwellings still standing and the other people — but a county losing eleven thousand people built a quarter of its housing while doing it.

refusals: Marion at 37.0 per cent and Richland at 38.0 read higher than Lima and this does not establish that they are older: 1,069 ± 235 of 2,886 ± 242 and 930 ± 195 of 2,449 ± 168 leave all three indistinguishable.
This does not establish why the housing was built where it was.

nodes.label: Allen County housing units, occupancy, tenure and value, 2023

properties.method: Tables B25002, B25003, B25077 and B25064 of the 2023 five-year file, joined on `GEO_ID`. Shares are computed here and medians are published. [verified] Owner-occupancy is of *occupied* units, so its denominator is 40,928 and not 44,697.
properties.parameter: housing units, occupancy status, tenure, median value and median gross rent

blocks.text: Housing units, vacancy, owner-occupancy, median value and median gross rent for the county, its thirteen civil subdivisions, the state and the nation. [verified] — [American Community Survey](../../catalog/census-acs-summary-file.md), 2023 five-year estimates.

**The county looks American and neither of its halves does.** Allen County is 68.3 per cent owner-occupied against 65.0 nationally — an unremarkable figure made of Lima at 46.4 per cent and twelve townships between 72.0 and 91.0, the city being the only subdivision below 70. [verified] — same source.

**Lima holds 35.4 per cent of the county's housing and 48.2 per cent of its empty housing**, 1,817 vacant units of 3,769. [verified] Four figures close exactly against the county's own row — 44,697 units, 40,928 occupied, 3,769 vacant, 27,960 owner-occupied — so the thirteen subdivisions partition the county four more times. [verified]

**A house in Shawnee Township is worth 2.2 times a house in Lima**, $210,200 against $95,900, on a combined margin of $17,965 for a gap of $114,300; the city's median value is 31.6 per cent of the nation's. [verified]

Perry Township's 17.0 per cent is the highest figure in the vacancy column, and this does not establish that it is the county's emptiest place: 290 vacant units ± 130 puts the rate between 9.4 and 24.7 per cent, straddling Lima's 11.5. [verified] The dashes are the file's unavailable-value sentinel and not a low rent. See [a survey is not a count](../../decisions/a-survey-is-not-a-count.yml).

refusals: Perry Township's 17.0 per cent is the highest figure in the vacancy column, and this does not establish that it is the county's emptiest place: 290 vacant units ± 130 puts the rate between 9.4 and 24.7 per cent, straddling Lima's 11.5.

properties.method: Sum of block-level `HU100` from the 2020 Census redistricting file, as served by TIGERweb. Total units, occupied and vacant together. [verified]
properties.parameter: total housing units

blocks.text: The county's total housing units at the 2020 census, summed over all 3,552 blocks. [verified] — [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md), 2020 vintage block layer, field `HU100`.

Against [the enumeration](allen-county-population-2020-census.yml) of 102,206 that is 2.29 people per housing unit. The figure varies across the county's thirteen civil subdivisions from 2.19 in [Lima](../place/lima.yml) and [American Township](../place/american-township.yml) to 2.57 in [Amanda](../place/amanda-township.yml) and [Richland](../place/richland-township.yml). [verified] — same source, by block composition.

**Both terms are now separated and the ratio has a replacement.** 40,935 of the 44,563 units were occupied and 3,628 were vacant, and 3,522 people were living outside households, which makes the county's average household **2.411 people**. [verified] — [the 2020 redistricting file](../../catalog/census-2020-redistricting-file.md), Tables H1 and P5; see [the occupancy](allen-county-occupancy-2020.yml) and [the group quarters](allen-county-group-quarters-2020.yml).

The open block that stood here named the right table and the wrong obstacle. It said the occupancy table was unavailable because TIGERweb does not serve it and the API will not release it without a key, both of which are true; what it did not consider is that the redistricting file the API is built over is a flat download that needs no key at all. [inference] The figure was one file away for two phases. This matters for a county whose [population has been falling for fifty years](../period/depopulation.yml), because a falling population that keeps its houses is a different thing from one that loses them, and Lima's vacancy rate is 11.2 per cent against 4.5 in Amanda Township.

nodes.label: Allen County household income and poverty, 2023

properties.method: 2023 five-year estimates from the table-based summary file. The twelve townships and Lima are county-subdivision and place summary levels and partition the county: they sum to 101,685 people and 12,815 below poverty, both equal to the county row. Margins are as published, at 90 per cent; combined margins are the root of the sum of squares. [verified]
properties.parameter: median household income (B19013) and poverty status (B17001)

blocks.text: Median household income and the share of people below the poverty line, for the county, its thirteen civil subdivisions, the state and the nation. [verified] — [American Community Survey](../../catalog/census-acs-summary-file.md), 2023 five-year estimates.

**Lima holds a third of the county's people and two thirds of its poor.** 35,304 of 101,685 residents — 34.7 per cent — and 8,214 of the 12,815 people below the poverty line, or 64.1 per cent. [verified] — same source. The county's twelve townships hold the other 4,601, and the two sums are exactly the county's own figures.

**Its median household income is 48 per cent of the township next door.** $43,370 against Shawnee Township's $91,134, a gap of $47,764 against a combined margin of $6,359. [verified] — same source. Against the nation it is 55 per cent, and against the county 70. [verified]

This does not establish that Lima has the lowest household income in the county. Perry Township's $53,272 is higher by $9,902 against a combined margin of $11,142, so the two cannot be ordered here. [verified] Nor is the county distinguishable from the state on poverty: 13.1 per cent against 13.2, against a combined margin of 1.2 points. [verified]

refusals: This does not establish that Lima has the lowest household income in the county.

properties.method: Read from the transportation, township and county chapters of the 1906 history, the 1921 history, and the 1917 federal directory. The 1905 figure of three counts names printed in one chapter; a fourth name appears in another chapter of the same book and is not added, because nothing establishes that it is a fourth company rather than a fourth name. [verified]
properties.parameter: interurban railway companies serving Lima

blocks.text: **The 1905 transportation chapter names three.** [The Western Ohio](../organization/western-ohio-railway.yml), completed spring 1901 and called the pioneer traction line of Northwestern Ohio; [the Fort Wayne, Van Wert & Lima](../organization/fort-wayne-van-wert-and-lima-traction-company.yml), "a close second in importance"; and the Lima & Toledo, "being projected and financed by the same gentlemen who own and control our excellent city traction system", with "a great deal of grading done". [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md).

**The township chapters of the same book name a fourth.** "The Lake Erie & Western Railroad and the Lima & Findlay traction line pass through [Richland township](../place/richland-township.yml) in a southwesterly direction", and through the village of [Beaverdam](../place/beaverdam.yml); at [Bluffton](../place/bluffton.yml), "an electric railway passes directly through Main street, starting from Toledo and ending in Cincinnati". [verified] — same source.

**A road can be running at Bluffton and unbuilt at Lima at the same time, and that resolves it.** The transportation chapter counts trains *landing passengers in Lima*; a line graded south from Findlay would appear in the township chapters as running and in the Lima count as absent. [inference] So the corpus records the north-eastern corridor as one route under three names — Lima & Findlay in 1905, Lima & Toledo in 1905, and by 1921 the Findlay end of the Western Ohio — without asserting that any two of the three are one company.

**The county chapter counts directions instead, and gets four.** "Traction lines cross the county through the county seat in four directions." [verified] — same source. West to [Delphos](../place/delphos.yml), [Elida](../place/elida.yml) and Fort Wayne; north-east through Bluffton and Beaverdam; south toward Dayton; and east, where [Lafayette](../place/lafayette.yml) in 1905 had only "our railroad, and soon-to-be traction line paralleling it". [verified] — same source. Three running and one promised is how a chapter counts four. [inference]

**By 1921 the count is two, and the sources agree on which two.** "There being two interurban railways, with their lines touching surrounding cities in every direction ... The Ohio Electric and the Western Ohio, with their freight and passenger service, open up a great deal of territory contributing to the commercial prosperity of Lima." [verified] — [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md).

**A federal census four years earlier says what the local books cannot: who owned whom.** The 1917 directory of operating electric railway companies lists the Ohio Electric as an operator, class A-Y, with the Fort Wayne, Van Wert & Lima printed in italics beneath it as a lessor, and lists the Western Ohio separately as B-X. Of the three companies named in 1905, one operates, one is leased, and the Lima & Toledo does not appear under its own name. [verified] — [Census of Electrical Industries, 1917](../../catalog/census-electrical-industries-1917.md).

nodes.label: Allen County land area by subdivision, 2000–2024

properties.method: Land and total area for all thirteen Allen County subdivisions read from the county-subdivision tables of the 2000 and 2010 Population and Housing Unit Counts volumes for Ohio, both born digital and extracted exactly rather than by OCR; annual figures from the Ohio place, county-subdivision and county gazetteer files for 2012 through 2024, converted from square metres at 2,589,988.11 m² to the square mile and 4,046.8564224 m² to the acre. [verified]
properties.parameter: land area by county subdivision

blocks.text: **The county's thirteen subdivisions, measured at two censuses and then every year for thirteen years.** Allen County is divided into twelve townships and one city that belongs to none of them, and those thirteen figures sum to the county. [verified] — [the 2000 volume](../../catalog/census-phc-3-37-ohio.md) and [the 2010 volume](../../catalog/census-cph-2-37-ohio-2010.md), county-subdivision tables, with [the gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md) for the annual series.

**The sum closes against the printed county in both years**, to a hundredth of a square mile — 404.42 against 404.43 and 402.48 against 402.50 — which is thirteen figures rounded to two places agreeing with a fourteenth. [inference] — addition performed here on [the two volumes](../../catalog/census-cph-2-37-ohio-2010.md). It closes again in the current geography: the twelve townships hold 388.927 square miles in the 2024 gazetteer and [Lima](../place/lima.yml) 13.619, together **402.546** against the county's own 402.545. [verified] — [the gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), Ohio county-subdivision, place and county files for 2024.

**Allen County's land area falls from 404.43 to 402.50 square miles between the two volumes**, and its total area does not move — 406.88 against 406.85. [verified] — the same tables. No land left this county in that decade; the county's only recorded boundary change since 1990 was a *gain*, from Putnam. [verified] — [the 2000 volume](../../catalog/census-phc-3-37-ohio.md), geographic change notes. Twelve hundred acres were reclassified from land to water on paper.

**So eleven of the twelve townships lost ground and none of them lost ground.** Every township but Spencer shows a smaller land area in 2010 than in 2000, and the three that actually gave ground to Lima — American, Bath and Perry — are not distinguishable in that column from Amanda and Marion, which gave nothing to anybody. [inference] — computed here from the two tables. Perry shows the largest fall of any subdivision, 474 acres, and Perry's real loss to Lima is somewhere inside it and cannot be recovered from it.

**Only Lima grows**, by 499 acres of land and 582 of total area, against 601 acres of annexation it reported in the same decade. [verified] — the same tables, against [the Boundary and Annexation Survey](../../catalog/census-bas-boundary-changes-ohio.md) as read in [the annexation record](allen-county-annexations-1990-2024.yml). That is the one subdivision whose area change is dominated by a real event rather than by a remeasurement, and it is dominated by it only because the event was large.

The gazetteer has published Ohio place and county-subdivision files every year since 2012, so the county's outline can be watched rather than sampled. [verified] — [the gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), 2012 through 2024.

**The clearest annexation in the whole thirteen years is a transfer of 4,483 square metres.** Between the 2021 and 2022 files Lima gains 4,483 square metres and Bath Township loses 4,484 — 1.11 acres, matched to one square metre by two rows that were computed independently. [verified] — same files. There is no record of it in [the annexation survey](../../catalog/census-bas-boundary-changes-ohio.md), whose last Lima entry is dated June 2017.

**Lima is the only municipality here whose annexations are visible at township level**, because it is the only one independent of any township: the Census Bureau tabulates Ohio villages inside the townships that contain them, so when Elida or Bluffton annexes, the township it annexes from does not change by a square metre. [inference] — the tabulation rule is [the 2010 volume's](../../catalog/census-cph-2-37-ohio-2010.md), the consequence is this corpus's. Elida gained 40.3 acres between the 2021 and 2022 files and American Township, which surrounds it, gained and lost nothing.

**And the biggest single-year jump in the series is not an annexation at all.** [Fort Shawnee](../place/fort-shawnee.yml) grows by 1,506 acres — 2.35 square miles, a fifth of Lima — between the 2012 and 2013 files, and in the same step its legal/statistical code changes from 47, village, to 57, census designated place. [verified] — same files. The village occupied 7.21 square miles at both the 2000 and 2010 censuses; the CDP drawn in its place occupies 9.51. [verified] — [the 2000](../../catalog/census-phc-3-37-ohio.md) and [2010](../../catalog/census-cph-2-37-ohio-2010.md) volumes and the 2020 gazetteer.

properties.method: Computed by the Census Bureau from the 2020 TIGER geography. A county's land area is not fixed across geographies — a later vintage may differ. [verified]
properties.parameter: land area

blocks.text: Land area of Allen County in the 2020 geography. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), national county file, field `ALAND_SQMI`. Water area is a further 4.306 square miles. [verified] — same record.
At the [2020 population base](allen-county-population-2020.yml) this is about 254 persons per square mile of land. [inference] — arithmetic this corpus's.

properties.method: Read from the Ohio agency list, selecting the county key ALLEN, which is the FBI's own assignment and not a geographic test — an agency serving two counties appears under a combined key and would be missed here. Dates are the file's `nibrs_start_date` verbatim. The population figures are each agency's own service population, which is not a census figure and does not sum to the county. [verified]
properties.parameter: law enforcement agencies reporting for Allen County

blocks.text: **Ten agencies report crime in Allen County, and the two that police most of it began last.** [verified] — [the FBI Crime Data Explorer](../../catalog/fbi-crime-data-explorer.md), Ohio agency list, county key ALLEN.
The dates are each agency's `nibrs_start_date` — when it changed from summary reporting to incident-based reporting. [verified] — same source.

**A village of nineteen hundred people converted sixteen years before the county seat.** Elida began in September 2005 and [Lima](../place/lima.yml) in January 2021. [verified] — same source. So a county-level crime series assembled from these agencies changes what it is made of in almost every year between 2004 and 2021, and changes most in the last two. [inference]

**Six of the ten are townships or a village; two are park rangers.** Three townships that ring Lima keep their own forces — [Shawnee](../place/shawnee-township.yml), [American](../place/american-township.yml) and [Perry](../place/perry-township.yml) — which is what a county looks like when its suburbs are unincorporated. [inference] — see [the townships](allen-county-outside-lima-1890-2020.yml).

**Two of the ten are held here and eight are not.** The Lima Police Department and [the Sheriff's Office](../office/allen-county-sheriff.yml) cover 34,552 and 24,079 people respectively — 58,631 of the county's 100,866, or 58 per cent. [verified] — same source and [the 2024 estimate](allen-county-population-2024.yml). The remaining eight were not fetched because the demonstration key ran out of requests, not because they are unavailable.

nodes.label: Allen County mortgage denial rates by applicant race, 2018-2024

properties.method: Rates use actions 1, 2 and 3. Race is the register's `derived_race`; 18 per cent of rows record none and are in no column here. Debt-to-income is grouped from a column that reports integers from 36 to 49 and bands elsewhere. Cells with fewer than ten white applications are dropped, which discards 17 per cent of Black applications rather than resting a rate on one or two files. [verified] Expected denials are the sum of the within-cell white rates over the matched Black applications; the standard deviation is that of the Poisson-binomial they define.
properties.parameter: mortgage denial rate by applicant race, and by race within four controls
properties.unit: ratio of observed to expected denials for Black applicants

blocks.text: Denial rates for the two races the register records in numbers this county can support, across seven years and inside every control the file carries. [verified] — [the HMDA register](../../catalog/hmda-loan-application-register.md).

**It is a pattern and not a year.** Pooled over the seven, 32.4 per cent of applications from Black applicants were denied against 17.8 per cent from white applicants, and the yearly gap runs between 5.9 and 17.0 percentage points without once reversing. [verified] — same source. The corpus opened this question saying 174 applications was one year of a small county; it is now 1,334 applications and 432 denials.

**It survives every control this register carries, taken one at a time.** Twenty-three strata across four dimensions — loan purpose, applicant income, debt-to-income and loan-to-value — and the gap is positive in all twenty-three. [verified] It is 7.7 points on a home purchase and 24.1 on a home improvement loan; 10.4 points under $30,000 of income and 4.6 above $150,000; 30.4 points in the lowest debt-to-income band and 1.1 in the 43-to-49 band; 23.0 points below 60 per cent loan-to-value and 3.3 between 90 and 100. The gap is widest where denial is rarest and compresses where it is common, which is what a ceiling does to a difference and not a finding about risk. [inference]

**Taken together rather than one at a time, it is a factor of 1.68.** Sorting every decision into a cell of loan purpose by income band by debt-to-income band by loan-to-value band gives 311 cells holding 955 Black applications — 83 per cent of those with all four controls present — in which at least ten white applications also sit. Those 955 drew **223 denials against 132.5 expected at the white rate in the same cells**, a ratio of 1.68 and 9.3 standard deviations from the null. [verified] — computed here from the same source. The same arithmetic run on white applications returns exactly 1.00, which is the check that it is arithmetic and not a thumb.

**Composition is real and it is small.** Inside those 311 cells the unadjusted rates are 23.4 per cent against 12.2, a gap of 11.1 points; reweighting the white rate to the Black applicants' own mix of loan purpose, income, debt and equity moves the comparison to 13.9, which closes 15 per cent of it. [verified] Black applicants in this county do apply for different loans on different terms, and that is not most of the difference.

refusals: This does not establish that any applicant was treated differently.

nodes.label: Life expectancy at birth in Allen County's census tracts, 2010–2015

properties.method: NCHS estimates for 2010–2015, on 2010 census tracts. The join to Lima is by tract identifier to the 2020 tract file and then by that tract's published internal point against the city's 2020 boundary polygon — so it is a statement about where a tract's centre falls and not about how many of its people live in the city. Two of the thirty tracts have no 2020 identifier and are excluded from every comparison, and are in the range and the median. Medians and weighted means are this corpus's arithmetic; every input is NCHS's or the Census Bureau's. [inference]
properties.parameter: life expectancy at birth, by census tract
properties.unit: years between the county's highest and lowest tract

blocks.text: How long people born here can expect to live, and how far it varies inside one county of a hundred thousand. [verified] — [NCHS USALEEP](../../catalog/nchs-usaleep.md), which builds an abridged life table for each census tract from death certificates and population.

**Thirty tracts, and 13.7 years between the highest and the lowest.** From **69.1** years in tract `39003012600` to **82.8** in `39003011300`, on a median of 78.0. [verified] — same source. The two ends are more than five combined standard errors apart, on published errors of 1.72 each, so the spread is not an artefact of small counts.

**A tract whose centre is inside Lima expects about five fewer years than one outside it.** Thirteen of the twenty-eight tracts this file can be joined to the 2020 geography have their internal point inside the city; their median is **72.7** years against **79.0** for the fifteen outside, and weighted by tract population, 73.9 against 79.1. [inference] — computed here from [the same file](../../catalog/nchs-usaleep.md) and [TIGERweb's place boundary](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md).

**The two groups barely overlap.** The highest Lima tract is 78.2 and the lowest tract outside the city is 74.0, so eleven of the thirteen inside sit below every tract outside but one. [inference] — computed here.

**Sixteen of the county's thirty-five tracts have their internal point inside Lima**, which is the same number the corpus reached by a different method — the sixteen whose 2020 block population is majority Lima. [verified] — same boundary file and [the lending register](allen-county-home-lending-2018-2024.yml). Two routes to the same count is not proof that they name the same sixteen, and this corpus has not checked that they do. [inference]

**The county's own figure is not stated here.** Population-weighted across the twenty-eight tracts that join, life expectancy is 76.9 years — but those tracts hold 82,484 of the county's 102,206 people, because two 2010 tracts were split in the 2020 redraw and seven 2020 tracts have no 2010 row. [inference] — computed here. Four fifths of a county is not a county, and NCHS publishes no county figure in this file.

**Against Ohio.** The state's 2,772 tracts run from 60.0 to 89.2 years on a median of 76.9, so Allen County's median sits half a year above the state's and its range is well inside it. [verified] — same file, all Ohio rows.

properties.method: Census of Agriculture, inventory taken at December 31 of the census year and sales for the calendar year, read from NASS's Quick Stats bulk county file and checked against the published county profile, which prints the same 2022 and 2017 inventories. `(D)` marks a cell NASS suppressed to avoid disclosing an individual operation and is not a small number; nothing here infers a value for one. Comparisons to 1910 set a count of animals on farms and off them against a count on farms alone, which in 1910 differed by about one per cent for swine. [inference]
properties.parameter: livestock inventory, Allen County

blocks.text: What the county keeps, and how few places keep it. [verified] — [USDA Census of Agriculture](../../catalog/usda-census-of-agriculture.md), county files.

**The hogs multiplied more than sevenfold while the places keeping them halved.** 31,741 head on 59 operations in 2002 against 235,800 on 28 in 2022 — an average herd of 538 becoming one of 8,421. [inference] — computed here from the five censuses. Nothing else moved: cattle ended where they began, and sheep, horses and milk cows are where they were or lower.
**The count, five censuses in one line.** 31,741 hogs in 2002, 62,910 in 2007, 80,372 in 2012, 178,781 in 2017 and 235,800 in 2022, kept on 59, 60, 46, 56 and 28 operations. [verified] — same source.

**Three quarters of the hogs sold were raised for someone else.** Of 377,816 head sold in 2022, 281,194 were produced under production contract on twelve operations — the census's own term for an animal fed by one party and owned by another. [verified] — same source. In 2017 it was 144,480 of 324,947 on twenty-one operations, so the contracted share went from 44 to 74 per cent while the number of operations doing it fell by nine.

**Hogs are now two fifths of everything the county sells.** $75,254,000 of $240,849,000, against $7,488,000 of $41,264,000 in 2002. [verified] — same source. The county ranks 4th in Ohio for hog sales and 23rd for agricultural sales altogether. [verified] — [the 2022 county profile](../../catalog/usda-census-of-agriculture.md).

**Against 1910: the swine outnumbered the people then by 59,695 to 56,580, and now by 235,800 to 100,866.** [inference] — computed here from [the 1910 animals](allen-county-domestic-animals-1910.yml) and [the 2024 estimate](allen-county-population-2024.yml). Two and a third hogs a head, where there had been one and a twentieth.

**Everything else in that 1910 count is gone.** 14,676 horses became 316; 41,240 sheep and goats became 1,499; 21,336 cattle became 8,576; and the 10,671 dairy cows became a figure the census will not print, because eight operations hold it and one of them is large enough that publishing the total would disclose it. [verified] — same sources, and Appendix A, which states the suppression rules. This corpus withholds figures for the same reason and by hand; see [what may leave the repository](../../decisions/what-may-leave-the-repository.yml).

properties.method: BEA CAEMP25S for 1969–2000 (SIC line 400) and CAEMP25N for 2001–2022 (NAICS line 500), read from the Ohio county files at GeoFIPS 39003. BEA counts jobs, including proprietors, part-time work, farm and government, where County Business Patterns counts employees of private establishments; the two are separate programmes and not one series. They agree on shape where they overlap, both placing the recent trough at the end of the 2000s and a recovery of about a fifth since. [verified]
properties.parameter: manufacturing employment, Allen County, all jobs

blocks.text: Fifty-four years of the mechanism this county's history is told through. [verified] — [BEA Regional Economic Accounts](../../catalog/bea-county-employment.md), county employment by industry.

**Manufacturing employment in Allen County peaked in 1973, at 18,400.** [verified] — same source. Not in 1969, and not before this corpus's [deindustrialization](../period/deindustrialization.yml) is said to begin. The county's factories were still adding workers into the late 1970s: 18,389 in 1979, within eleven of the peak six years earlier.

**The trough is 7,775, in 2009 — a fall of 58 per cent from the peak, across thirty-six years.** [verified] — same source. Employment has risen since, to 8,715 in 2022, and has not been below 7,775 in any year on this series.

**1986 was a recovery year, not a stage of the fall.** Manufacturing bottomed at 14,349 in 1982, rose four years running to 17,163 in 1986, and only then began the long decline. [verified] — same source. That matters because it is where [the corpus's other series](allen-county-manufacturing-employment-1986-2022.yml) opens, and because the last phase described this span, while calling it open, as a fall already under way. See [naming a gap is not leaving it empty](../../decisions/naming-a-gap-is-not-leaving-it-empty.yml).
**Almost the whole decline is after 1986.** From the 1973 peak to 1986 manufacturing lost 1,237 jobs, 7 per cent; from 1986 to 2009 it lost 9,388, 55 per cent. [inference] — computed here.

properties.method: County Business Patterns county files, one year in five from 1986. Checked by arithmetic self-closure: in 1986 the ten SIC divisions sum to the printed county total exactly, and in 2022 the twenty NAICS sectors do the same. Years between leave residuals of 2 to 239, each year carrying at least one sector with suppressed employment. Corroborated at the recent end by [the QCEW](../../catalog/bls-qcew.md), which gives 8,661 for 2023 against 8,573 for 2022. Government, the self-employed and farms are excluded throughout. [verified]
properties.parameter: manufacturing employment, Allen County, private employers

blocks.text: The measurement this corpus named a period after and did not have. [verified] — [County Business Patterns](../../catalog/census-county-business-patterns.md), private employers.

**Manufacturing employment in Allen County fell by 55 per cent between 1986 and 2010, from 15,762 to 7,127.** [verified] — same source. That is [deindustrialization](../period/deindustrialization.yml) measured for the first time in this corpus, in the period named for it.

**And then it stopped, and reversed.** From the 2010 trough manufacturing rose to 8,917 in 2020 and stood at 8,573 in 2022 — up a fifth from the bottom. [verified] — same source. The county's named mechanism of decline stopped operating around 2010 and the county kept shrinking. [inference]

**Total private employment peaked in 2005, not in 1986.** It rose from 45,917 to 52,699 while manufacturing was losing six thousand jobs, then fell to 42,814 by 2022. [verified] — same source. So the county replaced its manufacturing losses for twenty years and stopped being able to. [inference]

**After 2010 the losses were not in manufacturing.** Private employment fell 3,709 between 2010 and 2022 while manufacturing *rose* 1,446, so everything else fell by 5,155. [inference] — computed here.

**The sentence that stood here was wrong and is the reason this node is no longer the corpus's main employment series.** It said County Business Patterns "begins in 1986 with manufacturing already at 15,762 and already falling", and called this "the second half of a fall". A BEA series reaching back to 1969 shows 1986 as a recovery year — manufacturing bottomed at 14,349 in 1982 and had climbed four years running by 1986 — and shows the peak at 18,400 in 1973. [verified] — [the long series](allen-county-manufacturing-employment-1969-2022.yml). Nor was it the second half: 93 per cent of the fall from peak to trough happened after 1986. [inference] See [naming a gap is not leaving it empty](../../decisions/naming-a-gap-is-not-leaving-it-empty.yml).

nodes.label: When Allen County's municipalities were incorporated, 1842–1904

properties.method: Read from the full text of three county histories on archive.org, the 1885 book in two independent scans, and checked against the county's own cities-and-villages page. `as_of` is the latest founding date the corpus can state and not the query date, because the count is of corporations founded by then. Where two dates exist the table prints both and the `erected` property on each corporation carries the authorising one. Dates given only as a year are printed as a year; nothing here is promoted to a day. [inference]
properties.parameter: municipal corporations in Allen County with a recorded founding date

blocks.text: **Eight of the county's nine municipal corporations have a founding date, and every one of them was in a book this corpus already held.** [verified] — [1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md), [1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md) and [1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md).

**"Incorporated" is three different legal acts here and the corpus's one field flattens them.** Lima, Lafayette, Cairo and Beaverdam were organized on the county commissioners' authority, on a petition; Delphos and Spencerville by an act of incorporation; Bluffton by a ballot on 17 August 1861 that decided both the incorporation and the name. [verified] — same sources. **The field `erected` records the earliest of these, and the corpus says which kind it was in each node.** [inference] — see [a file has more than one date](../../decisions/a-file-has-more-than-one-date.yml).

**Authorisation and first election are not the same year twice over.** Lafayette was authorised 3 September 1867 and elected on 13 March 1868; Lima was petitioned for in 1841 and organized on 29 March 1842. The county's own website prints one date for each village, and for Lafayette it is the later one. [verified] — [the county's site](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md).

**Every one of the eight has a named first mayor in a nineteenth- or early-twentieth-century book, and this corpus holds a node for exactly one of them.** [verified] — same sources; the exception is [H. D. V. Williams](../person/henry-d-v-williams.yml).

**The four the corpus was missing were in books it had read for other things.** Delphos, Bluffton and Cairo were retrieved from the 1885, 1906 and 1921 histories in this phase; Lima's date had been held since the settlements phase and sat in prose without ever reaching the corporation's own field. [inference] — see [a count of absences is not an agenda](../../decisions/a-count-of-absences-is-not-an-agenda.yml).

**The gap that is left is one village and it is bounded.** Harrod's incorporation is in none of the three histories: the 1885 book names it as one of Auglaize Township's four post offices and gives no corporation; the 1910 census returns *Harrod village* at 269 people in 1890; the 1906 book prints a tax valuation for "Harrod corporation" in 1904. So the corporation existed by 1 June 1890 and not, on the 1885 book's silence, before that book went to press. [inference] — [the 1910 supplement](allen-county-townships-1890-1910.yml) and the histories above. The county's own site says 1884, which sits inside that window and is not corroborated here. [verified] — [the county's site](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md).

nodes.label: Allen County on the National Register, 1966–2004

properties.method: Layers 0 and 1 of the NPS `nrhp_locations` map service queried on `State='OHIO' AND County='Allen'` and unioned — 26 points and 3 polygons, no property in both. Polygon centroids computed here from the returned rings. Each of the 29 resulting coordinates put to the Allen County GIS township and section layers. Certification dates are the file's two-digit years read as 19xx above 30 and 20xx below. [verified]
properties.parameter: properties listed on the National Register of Historic Places

blocks.text: **Twenty-nine listings, and seventeen of them are one year.** Everything in Allen County on the National Register of Historic Places, with the day the Keeper signed each one. [verified] — [the NPS spatial dataset](../../catalog/nrhp-national-register.md), points and polygons queried together on `State='OHIO' AND County='Allen'`.

Written out: **twenty-nine listings between 15 October 1966 and 27 October 2004 — twenty-six buildings, two structures and one historic district — of which sixteen were signed on a single day, 7 October 1982, under the Lima Multiple Resource Area submission.** [verified] — same source. Seven listings precede 1982 and five follow it.

**The sixteen are a document, not a decade.** More than half of what this county has on the federal register arrived in one nomination, and the corpus reads that the way it read [its own sheriff roster](../../decisions/eighty-eight-rows-are-not-eighty-eight-nodes.yml): a list can look long and be one act. Between the Barr Hotel in May 1986 and Lima Stadium in March 2002 nothing at all was added, and nothing has been added in the twenty-one years since the last. [inference] — computed here from the certification dates.

Every one of the twenty-nine falls inside the county's own map, checked a point at a time. [verified] — [Allen County GIS](../../catalog/allen-county-gis-rest.md), point-in-polygon against the township and survey-section layers.

**Twenty of the twenty-nine stand in one square mile.** Survey section 31 of T3S R7E — downtown Lima — holds the courthouse, the theatre, the stadium and every block building of the 1982 submission. [verified] — same join. **Ten of the county's twelve townships hold nothing**, and neither does any village but Delphos: Bluffton, Elida, Cairo, Harrod, Lafayette, Beaverdam, Spencerville and Fort Shawnee have no listing of any kind. [verified] — same source against [the county's places](../place/allen-county.yml).

**Two listings name a town they do not stand in**, and the file says so in a field of its own. The Deep Cut is filed under Spencerville and lies in Spencer Township; the Griffith Breese Farm is filed under Lima, at 2875 Fort Amanda Rd, and lies in Shawnee Township. Both carry `Vicinity: True`. [verified] — same source. The federal register keeps a column for exactly the distinction this corpus had to argue for from a refinery — see [an address is not a municipality](../site/lima-refinery.yml).

**Allen County has a single National Historic Landmark and it is the Deep Cut**, a canal excavation two miles south of Spencerville, listed 15 October 1966 — the day the National Register began, when the existing Landmarks were entered into it as a body. [verified] — [the NPS dataset](../../catalog/nrhp-national-register.md), `Is_NHL` set on one of twenty-nine. It is also the county's oldest listing by eight years and the only one that is not a building or a district. See [the canal](../site/miami-and-erie-canal.yml).

**No industry.** Not the [locomotive works](../site/lima-locomotive-works-plant.yml), which built Shays and Berkshires and gave the county its name in the trade; not [the refinery](../site/lima-refinery.yml), running since 1886; not [the tank plant](../site/lima-army-tank-plant.yml) or [the Ford engine plant](../site/ford-lima-engine-plant.yml). [verified] — the county's whole list above. A county whose nineteenth and twentieth centuries were made of iron, oil and rolling stock has twenty-six commercial and domestic buildings and a stadium on the federal register, and nothing it made anything in. [inference] — observed here; see [a register records nominations](../../decisions/a-register-records-nominations.yml).

**One thing in this county has been judged eligible for the Register and is not on it.** The federal bridge inventory codes the 1909 Hay Road structure over the Auglaize River as eligible, and every other one of the county's 364 bridges as not applicable; no bridge appears among the twenty-nine listings above. [verified] — [the National Bridge Inventory](../../catalog/national-bridge-inventory.md); see [the Hay Road bridge](../site/hay-road-bridge.yml). Eligibility is a determination made in the course of federal review, and a nomination is a thing somebody files — which is what [a register records nominations](../../decisions/a-register-records-nominations.yml) says, met here from the other side. [inference]

refusals: The dataset carries `STATUS: Listed` on all twenty-nine and would simply omit a delisted property, so it cannot answer its own question.

properties.method: Births minus deaths, summed over the four full estimate years 2021–2024. The partial year 2020 — April to June, 293 births and 283 deaths — is excluded as not comparable. [verified]
properties.parameter: natural population change, four years to 2024

blocks.text: Across the four full years 2021 to 2024 the county recorded **4,763 births and 5,269 deaths** — a natural change of **−506**. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md), county file, fields `BIRTHS` and `DEATHS`.
Year by year the natural change was −213, −259, −41 and **+7**: deaths exceeded births in 2021, 2022 and 2023, and births exceeded deaths again in 2024. [verified] — same source.

**Deaths moved and births did not.** Births ran 1,171, 1,190, 1,202 and 1,200 — flat within three per cent. Deaths ran 1,384, 1,449, 1,243 and 1,193, peaking in 2022 and falling by 256 over the following two years. So the natural decrease of these four years is a deaths story, and the shape of it — a spike in 2021–2022 subsiding by 2024 — is the shape the pandemic left in county death counts across the United States. [inference] The corpus holds no cause-of-death data and cannot attribute it.

properties.method: Domestic plus international net migration, summed over the four full estimate years 2021–2024. The partial year 2020 is excluded as not comparable. [verified]
properties.parameter: net migration, four years to 2024

blocks.text: Across the four full years 2021 to 2024 the county's net migration was **−793**: a domestic net loss of **1,217** against an international net gain of **424**. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md), county file, fields `DOMESTICMIG` and `INTERNATIONALMIG`.

**The two components move in opposite directions and one of them is accelerating.** International migration ran 26, 100, 133 and 165 — rising every year without exception. Domestic migration ran −213, −530, −317 and −157, worst in 2022 and shrinking since. [verified] — same source.

In 2024 they crossed: 165 arriving from abroad against 157 leaving for elsewhere in the United States, for a net migration of **+8** — the first non-negative year in the series. [verified] — same source.

nodes.label: Allen County housing occupancy and household size, 2020

properties.method: Table H1, Occupancy Status, from the Ohio file of the 2020 Census Redistricting Data Summary File (P.L. 94-171), file segment 02, the last three fields of each record. Summed from the 3,552 block records for county 39003, joined to the geographic header on LOGRECNO and grouped by the header's county-subdivision code. [verified] Household size is population less group-quarters population, over occupied units, computed here for each subdivision. [inference] It is the definition the Census Bureau uses for average household size, and it is stated here rather than taken from a published table because no published table at this geography is held. Both closures were checked: the thirteen subdivision populations sum to the county's 102,206 and their units to 44,563, with no residual.
properties.parameter: occupied housing units, Allen County

blocks.text: The table this corpus asked for two phases ago and could not get: how many of Allen County's 44,563 housing units were lived in on 1 April 2020. **40,935 were occupied and 3,628 were vacant** — a vacancy rate of 8.14 per cent. [verified] — [the 2020 redistricting file](../../catalog/census-2020-redistricting-file.md), Table H1, summed from block records.

**With the group quarters count beside it the county's household size falls out exactly.** 3,522 people were not in households at all, so 98,684 were, in 40,935 occupied units: **2.411 people per household**. [inference] — computed here against [the group quarters](allen-county-group-quarters-2020.yml).
[verified] — same file, summed by county subdivision; household size computed here. The columns close on the county: the populations sum to 102,206 and the units to 44,563.

**One in nine housing units in Lima had nobody in it.** 11.2 per cent against 8.14 for the county and 4.5 for Amanda Township, and no township comes within three points of the city. [inference] — computed here. See [Lima](../place/lima.yml), whose emptiness this corpus has described from American Community Survey estimates and can now state from a count.

**And Lima's households are the smallest in the county.** 2.344 people against Amanda Township's 2.691, a spread of 0.35 of a person across thirteen subdivisions. [inference] — computed here. The city is not merely emptier by units; the units that are occupied hold fewer people.

**This settles a reading the corpus had refused.** The persons-per-unit ratio it had been using put group-quarters residents in the numerator and vacant units in the denominator, so it could not be read as household size. Both terms are now separated and the true figure is available for every subdivision. [inference] — see [the housing units](allen-county-housing-units-2020.yml), whose open block this closes.

properties.method: Subtraction of the city count from the county count at each census, both from Census publications this corpus already holds and cites. Not a published figure: no source states it, and it is tagged as this corpus's inference throughout. The `value` above is the series maximum. Boundaries are as reported at each census and are known to have moved in 1902, 1903, 1905, 1906, 1944 and between 1980 and 1990 — twice out of the city and four times into it. [inference]
properties.parameter: county population less the city of Lima, decennial

blocks.text: The county's population with [Lima](../place/lima.yml) taken out of it, at fourteen censuses. [inference] — subtraction performed here; every input is a Census count already held by this corpus.

Written out: **the county outside Lima held 24,663 people in 1890, 26,253 in 1900, 26,072 in 1910, 26,877 in 1920, 27,132 in 1930, 28,592 in 1940, 37,937 in 1950, 52,654 in 1960, 57,410 in 1970, 64,414 in 1980, 64,206 in 1990, 68,157 in 2000, 67,560 in 2010 and 66,627 in 2020.** [inference] — same subtraction. County figures from [1940–1990](allen-county-population-1940-1990.yml), [2000](allen-county-population-2000.yml), [2010](allen-county-population-2010.yml) and [the 2020 census count](allen-county-population-2020-census.yml), with 1930 from [the 1950 townships table](allen-county-townships-1930-1950.yml) and 1890 to 1910 from [the 1910 one](allen-county-townships-1890-1910.yml); Lima from [1850–1960](lima-population-1850-1960.yml), [1970–1990](lima-population-1970-1990.yml), [2000](lima-population-2000.yml), [2010](lima-population-2010.yml) and [2020](lima-population-2020-census.yml). The 2020 pair is census-to-census; the estimates base gives 102,217 and 35,531 for the same date and would put this series' last term at 66,686.

**Four of the fourteen terms are measured as well as derived.** The townships in [the 1950 volume's Table 6](allen-county-townships-1930-1950.yml) sum to 27,132 for 1930 and 28,592 for 1940, and the twelve outside Ottawa in [the 1910 supplement](allen-county-townships-1890-1910.yml) sum to 24,657 for 1890 and 26,072 for 1910 — the same numbers this subtraction produces, from sources that never perform it. [verified] — those tables. The 1890 pair differs by six, and correctly: the twelve exclude Ottawa Township, which held six people outside Lima city that year and none afterwards.

**The 1921 history performs this subtraction for 1920 and gets it wrong by a thousand.** Listing the county's nine incorporated places — Beaver Dam 394, Bluffton 1,950, Delphos (in Allen County) 3,169, Elida 509, Harrod 389, Lafayette 383, Lima 41,306, Spencerville 1,543, West Cairo 380 — it concludes "that out of a total population of 68,203 in Allen County, only 17,180 persons live in the country". [verified] — [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md). Those nine sum to 50,023, and 68,203 less 50,023 is **18,180**. [inference] — computed here.

**Two errors, and the corpus can separate them.** Its Lima figure is 41,306 where the census prints 41,326, twenty low; correcting that gives 50,043 and a remainder of **18,160**. And 18,160 is what this table's own 1920 term gives independently — 26,877 less the eight non-Lima villages' 8,717. [inference] — same computation, against [Lima's series](lima-population-1850-1960.yml). **Two routes agree on 18,160 and the book prints 17,180**, which is a transposition of its own subtraction and not a different definition.

**The first fifty years of this series are almost flat, and that is the finding.** From 24,663 in 1890 to 28,592 in 1940 the county outside Lima grew 16 per cent, while the county grew 80 per cent and Lima 180. [inference] — computed here. Then it reversed: the balance is up 133 per cent since 1940 and the city is down a third since 1970. **Lima's share of the county peaked in 1940 at 61.0 per cent, having been 39.3 in 1890 and 34.8 in 2020** — a rise and a fall of almost exactly the same size, hinged on one census. [inference]

**This answers a question [depopulation](../period/depopulation.yml) left open.** That node said the ring around Lima grew while the city emptied, and that "when the ring turned is not established here". **It turned between 2000 and 2010.** The county outside Lima grew at every census from 1910 to 2000 except one, and has fallen at the two since. It fell once before that too, between 1900 and 1910. [inference]

**So the county has three peaks and they are thirty years apart.** Lima peaked in 1970, the county as a whole in 1980, and the county outside Lima in 2000. [inference] — from the three series above. A single line labelled "Allen County" hides all of this: from 1970 to 2000 the county was falling and two thirds of it was growing.

**The exception is the decade the boundary moved, and it moves the right way.** Between 1980 and 1990 the balance fell by 208 — the only fall before 2000 — and it is the one decade in which Lima is known to have annexed, from American, Bath and Shawnee townships. [verified] — [1990 Census, Population and Housing Unit Counts, Ohio](../../catalog/census-cph-2-37-ohio.md), Geographic Change Notes. Annexation moves people from the balance into the city without anybody moving house, so it pushes this series down and the city's up. The 1980s fall is therefore an upper bound on a decline and may be no decline at all. [inference]

**Lima's share of the county rose at every census from 1890 to 1940 and has fallen at every one since, including the three at which the city grew.** 39.3% in 1890 to 61.0% in 1940, then down to 34.8% in 2020, through a decade in which the city gained 5,535 people and still lost four points of share. [inference] — computed above. The county was redistributing before it was declining, and the two processes are seventy years out of phase.

**What the corroboration reaches and does not.** Between 2000 and 2010 the Census Bureau's own "balance of county" — everything outside *every* incorporated place, a narrower base than this one — fell from 50,809 to 50,048. [verified] — [Census Intercensal Estimates, 2000–2010](../../catalog/census-intercensal-2000-2010.md). Same direction, different denominator: the difference between the two is Delphos, Bluffton, Spencerville, Elida and the smaller villages, which this series keeps and that one removes.

**Lima did annex after 2000, and the last two terms of this series are affected by it.** The city took 601 acres in eight annexations between June 2002 and December 2009, and one more in June 2017. [verified] — [the Boundary and Annexation Survey](../../catalog/census-bas-boundary-changes-ohio.md), as read in [the annexation record](allen-county-annexations-1990-2024.yml). So the 2010 and 2020 terms subtract a Lima about a square mile larger than the 2000 term's, and the balance of the county is correspondingly a square mile smaller: the fall outside Lima since 2000 is overstated and the fall inside it understated. [inference] — computed here. How much is not recoverable from the area figures, because those cannot be differenced across censuses; see [the control is the figure that cannot move](../../decisions/the-control-is-the-figure-that-cannot-move.yml).

properties.method: Decennial census counts as compiled in 1906 from published returns, with the 1906 figure an estimate by the compilers. Not read from a Census Bureau publication. [verified]
properties.parameter: total resident population, decennial

blocks.text: The county's decennial census counts for its first seventy years. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md), both scans agreeing figure for figure.

**The oil decade is visible in it.** The largest gain of the seven is 1880 to 1890, **9,330 people or 29.7 per cent**, and the 1906 compilers attribute it without hesitation: "the marked increase in the decade preceding 1890 is accounted for by the discovery of oil in 1885. During this decade the city of Lima doubled her population." [verified] — same source. That is the demographic signature of [the strike](../event/lima-oil-strike.yml), from men who watched it happen.

**The series is not continuous across 1848 and the corpus will not smooth it.** The first two figures describe a county that included eight townships now in Auglaize County and excluded four that are in Allen today, and the [reorganization of February 28, 1848](../event/reorganization-of-1848.yml) cost it a net 138 square miles. So 578 and 9,079 count different ground from everything after them. [inference]

properties.method: Read from Table 3 by counting column positions against the header printed earlier in the document, and checked against the 1970 count this corpus already held from a different Census product. The `value` above is the series maximum, not its last term. [verified]
properties.parameter: total resident population, decennial

blocks.text: The county's decennial counts for the six censuses this corpus was missing. [verified] — [1990 Census, Population and Housing Unit Counts, Ohio](../../catalog/census-cph-2-37-ohio.md), Table 3.

**The county's peak is 1980, not 1970, and the corpus has been saying 1970 since genesis.** 112,241 against 111,144 — a rise of 1,097 across the decade the corpus described as the start of a decline. [verified] — same source. Every figure this corpus held began at 1970 or later, so the sentence "no reversal at any measured point" in [depopulation](../period/depopulation.yml) was true of the data and false of the county. See [that node](../period/depopulation.yml), which now says so.

**The 1970 figure matches an unrelated source exactly**, which is how the reading of these columns was checked: 111,144 here and 111,144 in the [1970–1979 county estimates](../../catalog/census-county-estimates-1970s.md), from a different Census product. [verified]

**Housing grew when population did not.** Between 1970 and 1990 the county gained 7,281 housing units and lost 1,389 people. [inference] — computed from the figures above. Household size fell across the United States over those decades, so this is not peculiar to Allen County; what it does mean is that the county's building stock and its population stopped moving together around 1970, and the corpus's account of decline has until now been a population account only.

**1930 is no longer a gap: 69,419.** [verified] — [1950 Census, Number of Inhabitants, Ohio](../../catalog/census-1950-number-of-inhabitants-ohio.md), Tables 5 and 6, which give it twice. So the county ran 68,203 in 1920, **69,419 in 1930** and 73,303 in 1940 — a gain of 1,216 in the 1920s and 3,884 in the 1930s. [inference] — computed here; the source prints the second as 5.6 per cent and this corpus's arithmetic agrees. The county grew three times faster through the Depression decade than through the boom before it, which is the opposite of the shape the decades' reputations suggest and is [true of Lima too](lima-population-1850-1960.yml), at 2.3 per cent then 5.7.

**And 1910 is closed too: 56,580.** [verified] — [Abstract of the Thirteenth Census, Supplement for Ohio](../../catalog/census-1910-abstract-supplement-ohio.md); see [the 1890–1910 divisions](allen-county-townships-1890-1910.yml). **The county now has a count for every decennial census from 1830 to 2020 and an estimate for 2024, with no gaps.** Twenty-one observations, every one from a published table. [verified] The two figures that were open when this node was written are both closed, one phase apart, and both by volumes older than the one this node is named for.

properties.method: Decennial enumeration, unrounded. The estimate columns in the same file are rounded to hundreds; this column is not. [verified]

blocks.text: The 1970 decennial census count for Allen County. [verified] — [Preliminary Estimates of the Intercensal Population of Counties, 1970–1979](../../catalog/census-county-estimates-1970s.md), first block, column headed `Census 1970`, FIPS 39003.

This is the earliest population figure in the corpus and the anchor the [depopulation](../period/depopulation.yml) claim rests on. Against the [2024 estimate](allen-county-population-2024.yml) of 100,866 the county has lost 10,278 people, or 9.2%, over 54 years. [inference] — arithmetic this corpus's; both figures verified.

blocks.text: The April 1, 2000 estimates base for Allen County. [verified] — [Census Intercensal Estimates, 2000–2010](../../catalog/census-intercensal-2000-2010.md), county file, field `ESTIMATESBASE2000`.
An intercensal series is fitted between two known censuses rather than projected from one, so this figure is the 2000 enumeration as revised with the 2010 count in hand. [verified]

properties.parameter: total resident population
