The same value appears in the Vintage 2020 county file, a separate release built for a different purpose. [verified] Two files agreeing on a census count is weak confirmation — they rest on the same enumeration — but a disagreement would have been strong evidence of a transcription error, and there was none.

nodes.label: Allen County population, 2020 census

properties.method: Sum of block-level `POP100` from the 2020 Census redistricting file, as served by TIGERweb. Not a modelled figure and not subject to later revision. [verified]
properties.parameter: total resident population

blocks.text: The 2020 decennial enumeration for Allen County as published for redistricting, obtained by summing `POP100` over all 3,552 census blocks in the county. [verified] — [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md), 2020 vintage block layer.

The figure is a sum and not a published total, so it carries the sum's own check: the Allen County portions of the twelve school districts covering the county also sum to 102,206, from a different partition of the same blocks. [verified] — [2020 Census Block Assignment Files](../../catalog/census-block-assignment-2020.md).

**This count was taken inside a federally declared disaster.** The COVID-19 incident window for Allen County runs 20 January 2020 to 11 May 2023, and Census Day is 1 April 2020. [verified] — [the COVID-19 declaration](../event/allen-county-declared-for-covid-19-2020.yml). The corpus does not assert that the enumeration was affected — nothing held here would establish it — and records the overlap because a reader of this figure should know it and could not otherwise learn it here. [inference]

refusals: The corpus does not assert that the enumeration was affected — nothing held here would establish it — and records the overlap because a reader of this figure should know it and could not otherwise learn it here.

properties.method: Decennial enumeration as revised for the Vintage 2024 estimates base. A later vintage may revise it again. [verified]
properties.parameter: total resident population

blocks.text: The Census Bureau's April 1, 2020 estimates base for Allen County. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates, Vintage 2024](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md), county file, field `ESTIMATESBASE2020`.

This is the 2020 enumeration as subsequently revised, not a modeled estimate — which is why it is the right figure to anchor a series on and the wrong one to describe as "the 2020 census count" without qualification. That caution is now measured: [the enumeration itself](allen-county-population-2020-census.yml) is 102,206, eleven fewer. [verified] — [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md), summed over the county's 3,552 blocks.

blocks.text: The Vintage 2024 estimate for Allen County. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates, Vintage 2024](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md), county file, field `POPESTIMATE2024`.

Against the [2020 base](allen-county-population-2020.yml) of 102,217 this is a fall of 1,351, or about 1.3% over four years. [inference] — the arithmetic is this corpus's; both figures are verified. The intervening years in the same file run 102,137 / 101,800 / 101,086 / 100,851, so the 2024 figure is a slight rise on 2023 rather than a continuation of the fall.

properties.method: Summed by candidate over the county's 88 precincts. The 2016 file carries no registered-voter or ballots-cast column, so no turnout rate is derivable from it. [verified]
properties.parameter: presidential votes cast

blocks.text: Of 45,815 presidential votes cast in the county, **30,487 for Trump and 13,294 for Clinton** — 66.5 per cent against 29.0, with 1,486 for Johnson and 323 for Stein. [verified] — [OpenElections](../../catalog/openelections-ohio.md), summed over the county's 88 precincts.

**Thirteen precincts went to Clinton**, twelve of them in [Lima](../place/lima.yml) and the thirteenth `AMERICAN D`, in the township wrapped around the city. Four years later [eleven went to Biden](allen-county-presidential-vote-2020.yml): `LIMA 1A` and `LIMA 1C` crossed over and nothing crossed the other way. [verified] — same source.

The 1,486 votes for Johnson are the largest third-party showing in the three elections this corpus holds — three times Jorgensen's 590 in 2020 on a similar total vote. [verified] — same source. What that means is not recorded here; it is the kind of thing two data points cannot carry.

properties.method: Summed by candidate over the county's 88 precincts. The total is 360 fewer than the 48,353 ballots cast — an undervote of 0.7 per cent. [verified]
properties.parameter: presidential votes cast

blocks.text: Of 47,993 presidential votes cast in the county, **33,116 for Trump and Pence and 14,149 for Biden and Harris** — 69.0 per cent against 29.5, with 590 for Jorgensen and Cohen and 138 for Hawkins and Walker. [verified] — [OpenElections](../../catalog/openelections-ohio.md).

**Eleven of the county's 88 precincts went to Biden, and ten of them are in Lima.** The eleventh is `AMERICAN D`, in the township wrapped around the city's west and north. Every other precinct in the county — all twelve townships' rural ground, both cities' outer wards, every village — went the other way. [verified] — same source. The most Republican precinct is `MONROE E` at 90.6 per cent; the most Democratic is `LIMA 6C` at 87.9. A county that votes 69–29 contains precincts ninety points apart.

**It is the third of three, and the county is drifting.** Republican share of the top-of-ticket vote ran 66.5 per cent in [2016](allen-county-presidential-vote-2016.yml), 67.3 in [2018](allen-county-governor-vote-2018.yml) and 69.0 here — a move of 2.5 points across two presidential elections, against a median precinct move of 1.5. [verified] — same source.

**Every precinct Clinton won in 2016 moved toward the Republicans**, all thirteen of them, by a mean of 4.5 points; `LIMA 1A` and `LIMA 1C` crossed over entirely. Across the 88 the correlation between 2016 Republican share and the 2016–2020 swing is **−0.39**: the more Democratic a precinct was, the harder it moved. [verified] — computed here from the three [OpenElections](../../catalog/openelections-ohio.md) files.
Down-ballot in 2020, Jim Jordan took 33,201 to 13,080, Matt Huffman 34,303 to 12,645, and Bob Cupp ran unopposed with 38,882. [verified] — same source.

nodes.label: Allen County population by race, 2023

properties.method: 2023 five-year estimates. Race categories are "alone" except the two-or-more column; Hispanic origin is asked separately and overlaps every race column, so the rows do not sum to 100. The twelve townships and Lima partition the county: 2,515 plus 8,290 is 10,805, the county row. [verified]
properties.parameter: population by race (B02001) and Hispanic origin (B03003)
properties.unit: residents identifying as Black or African American alone, Allen County

blocks.text: Race and Hispanic origin for the county, its thirteen civil subdivisions, the state and the nation. [verified] — [American Community Survey](../../catalog/census-acs-summary-file.md), 2023 five-year estimates.

**Lima holds a third of the county's people and three quarters of its Black residents.** 8,290 of 10,805, or 76.7 per cent ± 4.6, against a 34.7 per cent share of the population. [verified] — same source. The twelve townships hold the other 2,515, and the two sum exactly to the county's figure.

**Eight of the twelve townships have fewer than a hundred Black residents**, and two report none. [verified] Outside Lima and the two townships that adjoin it — American at 10.1 per cent and Shawnee at 4.1 — the county is between 90 and 97 per cent white. [verified]

nodes.label: Allen County's railroads, 1872–1921

properties.method: Read from the full text of three county histories on archive.org, the 1885 book in two independent scans. The mileage is the 1885 book's, compiled from official records of 1883 and prefaced "about". The employment figures are as the sources print them: a range for 1879, a floor for the shops in 1906, and an exact count for the yards and freight offices in 1905. Nothing here averages a range or treats "more than 500" as 500, and the three are not added together. [verified]
properties.parameter: railroad main track in the county

blocks.text: The network three county histories describe, and what it employed. [verified] — [1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md), [1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md) and [1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md).

**In 1883 there were about 102 miles of main track and 22 miles of side track in the county.** [verified] — [the 1885 history](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md), compiling the official records of 1883. It is the only measurement of the county's railroad extent this corpus holds from any year, and it comes two years before [the oil strike](../event/lima-oil-strike.yml).

**The county voted for two of those lines and eight people voted against.** The Boesel railroad bill passed the Legislature in April 1872, and at a special election on 25 May 1872 Lima and Ottawa Township voted on $100,000 of bonds for the Lima, Lafayette & Mississippi and the Lake Erie & Louisville. "Something over 700 votes were cast and only eight of those were against the appropriation." Both roads were put through in 1872 and later consolidated as the Lake Erie & Western. [verified] — [the 1906 history](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md).

**Lima was a railroad town six years before it was an oil town.** In March 1879, at a population of about 7,000, the *Allen County Republican* described the city as standing at the crossing of the Pittsburg, Fort Wayne & Chicago, the Dayton & Michigan and the Lake Erie & Louisville, with all three keeping repair shops there, a street railroad running from the Union Depot, and the Dayton & Michigan shops covering some eight acres and employing 200 to 300 men. [verified] — same source, quoting the paper of 14 March 1879.

**Those shops were the largest employer in the county on any figure the corpus holds for that decade**, and there is no rival in the 1879 list: the next largest establishments named are furniture factories of seven to twenty-five hands. [inference] — computed from the same list.

**By 1906 two shops employed more than five hundred men each** — the Cincinnati, Hamilton & Dayton, successor to the Dayton & Michigan, and the Lake Erie & Western, whose shops came to Lima about 1880 — and the city was "one of the five great trunk lines, which center in this city". [verified] — same source. Ten fast passenger trains a day passed through Lima on the Chicago & Erie alone, besides the mails and the limited express.

**The lines, and when each arrived.** [verified] — the three histories together; see [the first railroad](../event/the-first-railroad-reaches-allen-county.yml) for the three years the sources give for the first of them, and [Benjamin Faurot](../person/benjamin-faurot.yml) for the last.

**Delphos kept a roundhouse.** In 1921 it held 100 railway employees besides the engineers and conductors living in the town, the shops of the Toledo, Delphos & Western — the Clover Leaf — and a terminal on the Northern Ohio Railway, with interurban service to Lima and Fort Wayne. [verified] — [the 1921 history](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md).

**Two of the three gaps this node opened are closed.** There is now an employment count rather than a range: 108 men in Lima's railway yards and 74 in the freight offices in 1905, **182** exactly. [verified] — [the traffic of 1905](lima-railroad-traffic-1905.yml). And the interurban is held — three companies named in 1905, two serving Lima in 1921, and a federal directory's word on who owned whom. [verified] — [the interurban](allen-county-interurban-1901-1921.yml).

**The mileage gap is not closed and the second figure shows why.** 1905 gives 73 miles of *aggregate yard trackage in Lima*, against 1883's 102 miles of *main track in the county*. The two cannot be differenced, subtracted or trended: they count different things over different ground. [inference] — see [the control is the figure that cannot move](../../decisions/the-control-is-the-figure-that-cannot-move.yml).

refusals: The corpus cannot say how large the railroad workforce of this county ever was.

nodes.label: Allen County's railroads, 2026

properties.method: Current Form 71 inventory as of retrieval, filtered to FIPS 39003, counting rows whose `crossingclosed` field is `No`. 95 of the 201 open rows were last revised in 2025 and 92 in 2026; twelve carry revisions from 2014 to 2024 and are stale to that degree. A crossing is a place a road meets a track, so a railroad with many crossings is not necessarily a railroad with much track or much traffic — the train counts are recorded separately and are used here for that. [verified]
properties.parameter: open highway-rail grade crossings

blocks.text: What is left of the network, counted at every place a road crosses it. [verified] — [FRA Highway-Rail Grade Crossing Inventory](../../catalog/fra-crossing-inventory.md).

**Not one of the 201 open crossings sees a passenger train.** [verified] — same source, which records passenger trains per day at every crossing and records zero at all of them. In 1906 ten fast passenger trains a day passed through Lima on the Chicago & Erie alone, besides the mails and the limited express, and in 1921 a traveller could go to bed in Allen County and wake in Chicago or New York. [verified] — [the network then](allen-county-railroads-1883-1921.yml).

**One line carries most of the traffic and it is not the one with most of the crossings.** CSX runs up to 24 through trains a day at 60 miles an hour on two main tracks at Robb Avenue in Lima; the Chicago, Fort Wayne & Eastern, which has 65 open crossings to CSX's 42, runs at most 10 a day at 40, on one track. Norfolk Southern's 40 open crossings see at most two trains a day at ten miles an hour. [verified] — same source.

**The closed crossings are the record of who left.** 104 of the county's 305 crossing records are marked closed, including every one of Conrail's 24 and every one of Grand Trunk Western's 3. [verified] — same source. Norfolk Southern has more closed crossings in this county than open ones.

**The busiest railroad in the county is a short line named for Fort Wayne.** The Chicago, Fort Wayne & Eastern's crossings sit in Lima, Lafayette, Delphos and Elida — east of Lima and west of it, on the axis the Ohio & Indiana was built along in 1854. [inference] — the towns are the source's, the identification is this corpus's, and it rests on route and name rather than on any corporate record. See [the first railroad](../event/the-first-railroad-reaches-allen-county.yml).

**Lima holds 108 of the 201.** Then Spencerville with 16, Lafayette 15, Beaverdam 14, Delphos 13, Elida 12, Cairo 10 and Bluffton 7. [verified] — same source. 171 of the 201 are at grade; 21 pass under the railroad and 9 over it.

refusals: The inventory counts crossings and not track, so nothing here is comparable to the 102 miles of main track the county had in 1883, and this corpus cannot say whether the network shrank, moved or merely changed hands.

nodes.label: The school boards of Allen County's twelve districts, 2026

properties.method: Fetched from the Ohio boards of elections lookup by posting the district-type form with `cmbDistrictCat` = 8, which returns every school board in a county in one response — the same database the corpus previously read as eighty-eight separate precinct pages. Seats are the roster's own `Total Seats`. Names are printed as the Allen County view renders them, which is not always as a neighbouring county renders the same person; where they differ both are given and neither is corrected. Treasurers are excluded: they are appointed officers and not elective seats. [inference]
properties.parameter: boards of education of school districts holding ground in Allen County

blocks.text: **Twelve boards of education, sixty seats, and only forty-five of them are on a ballot in this county.** [verified] — [the elected officials lookup](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md), Allen County, queried by district type.

**The county's own roster answers this question two ways and the two answers differ.** Queried by district type it returns all twelve boards with their members. Queried precinct by precinct across all eighty-eight precincts it returns nine, and never [Columbus Grove](../jurisdiction/columbus-grove-local-school-district.yml), [Pandora-Gilboa](../jurisdiction/pandora-gilboa-local-school-district.yml) or [Waynesfield-Goshen](../jurisdiction/waynesfield-goshen-local-school-district.yml). [verified] — same source, both views read here.

**They are not in conflict; they answer different questions.** The precinct view lists what an Allen County elector votes on, and no elector here votes on those three boards. The district-type view lists the boards of every district holding ground in this county. [inference] The corpus had read only the first and had concluded that the three boards were absent from the roster. They were absent from the ballot.
**The fifteen people the corpus said it could not name.** [verified] — same source.

**The neighbouring counties' rosters carry the same fifteen people under different names.** Putnam County gives Angela Lynn Basinger for Angie Basinger, Brian E. Jones for Brian E Jones; Auglaize gives Kevin D Ewing, David J Pepple, Michelle R Steinke and Brad V Vorhes. **Eight of the fifteen are rendered identically and seven are not**, across two boards of elections publishing from the same state system. [verified] — [the same lookup](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md) at its Putnam and Auglaize addresses; counted here.

nodes.label: Children in poverty in Allen County's school districts, 2023

properties.method: Joined on the five-digit LEA code prefixed with the state FIPS, matching the `fips_code` these district nodes carry. [verified] Rates are computed here as the poverty count over the 5-to-17 population; the file publishes neither the rate nor an interval.
properties.parameter: children aged 5 to 17 in poverty, by school district
properties.unit: children in poverty across the twelve districts

blocks.text: The modelled number of children aged 5 to 17 in poverty in each district holding ground in Allen County, with the district's whole population. [verified] — [SAIPE school district estimates](../../catalog/census-saipe-school-districts.md), 2023.

**Lima City Schools is 31.7 per cent child poverty and Bluffton is 5.6.** Lima holds a quarter of the twelve districts' school-age children and very nearly half of their poor ones — 1,626 of 3,368. [verified] — same source, and computed here.

**This is the same sorting the corpus has already measured, arriving through a third instrument.** Lima is 34.7 per cent of the county's people, 64.1 per cent of its poor, 46.4 per cent owner-occupied where every township is above 72, and its median house is worth 46 per cent of Shawnee Township's. [verified] — [race](allen-county-race-2023.yml), [income](allen-county-income-and-poverty-2023.yml) and [housing](allen-county-housing-stock-2023.yml). A survey, a model and a finance return describe one shape. [inference]

**Perry is the district that does not fit either story.** 22.1 per cent child poverty on 602 children — the county's second-highest rate — in a township whose median household income the margins would not let this corpus call lower than Lima's. [verified] The district and the township are not the same ground: Perry Local reaches into Lima. [inference]

**These twelve are not the county and their sum is not a county figure.** 117,057 people against the county's 101,685, because five of the districts hold ground in Putnam, Auglaize, Van Wert or Hancock. The 16.5 per cent in the last row is a rate for twelve districts, not for Allen County. [verified]

refusals: This does not establish a rate that can be ranked against another district.

nodes.label: Enrolment in Allen County's twelve school districts, 2010-2023

properties.method: `ENROLL` from the annual survey, read by column name across three column layouts and joined on `NCESID`, which is the `fips_code` these district nodes already carry. [verified] Twelve of twelve matched in all fourteen years. Percentage changes are computed here from the endpoints.
properties.parameter: fall enrolment, by school district

blocks.text: Fall enrolment in every school district holding ground in Allen County, annually for fourteen years. [verified] — [the school finance survey](../../catalog/census-school-system-finances.md).

**The schools are emptying about twice as fast as the county.** The twelve lost 1,872 pupils, 10.4 per cent, over a span in which Allen County's population fell 3.9 per cent to the 2020 census and 5.1 per cent to the 2024 estimate. [verified] — same source, and [the county](../place/allen-county.yml).

**Three districts lost a fifth and one grew.** Lima at −20.7 per cent, Waynesfield-Goshen at −20.0 and Delphos at −20.2; Bluffton is up 8.8 per cent and Allen East has not moved. [verified] — same source. The loss is as concentrated inside the school geography as [the population loss is inside the county](../period/depopulation.yml). [inference]

This is not a measurement of Allen County. Five of these districts hold ground in Putnam, Auglaize, Van Wert or Hancock counties, and the twelve together held 117,057 people in 2023 against the county's 101,685. [verified] — [the poverty file](allen-county-school-district-poverty-2023.yml). A school geography is the first one in this corpus that does not close against the county.

nodes.label: What Allen County's school districts spend and where it comes from, 2023

properties.method: `PPCSTOT` for spending, `PCTLTOT`/`PCTSTOT`/`PCTFTOT` for the shares, and `LOCRPROP` divided by `ENROLL` for property tax per pupil, which the file does not publish and the corpus computes. [verified] Dollars are nominal and this is one year, so nothing here needs a deflator; a level quoted against another year would.
properties.parameter: current spending per pupil, revenue by source, and property tax per pupil
properties.unit: dollars of current spending per pupil, Lima City Schools

blocks.text: Current spending per pupil and the source of every revenue dollar, for the twelve districts holding ground in Allen County, fiscal 2023. [verified] — [the school finance survey](../../catalog/census-school-system-finances.md).

**The district that spends the most per pupil raises the least of it.** Lima City is the county's largest district and its highest spender at $19,321, and 18.4 per cent of its revenue is local where every other district here is between 37.0 and 65.8: 59.2 per cent comes from the state and 22.4 from the federal government. [verified] — same source. That is compensatory aid working the way it is designed to, and it is worth saying plainly rather than as a surprise. [inference]

**Under it is the property tax, and under that is the housing.** Lima raises $3,098 a pupil in property tax where Shawnee raises $7,727 — a ratio of 2.49. The median house in Lima is worth $95,900 and in Shawnee Township $210,200, a ratio of 2.19. [verified] — [the housing stock](allen-county-housing-stock-2023.yml). The two ratios are not the same number and they are close, and a district's tax base is what its houses are worth. [inference]

**High spending per pupil has two different causes here and only one of them is poverty.** The three smallest districts — Waynesfield-Goshen at 472 pupils, Pandora-Gilboa at 521 and Columbus Grove at 756 — are the second, third and fourth highest spenders in the county, on child poverty rates between 6.6 and 10.2 per cent against Lima's 31.7. [verified] — [the poverty file](allen-county-school-district-poverty-2023.yml). A school has costs that do not divide, and a district of five hundred divides them by five hundred. [inference]

refusals: This does not establish that any district is spending well or badly.

nodes.label: Offenses reported by the Allen County Sheriff, 2015–2024

properties.method: Monthly counts summed to calendar years. The two periods are divided at the office's own incident-based reporting start of 1 December 2020, so 2020 sits in the earlier period and 2021 in the later; the one month of overlap is not adjusted for. No figure here is computed across the two periods except the ratio, which is reported precisely to show that the two measures move opposite ways. [inference]
properties.parameter: violent offenses reported by the Allen County Sheriff's Office

blocks.text: **The sheriff's violent offenses nearly tripled between 2020 and 2021, and his property offenses fell.** [verified] — [the FBI Crime Data Explorer](../../catalog/fbi-crime-data-explorer.md), Allen County Sheriff's Office.

**The line between those two periods is 1 December 2020, and it is in a different file.** That is the date the office began incident-based reporting. [verified] — same source, Ohio agency list; see [the agencies](allen-county-law-enforcement-agencies-2026.yml). Nothing in the monthly series marks it.

**A change that triples one measure and lowers another at the same agency in the same month is a change in counting.** A rise in violence would not spare property crime, and a better-resourced office would not report fewer burglaries. The corpus reads the step as definitional and does not publish a crime trend across it. [inference] — see [a reporting change has a date and a control](../../decisions/a-reporting-change-has-a-date-and-a-control.yml).

**What can be said about each half.** Before the change: 27 to 50 violent offenses a year over 23,000-odd people, a rate near 120 per hundred thousand. After: 79 to 114, a rate near 380. Property offenses fell in both halves and stand at 483 in 2024, the lowest of the ten years. [verified] — same source, computed here.

**This office polices what nobody else does.** Its service population is 24,079, a quarter of the county — the unincorporated ground outside [Lima](../place/lima.yml) and outside the three townships that keep their own forces. [verified] — same source. It is the same office whose thirty-nine holders since 1831 are the largest single line in this corpus. [verified] — [the office](../office/allen-county-sheriff.yml).

properties.method: Seventy-seven annual detail files downloaded whole from the NCEI bulk directory and filtered locally on `STATE` = OHIO and `CZ_NAME` = ALLEN; there is no county query. The 390 rows are 287 county-designated and 103 zone-designated, and the split follows NWS Directive 10-1605 exactly. Decade counts for the 2020s are omitted from the table above because the decade is not over — it stood at 60 when this was compiled. Damage is summed from the file's `K`/`M` suffixed estimates in nominal dollars of the year of each event, undeflated, and the file's own documentation calls them estimates. [verified]
properties.parameter: severe weather events recorded for Allen County

blocks.text: **Three hundred and ninety events in seventy-six years, and the series is a history of observation before it is a history of weather.** [verified] — [the Storm Events Database](../../catalog/noaa-storm-events.md), filtered to Ohio, county Allen.
**The count rises monotonically across seven decades and the tornadoes do not.** [verified] — same source, counted here.

**The seven decade totals are 4, 8, 12, 32, 58, 95 and 121, and the tornado column beside them is 1, 2, 4, 3, 2, 3, 4.** The first series is in strictly increasing order, which is one arrangement of the 5,040 that seven distinct numbers can take; the second is not ordered at all, and four events in the 1950s against 121 in the 2010s is a factor of thirty. [inference] — computed from the same source. **Tornado is the only category counted in every one of those decades**, which is what makes it the control. [verified] — same source; see [the tornadoes](allen-county-tornadoes-1950-2026.yml).

**Sixteen event types appear here and thirteen of them start in 1996 or later.** Tornado begins in 1950, thunderstorm wind in 1955, hail in 1959; then nothing new for thirty-seven years, and then flash flood, ice storm, winter storm and cold/wind chill all first appear in 1996, flood and high wind in 1997, heavy snow in 1999, strong wind in 2004, lightning in 2006, blizzard in 2007, winter weather in 2010, extreme cold in 2014 and heavy rain in 2020. [verified] — same source, first year of each type computed here. See [a category has a birthday](../../decisions/a-category-has-a-birthday.yml).

**So the two halves are 1.63 events a year and 10.16.** Seventy-five events in the forty-six years to 1995 against 315 in the thirty-one years from 1996 — six times the rate — while the tornado rate goes from 0.24 a year to 0.39 on counts of eleven and twelve. [inference] — computed here. The corpus reports the halves and refuses the trend across them.

**Eleven people have been killed by weather in this county since 1950 and all eleven died in the same minute.** The file's only fatalities are the eleven of the tornado of 11 April 1965. Of 134 direct injuries, 130 are that tornado's hundred and the thirty of July 1950. [verified] — same source; see [that evening](../event/the-tornado-of-11-april-1965.yml).

**Three episodes are three-quarters of all the damage.** $9,408,250 of property damage is recorded across the whole file, and the tornadoes of 1950 and 1965 at $2.5 million each and the windstorm of 22 June 2006 at $1,970,000 are $6,970,000 of it — 74.1 per cent. [verified] — same source, summed here. Crop damage across seventy-six years is $55,000.

**The record is written by the county's own residents.** Of the 293 rows that name a reporter, 240 name a person — trained spotters, emergency managers, police, broadcast media, amateur radio operators, newspapers and the public — 43 name an instrument, eight are National Weather Service storm surveys and two say "unknown". [verified] — same source. **That is the mechanism behind the rising count**: a file filled by people telephoning a forecast office grows when there are more people willing to telephone, and the reporter field is empty on all eighty-nine rows before 1998. [inference]
**More than half of it falls in four months of twelve.** May through August hold 219 of the 390 rows, June and July alone hold 144, and October holds five. [verified] — same source, counted here.

nodes.label: Allen County survey sections, 2026

properties.method: Layer 55 returned in one request under the service's 1000-record cap; three zero-area duplicate polygons removed, leaving 404. Areas are the layer's own `SHAPE.area` in square feet. Points were projected onto EPSG:3734 in `crates/ground` and located by crossing-number test; the projection was checked against the county's server, which was asked to project the same seven points itself and named the same seven sections. [verified]
properties.parameter: sections of the rectangular survey, and their area

blocks.text: The rectangular survey grid the county is drawn on: **404 sections across fifteen township-range cells**, T1S–T4S by R4E–R8E, numbered 1 to 36 within each. [verified] — [Allen County GIS REST](../../catalog/allen-county-gis-rest.md), layer 55.

**It closes against the county to within five hundredths of a square mile.** The sections total **406.805 square miles**; the county's own gazetteer record is 402.545 land plus 4.306 water, **406.851**. [verified] — same layer and [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md). Two sources that share no method — the Census Bureau computing from a boundary file, the county from its own survey — and a mean section of 639.7 acres against a nominal 640. This is the corpus's first measurement of the county as *land* rather than as population or jurisdiction. [inference]

**Why the corpus wanted it.** Every question this corpus has failed to close in the last two phases was a question about ground rather than about jurisdiction: where the county jail stood in 1933, where the Lima Tank Depot stood in 1943, whether the Depot is the ground the tank plant occupies now, when the Ford engine plant was built. Land through time is indexed by the survey, because that is how the Recorder's tract books are organized. [inference]
**The ground each of the corpus's own sites stands on**, computed from its coordinates. [verified] — same layer, cross-checked against layer 51 parcel numbers:
The volume names come from the Recorder's own book list. [verified] — [Section Ground book list](../../catalog/allen-county-recorder-section-ground.md).

**The code is written two ways and the two are different strings.** Layer 55 writes the section as the county writes it and a parcel number pads it to two digits, so T4S R6E §1 is `461` in one place and `4601` in the other. **Ninety-six of the 404 sections have a single-digit number**, so a string join between the forms silently drops 24 per cent of the county. [verified] — same layer, checked against every parcel prefix on that ground.

**Two witnesses, twenty-seven agreements.** All 29 nodes in this corpus that carry a point were located twice: by polygon against layer 55, and by the leading digits of the parcel containing the same point. [verified] — same sources.

**One polygon in the layer is two sections.** T3S R8E §5 is 1,282.2 acres on a footprint 1.04 by 2.01 miles, where its thirty-five neighbours average 641 and none is missing. [verified] — same layer. It is one section's number drawn over two sections' ground.

**The Recorder's thirty volumes nearly partition the same grid.** Their section runs expand to 416 slots: 402 sections in exactly one book, T4S R5E §8 in two, T4S R5E §18 in none, and thirteen in a book but not in the county's grid. [verified] — [the book list](../../catalog/allen-county-recorder-section-ground.md).

refusals: The corpus does not assert Bluffton's section.

properties.method: Rows where `EVENT_TYPE` is Tornado in the county's 390-row extract, sorted by begin date. Scale is the file's `TOR_F_SCALE`, which mixes the Fujita scale used before February 2007 with the Enhanced Fujita scale used after and marks neither; the two are printed as the file prints them and are not treated as one series. The 1970 row carries no rating at all. Damage is the file's nominal-dollar estimate; a blank means the field is empty, which is not the same as `$0` and seven rows have one or the other. Place names in the last column are this corpus's, taken as the nearest node to the file's coordinates, except where the file names a location itself. [inference]
properties.parameter: tornadoes recorded in Allen County

blocks.text: **Twenty-three tornadoes in seventy-six years, and two of them are almost everything.** [verified] — [the Storm Events Database](../../catalog/noaa-storm-events.md).

**One tornado has killed anyone here and one other has injured more than one person.** Eleven deaths and a hundred injuries on 11 April 1965; thirty injuries on 19 July 1950; one injury in April 1980; nothing else. [verified] — same source. **Fourteen of the twenty-three did less than $25,000 of measured damage, and seven of those fourteen did none the file records** — five rows read zero and two are blank. [verified] — same source, counted here.

**The strong ones are all in the first half.** The three tornadoes rated F3 or F4 fall in 1950, 1965 and 1971, and nothing since 1981 has been rated above F1: of the thirteen from 1992 on, ten are F0 or EF0 and three are F1 or EF1. [verified] — same source. **This is not evidence that the tornadoes weakened.** Ratings before the 1990s were assigned retrospectively from damage reports and the modern ones from ground surveys, and a survey that finds no damage rates EF0. [inference]

**The track lengths close on their own coordinates, and one of them leaves the county.** The 1965 track's endpoints are 17.92 miles apart against a stated 17.8; 1950's are 9.53 against 9.7; 1971's are 31.33 against 31.5. But 1971's endpoint is 25.6 miles east of Bluffton, far outside Allen County: **`TOR_LENGTH` is the length of the tornado, not the length of it that was in this county**, and the column cannot be summed to a figure about this ground. [inference] — computed here from the file's own latitudes and longitudes.

**The coordinate field changed meaning about 2010 and the file does not say so.** Every tornado from 1998 through 2006 has an identical begin and end coordinate on a five- or sixtieth-of-a-degree grid, against a stated track of a tenth of a mile — those are the nearest town's position. Every tornado from 2010 on reproduces its stated track length from its coordinates to two decimal places. [inference] — same computation. See [a file has more than one date](../../decisions/a-file-has-more-than-one-date.yml).

properties.method: BEA CAEMP25S line 10 for 1969–2000 and CAEMP25N line 10 for 2001–2022, Ohio county files at GeoFIPS 39003. Counts jobs rather than people, so a person holding two jobs is counted twice, and includes farm, government and proprietors. Not comparable with [County Business Patterns](allen-county-manufacturing-employment-1986-2022.yml), which counts private employees only. The comparison with population is a comparison of two programmes. [inference]
properties.parameter: total employment, all jobs, Allen County

blocks.text: Every job in the county, counted the same way for fifty-four years. [verified] — [BEA Regional Economic Accounts](../../catalog/bea-county-employment.md), total employment including proprietors, part-time work, farm and government.

**The county's jobs rose for thirty-one years while its people fell.** Employment went from 56,562 in 1969 to 72,973 in 2000 — a gain of 16,411, or 29 per cent. [verified] — same source. Over the same span the county's population fell from 111,144 to 108,464. [verified] — [the county series](../place/allen-county.yml).

**Jobs peaked twenty years after people did.** The county's population peaked in 1980 and its employment in 2000. [inference] — the two peaks are read from different sources and compared here. Whatever this county lost between 1980 and 2000, it was not work.

**Employment has fallen since, and by less than manufacturing did.** From 69,825 in 2001 to 64,238 in 2022, a loss of 5,587 or 8 per cent, against [manufacturing's](allen-county-manufacturing-employment-1969-2022.yml) fall of 3,182 over the same years. So manufacturing accounts for more than half the county's total job loss since 2001 while being about a seventh of its jobs. [inference] — computed here.

properties.method: Read from a rendered image of a 400-dpi scan; the volume's OCR text layer was used to find the page and not to read the columns. Checked against three arithmetic closures the table supplies and against two columns, 1900 and 1890, that this corpus already held from an unrelated county history. The `value` above is the county total for 1910, the figure this table was fetched for. [verified]
properties.parameter: total resident population by minor civil division, decennial

blocks.text: The county's thirteen minor civil divisions at three censuses — twelve townships and Ottawa, which was Lima. [verified] — [Abstract of the Thirteenth Census, Supplement for Ohio](../../catalog/census-1910-abstract-supplement-ohio.md), minor civil divisions table.

Written out: **Allen County held 56,580 people in 1910**, and the twelve townships outside Lima held 26,072 of them. [verified] — same source. That 1910 count was the last gap in the county's decennial record, which now runs unbroken from 1830.

**Three columns and every one closes.** The thirteen divisions sum to the printed county total in 1910, 1900 and 1890 alike, with no residual, and Lima's four wards — 5,150, 8,010, 7,830 and 9,518 — sum to its 30,508. [verified] — computed here from the printed figures.

**Ottawa Township is measured here, by name, and the coextension is datable.** The row reads "Ottawa township, coextensive with Lima city" and gives 15,987 for 1890 against the city's 15,981. Six people, and they are real rather than a misprint: without them the 1890 column does not sum to 40,644. [verified] — same source and the arithmetic above. So Ottawa held six residents outside Lima in 1890 and none at either census after. **The township and the city became exactly the same ground between 1890 and 1900.** [inference] See [what became of German and Ottawa townships](../question/what-became-of-german-and-ottawa-townships.yml).

**German Township is still German**, at all three censuses; it became [American](../place/american-township.yml) in 1918. And Cairo is still **West Cairo**, which is a third source for the older name and the first federal one. [verified] — same source.

**The countryside was shrinking while the county grew.** Five of the twelve townships outside Lima held fewer people in 1910 than in 1890, and eight of them reached their lowest recorded count somewhere between 1900 and 1940. [inference] — computed from this table and [the 1930–1950 series](allen-county-townships-1930-1950.yml). Allen County outside Lima went from 24,663 in 1890 to 28,592 in 1940, a rise of 16 per cent, while the county rose 80 per cent and the city 180. [inference] Everything that happened to this county between 1890 and 1940 happened in one municipality.

properties.method: Read from rendered images of a 300-dpi scan; the volume's own OCR text layer was used as a second reader and its column association across a three-up table was not trusted. Checked against three arithmetic closures the table itself supplies. The 1940 and 1930 columns are on 1950 boundaries where the source could put them there and exclude Lima entirely; the `value` above is the twelve-township sum for 1930, which is the county less the city. [verified]
properties.parameter: total resident population by minor civil division, decennial

blocks.text: Every one of the county's twelve townships at three censuses, and the villages inside them. [verified] — [1950 Census, Number of Inhabitants, Ohio](../../catalog/census-1950-number-of-inhabitants-ohio.md), Table 6, *Population of counties by minor civil divisions: 1930 to 1950*.

Written out, because a table is not prose: in 1930 **Marion Township was the county's largest outside Lima, with 4,959 people, and Perry its smallest at 1,515**; by 1950 Perry held 14,207 and American 25,151, because the city had crossed into both. [verified] — same source.

**Every figure sits inside an arithmetic closure.** The twelve 1950 counts sum to 88,183, which is the county total, and Lima's four parts inside them — 19,270 in American, 17,469 in Bath, 10,895 in Perry, 2,612 in Shawnee — sum to 50,246, which is Lima's own. The 1940 and 1930 columns exclude Lima, as the table's head warns they may, and they miss the county by exactly Lima: 28,592 + 44,711 = 73,303, and 27,132 + 42,287 = 69,419. [verified] — computed here from the printed figures. Three closures, no residual, and every number in the block participates in one.

**The 1940 column is a figure this corpus had already computed and published as an inference.** A phase ago it derived "the county outside Lima in 1940" as 73,303 − 44,711 = 28,592. The twelve townships sum to 28,592. [verified] — same source. A derived figure and a measured one meeting to the person is the best evidence this corpus has yet had that its subtraction is doing what it says.
**So the county outside Lima now begins in 1930, at 27,132**, and rose to 28,592 by 1940 and 37,937 by 1950. [inference] — see [the balance series](allen-county-outside-lima-1890-2020.yml).

**The city is what moved, and the townships mostly did not.** Between 1930 and 1940 seven of the twelve gained and five lost, and the whole balance moved by 1,460 people on a base of 27,132 — five per cent across a decade. [inference] — computed above. Lima gained 2,424 in the same decade. Whatever was happening to this county in the 1930s was happening in one municipality.

**Every one of the twelve is larger now than it was in 1930, and the comparison is sound.** The 1930 and 1940 columns exclude Lima, and so do today's township figures, because the Census treats the city as its own county subdivision — which is why the modern twelve sum to 66,686, exactly the 2020 estimates base less Lima. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md), sub-county file, and arithmetic here. Against 1930:

The whole balance is two and a half times its 1930 size while the county is below its 1980 peak and the city has lost a third of itself. [inference] The two that grew sixfold, Shawnee and American, are the two Lima borders on its south and west.

**But 1930 was near the bottom, and the second column is why that matters.** Eight of the twelve reached their lowest recorded count somewhere between 1900 and 1940, and five held fewer people in 1910 than in 1890. [inference] — see [the 1890–1910 divisions](allen-county-townships-1890-1910.yml). Measured from 1890 the twelve still all grew, and six of them grew *less*: Monroe by three per cent rather than by a third, and Amanda by a half rather than by double. A baseline is a choice, and this one was made by which volume happened to arrive first.

**In 1950 the four townships Lima had reached still net out correctly.** Taking the city's parts back off them gives American 5,881, Bath 5,450, Perry 3,312 and Shawnee 3,796, and all twelve then sum to 37,937 — the county less Lima. [verified] — computed here. That is the fourth closure this one table supports, and it is what makes the four affected townships comparable across the century rather than only from 1950.

Also recorded here because no node yet holds it: **Westwood**, an unincorporated place of 2,296 people in 1950, split 1,968 in American and 328 in Shawnee. [verified] — same source. It is not in the corpus's places and this is the only figure it has for it.

nodes.label: Allen County facilities reporting to the Toxics Release Inventory, 1987–2024

properties.method: The Envirofacts facility register for Allen County joined to `tri_reporting_form`, paged at 1,000 rows — 5,372 forms across 49 facility identifiers, reporting years 1987 to 2024. A facility is counted as filing in a year if any form carries that year. One register entry, Heat Treating Tech Inc, has no forms at all. [verified]
properties.parameter: facilities filing a TRI reporting form, Allen County

blocks.text: Every facility in the county that filed for 2024, with the years it has filed and the parent company named against it now. [verified] — [EPA TRI](../../catalog/epa-tri.md).

**Twenty facilities filed for 2024, and the register holds forty-nine.** Twenty-eight of the forty-eight that have ever filed did not file for 2024, and only three of those twenty-eight carry the register's closure flag. [verified] The flag is not a currency test; a filing is. See [a register is not a census](../../decisions/a-register-is-not-a-census.yml).

**Six have filed in all thirty-eight years** — the refinery, Dana, Ford, INEOS, FXI and Chemtrade at Cairo. [verified] Sixteen of the twenty have filed in twenty-seven years or more, and sixteen have no gap between their first year and their last, so the county's reporting industry is old and it has stayed. [verified] The column above is first year and last, not every year between: Procter & Gamble's span is thirty-eight years and its filings are thirty. [verified]

Every parent above is a parent **now** — the register's attributes are current-state and say nothing about who owned any of these facilities earlier. And this is not a list of the county's employers: TRI covers facilities over a size threshold that handle listed chemicals, so it sees a foundry and not a hospital. No employment figure here rests on it. [verified]

properties.method: Sum of the `ballots_cast` field over the 88 Allen County precincts, from a volunteer transcription of the certified returns. Registered voters summed the same way: 67,374. [verified]
properties.parameter: ballots cast, general election

blocks.text: 48,353 ballots cast against 67,374 registered voters at the general election of 3 November 2020 — **71.8 per cent**, summed over the county's 88 precincts. [verified] — [OpenElections](../../catalog/openelections-ohio.md).

**The county figure hides a fifty-two point spread.** Turnout ran from 35.4 per cent in `LIMA 3B` to 87.8 per cent in `DELPHOS 1B`. No other quantity this corpus holds varies that far across the county: population per housing unit runs 2.19 to 2.57, and land area per subdivision by a factor of four. [verified] — same source, precinct by precinct.

Registration itself varies as much and is the more interesting number. Across the 88 precincts registered voters run from 0.28 to 0.84 per resident, and the low end of that range is where the county's [group quarters](../question/who-lives-in-the-county-without-housing.yml) are. [verified] — same source against [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md) block population.

properties.method: Distinct values in the VTD assignment file over the 3,552 blocks whose GEOID begins 39003, cross-checked against the 88 features TIGERweb returns for the county. [verified]
properties.parameter: voting districts

blocks.text: The 88 voting districts into which Allen County's 3,552 census blocks are divided in the 2020 geography, named. [verified] — [2020 Census Block Assignment Files](../../catalog/census-block-assignment-2020.md) for the assignment and [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md), layer 58, for the names, populations, housing units and areas.

**The precinct grid nests inside the civil geography exactly.** Not one of the 88 crosses a county-subdivision line. [verified] — the assignment files crossed with TIGERweb block geography, block by block — the sharp contrast with [the school districts](../jurisdiction/), which cross county and township lines freely. [Lima](../place/lima.yml) holds 23 and [Sugar Creek Township](../place/sugar-creek-township.yml) holds [one](../division/voting-district-sugar-creek-2020.yml); their populations sum to 102,206, which is [the county's own enumeration](allen-county-population-2020-census.yml).

**A second, unrelated pipeline confirms the names.** The 88 the county board of elections used on its certified returns are identical, string for string, to the 88 the Census Bureau publishes. [verified] — [OpenElections](../../catalog/openelections-ohio.md) against TIGERweb. That joins [turnout](allen-county-turnout-2020.yml) and [the vote](allen-county-presidential-vote-2020.yml) to census geography with no crosswalk, and those show the 88 are far from interchangeable.

nodes.label: What work pays in Allen County, 2024

properties.method: QCEW annual averages, aggregation level 74 for the sector table and 70 for the county total, read from the BLS open CSV API. Sector figures are summed across ownership codes, so a sector's row includes its government establishments; average annual pay per sector is total annual wages divided by average annual employment, which is this corpus's arithmetic over the source's two published fields. The eighteen sectors sum to 49,113 jobs against the county total of 49,690; the residual is employment the file places at aggregation levels this table does not read. [verified]
properties.parameter: average weekly wage, all industries, all ownerships

blocks.text: Thirteen phases measured how many people work here and not one measured what they are paid. [verified] — [Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages](../../catalog/bls-qcew.md), annual averages for 2024, all ownerships.
**49,690 covered jobs in 2,586 establishments, at an average weekly wage of $1,131 and an average annual pay of $58,790.** [verified] — same source.

**That is 89.3 per cent of the Ohio average weekly wage and 77.8 per cent of the national one** — $1,131 against $1,267 and $1,454. [inference] — computed here from the same source's Ohio and national files. A worker in this county earns about four fifths of what a worker in the country does.
[verified] — same source, county by NAICS sector, summed across ownerships.

**The five largest sectors, in jobs and in pay.** Health care 9,767 jobs at $60,502 a year; manufacturing 8,779 at $92,088; retail trade 5,261 at $34,261; accommodation and food services 4,737 at $20,844; educational services 3,899 at $47,735. [verified] — same source.

**Manufacturing is 17.9 per cent of the jobs and 28.0 per cent of the wages.** [inference] — computed here. It is the only sector in the county whose share of pay is more than half again its share of employment.

**Retail trade and food service together employ more people than manufacturing and pay a tenth of the county's wages.** 9,998 jobs against 8,779, and 9.7 per cent of $2,884,327,418 in total annual wages. [inference] — computed here. Health care, the largest employer of all, takes 20.5 per cent of the wages on 19.9 per cent of the jobs.

**The two extremes are 4.4 times apart.** Utilities pays $93,106 a year across 202 jobs and accommodation and food services $20,844 across 4,737. [verified] — same source. Information employs fifty-two people in the whole county.

properties.method: Fetched from the USGS site service with `siteStatus=all`, which is required or discontinued gauges are omitted — and the discontinued ones carry most of the county's long record. Site types are the service's own two-letter codes, collapsed here to their first letter group. The count is of sites the service lists for this county whatever their status or period of record, and is not a count of instruments now running. [verified]
properties.parameter: USGS water monitoring sites in Allen County

blocks.text: **The county holds 184 water monitoring sites and two usable stream records.** [verified] — [USGS NWIS](../../catalog/usgs-nwis.md), site service, county 39003, all statuses.

**Twenty-nine stream sites and two annual peak records between them.** The rest are levels, samples or one-off measurements; three of the county's larger stream gauges answer the peak-flow service with a 200 and no rows. A county can be thick with instruments and thin with measurements. [inference] — computed here; see [the peak flows](ottawa-river-peak-flows-1924-2025.yml).
**The drainage areas put the county's rivers in order.** [verified] — same source.

The Auglaize is the larger river and the Ottawa is the gauged one, which is [the same asymmetry the bridges show](allen-county-bridge-crossings-2025.yml): forty-one crossings of the Ottawa against twenty-two of the Auglaize. Both follow from the same fact, which is that [Lima](../place/lima.yml) sits on the Ottawa. [inference]

**Every one of the 184 sites drains to Lake Erie.** 168 are in the Auglaize subbasin `04100007`, 14 in the Blanchard `04100008`, and two in other Maumee units; none is in an Ohio River unit. [verified] — same source. **That is an absence of instruments and not evidence about the divide**: the corpus has already established that four census blocks in [Auglaize Township](../place/auglaize-township.yml), holding ninety-nine people, drain to [the Scioto](../natural-feature/scioto-river-basin.yml), and ninety-nine people do not get a gauge. [inference] — see [silence from a source that would have spoken](../../decisions/silence-from-a-source-that-would-have-spoken.yml), which this is not an instance of.

**The thirty-one lake and reservoir stations are the drinking water.** Allen County has no natural lakes; Lima's water system owns six named reservoirs, each with an intake, and Delphos a seventh. [verified] — [the water systems](allen-county-water-systems-2026.yml). A monitoring network concentrated on standing water in a county with none of it is a network watching a city's supply. [inference]

properties.method: Selected on the `OH02` identifier prefix, which is Ohio's county code for Allen, and restricted to `pws_activity_code` A and `pws_type_code` CWS. The thirty-three active non-community systems — rest areas, campgrounds, schools, a tavern — are excluded, because they serve people who are passing through or at work and counting them against a resident population would double-count. Populations are as each system reports them and are service populations, not residents of any boundary this corpus holds. [verified]
properties.parameter: people served by community water systems in Allen County

blocks.text: **Eight community water systems serve 84,476 people, and six of them are the town.** [verified] — [EPA SDWIS](../../catalog/epa-sdwis.md), systems with identifiers beginning `OH02`, active only.

**Lima's system serves more than the county seat by a factor of two.** Lima held 35,579 people at the 2020 census and its water system reports serving 65,619 — sixty-five per cent of the county — before counting the 4,109 it sells to [Elida](../place/elida.yml). [verified] — same source and [the 2020 count](lima-population-2020-census.yml).

**Everything Lima drinks is surface water, and it is stored.** Its facility list carries six named reservoirs — Ferguson, Bresler, Metzger, Williams, Twin Lakes and Lost Creek — with an intake on each, and four more intakes on [the Ottawa](../natural-feature/ottawa-river.yml) and [the Auglaize](../natural-feature/auglaize-river.yml). [verified] — same source, facility table. **That is what the thirty-one lake and reservoir monitoring stations in a county with no natural lakes are.** [inference] — see [the gauges](allen-county-water-gauges-2026.yml).

**The city drinks from the river nobody measures.** Two of its intakes are on the Auglaize, which has 219 square miles of drainage above Spencerville and not one year of recorded peak flow. [verified] — [the peak flows](ottawa-river-peak-flows-1924-2025.yml). [inference]

**Two of the eight own no surface source and are coded as surface anyway.** Elida buys from Lima; Bluffton owns eight wells and buys surface water from Ottawa Village in Putnam County. The system-level `gw_sw_code` describes the water in the pipe and not the ground it came from. [verified] — same source, facility table.

**About one person in six is on none of them.** The eight report 84,476 against the county's 100,866 in 2024 — 84 per cent. The residual is not a count of private wells: these are self-reported service populations, and Bluffton and Delphos both straddle county lines. [inference] — computed against [the 2024 estimate](allen-county-population-2024.yml).

nodes.label: Drinking water violations in Allen County, 1984–2026

properties.method: All rows for systems whose identifier begins `OH02`, whatever the system's type or current status — so a tavern that closed in 1998 is counted. Health-based is the file's own `is_health_based_ind`, not a threshold chosen here. Distinct problems are counted by grouping on system and return-to-compliance date, which merges Bluffton's ten quarterly rows and leaves every other health-based violation on its own. The 2020s figure covers six years and eight months, not ten. [verified]
properties.parameter: recorded drinking water violations in Allen County

blocks.text: **197 recorded violations across thirty-eight systems in forty-two years, of which twenty concern the water.** [verified] — [EPA SDWIS](../../catalog/epa-sdwis.md), violations for systems beginning `OH02`.
The twenty health-based violations are exactly the fourteen `MCL` and the six `TT`, and nothing else in the file is flagged health-based. [verified] — same source, counted here.

**Twenty violations, ten resolutions.** Every one has returned to compliance, and the return dates group them in pairs: ten of Bluffton's are one problem. [verified] — same source; see [the file carries its own grouping key](../../decisions/the-file-carries-its-own-grouping-key.yml).

**Bluffton Village was over a standard for ten consecutive quarters**, October 2013 to March 2016, on contaminant 2950 — 0.104 milligrams per litre against a limit of 0.08 in the first quarter — and returned to compliance on 7 April 2016, closing all ten at once. [verified] — same source.

**Lima City has exceeded the same standard twice**, in the first quarter of 2022 and the second of 2024, the latter at 0.087 against 0.08, and cleared each within months. It also missed a treatment step in December 2016. [verified] — same source. Both Lima and Bluffton drink surface water; five of the seven systems with a health-based violation are the county's smallest — a campground, a chiropractor's office, a rescue mission, a community centre and a school. [verified] — same source.

**The count rises steeply and the water is not the reason.** Two violations in the 1980s, 24 in the 1990s, 25 in the 2000s, 61 in the 2010s and 85 in the six years since 2020. Nearly all of the increase is monitoring and reporting, and the number of federal drinking water rules to be monitored under grew across the same span. [inference] — computed here. The corpus records the count and refuses the trend, as it does for [the disaster declarations](allen-county-disaster-declarations-1965-2020.yml).

properties.method: Every line of the printed honour roll matching `Surname, Given`, counted from the single digitization of the 1921 history. Two rejected lines were identified as wrapped continuations of accepted names and are not additional men. Overlap with the service roster computed on normalised surname plus first initial. [inference]
properties.parameter: Allen County men who died in service, First World War

blocks.text: **Ninety-five names under the heading "On Fame's Eternal Camping Ground".** The county's honour roll of men who died in military or naval service in the First World War, printed alphabetically from Harry Apostol to Thor Zetlitz. [verified] — [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md), the closing pages of chapter XLIV; count performed here, and it is a floor for the same reason [the service roster's is](allen-county-world-war-service.yml).

The parse accepted 95 name lines and rejected two — `Ross` and `Alexander` — which are the second halves of `MacDonnell, Duncan` and `Turner, Aberdeen`, wrapped across a line. So the list is 95 men and the parse and the page agree. [inference] — read here.

**It was compiled by different hands from the service roster.** Elmer McClain says "especial care was taken" over the mortuary list: every newspaper in the county was asked to help, the William Paul Gallagher Post of the American Legion was appealed to, and he credits Mrs. Irene Mills Jackson of the Home Service Bureau of the American Red Cross and Mrs. James Pillars, secretary of the Allen County Historical and Archaeological Society. [verified] — same source.

**At most forty-seven of the ninety-five dead are absent from the roster of the served**, matched on surname and first initial. At least forty-eight are present. [inference] — computed here; the direction is fixed, because any OCR failure in either list breaks a match and pushes the absences up, never down.

**One of the absent is the man the post is named for.** The honour roll carries `Gallagher, William Paul`. The service roster is alphabetical and the slot where he belongs is occupied by other men: `Galberach, William H.` then `Gallant, William H,` then `Gallapool, C. Ralph`, `Gallaspie, Edward L.`, `Gallont, Charles J.`, `Galloway, Earl D.` No *Gallagher*, in any spelling a search of the five thousand lines will find. [verified] — [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md), the two lists read against each other. The American Legion post in Lima is the William Paul Gallagher Post No. 96; it helped compile the honour roll; and the list of who served, assembled with that post's help, does not have him.

That is not a defect in either list. It is what two lists made by different people out of different sources look like when they are set next to each other, and it is the measure of how far either can be trusted alone. [inference] — see [one scan is a floor and a residue](../../decisions/one-scan-is-a-floor-and-a-residue.yml).

**One in forty-four, against one in eleven.** Ninety-five dead out of at least 4,158 who served is 2.3 per cent. The county's Civil War roster of 1,920 names records 170 deaths, 8.9 per cent. [inference] — computed here from [the service roster](allen-county-world-war-service.yml) and [the Civil War dead](allen-county-civil-war-dead.yml). Four times as many men went and a quarter as many of them died, in a war a fifth as long.

nodes.label: Allen County in the World War — how many served

properties.method: Every line of Elmer McClain's printed roster matching `Surname, Given` or `Surname. Given`, counted from the single archive.org digitization of the 1921 history — 4,088 plus 70. Ninety-six further lines were rejected and are reported rather than estimated. Duplicates were not removed from the published figure; they are counted separately. [inference]
properties.parameter: Allen County men in military or naval service, First World War

blocks.text: **The narrative says about thirty-five hundred and the roster twenty pages later holds more than four thousand names.** Both are in the same chapter of the same book. [verified] — [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md), chapter XLIV, "Allen County in the Wars".

Written out: **the American Legion's figure is 3,260 enlistments, rising to about 3,500 with officers and men credited elsewhere; the printed roster yields at least 4,158 names.** [verified] for the first three — same source; [inference] for the last, counted here.

**The roster is a document with a compiler and a method.** It is the "World War Military and Naval List" of Elmer McClain, an Allen County man who enlisted and did transport duty and kept a card system. He appealed to the newspapers, checked his cards against other lists, and drew on twelve named sources: ex-service men, the YMCA at the camps and in Lima, the American Legion, the Federal Employment Bureau, a local citizens committee, the county recorder's office, the 1919 Lima city directory, the township chairmen of the Victory Loan campaign, the Knights of Columbus, the Red Cross, the local draft board and the Allen County Historical Society. [verified] — same source, which gives the list numbered.

**And he says what it is worth.** "In spite of all effort to make it so, the compiler knows that it is not in every respect either perfectly complete or perfectly accurate, but it is the most complete and accurate list in existence"; and, on why: "Many young men from Allen County enlisted in various parts of the United States throughout the war, and no official list of these men exists." [verified] — same source.
**The book cannot spell him.** He is "Elmert McClain" in the paragraph introducing the list and "Elmer McClain" in the line above the first name. [verified] — same source, two lines apart.

4,158 is a floor and the residue proves it. The parser accepted 4,088 lines of the form `Surname, Given` and a further 70 where the comma had been read as a full stop; it left 96 lines it could not classify, and those visibly include names whose comma was lost altogether — `Augsburger Donald`, `Beamer Ray`, `Biederman William`, `Bixler Aurora`, `Creps Clark W.` — and fragments of names broken across a line. [inference] — parse performed here on the one scan that exists; see [one scan is a floor and a residue](../../decisions/one-scan-is-a-floor-and-a-residue.yml).

**Thirty-six of the accepted lines repeat a name already in the list.** [inference] — computed here on surname and given name normalised. The compiler warned that the list is not perfectly accurate and this is one shape that takes.

**One in sixteen.** Against the county's 68,203 at the 1920 census, 4,158 is 6.1 per cent of everybody — one person in sixteen, counting women, children and the old. The Civil War figure was one in ten. [inference] — computed here from [the population series](allen-county-outside-lima-1890-2020.yml) and [the Civil War service](allen-county-civil-war-service.yml).

nodes.label: Municipal elections in Bluffton and Beaverdam as their paper reported them, 1939–1959

properties.method: The election-week issue of each odd year from 1939 to 1959 that the archive holds, read page by page from the ALTO OCR: 1939, 1943, 1945, 1947, 1955, 1957 and 1959. 1941, 1949, 1951 and 1953 have no issue in the week after the election and are absent for that reason and not because nothing was printed. Six of the seven read carry a Bluffton mayoral result and two carry Beaverdam's, which is the eight counted below; 1947 carries the campaign and not the count. Vote totals are as printed, including the ones the paper itself labels unofficial. [verified]
properties.parameter: municipal elections in Allen County villages reported with returns

blocks.text: **The village's weekly reported its own elections office by office and vote by vote, and that is the control on what the same paper knows about [Lima](lima-mayors-1939-1956.yml).** [verified] — [The Bluffton News](../../catalog/chronicling-america.md), the election-week issue of each year below read in full.

**1939 — the whole government in one story.** W. A. Howe (R) was elected mayor 713 to 322 over A. D. Wells (D) in "one of the heaviest off year balloting in the history of the town". James West (R) took the clerk's office 733 to 289; Samuel Bixel (D) was re-elected treasurer 544 to 413; Lee Coon (D) was returned as marshal for a third term 779 to 248. Council came out three and three — Munson Bixel, Armin Hauenstein and Cleon Triplett against Menno Badertscher, Evan Basinger and R. A. Patterson. [verified] — same source, 9 November 1939.

**And the same story records how the seat had been filled the year before.** Howe was the sitting mayor, and had become mayor in 1938 as president of the town council, "filling the vacancy caused by the resignation of J. Norman King who was elected to that office two years ago". [verified] — same source. It is the earliest account this corpus holds of a municipal vacancy in this county being filled, and the rule it shows — the president of council steps up — is the same one [Lima used in 1945](lima-mayors-1939-1956.yml) when its mayor took a week's holiday. [inference]

**1943 — unopposed, and most of the village stayed home.** Howe was re-elected for a third consecutive term with no opponent. 468 votes were cast out of an eligible vote the paper estimated at over 1,200, and 330 of them were for mayor. [verified] — same source, 4 November 1943.

**1945 — a write-in beat a man who had no opponent.** Charles Aukerman (R) was elected mayor over W. A. Howe (R) by 225 to 208, in "one of the biggest upsets in the history of Bluffton politics". Howe was on the ticket seeking a fourth term and had drawn no Democratic opposition; the paper attributed the result to "local Republican factional differences". 619 ballots were cast in the village's four precincts and only 433 of them were marked for mayor. [verified] — same source, 8 November 1945.

**186 electors who voted did not vote for mayor**, which is what an uncontested office does to a ballot and is the reason a write-in needed only 225 votes to carry it. [inference] — computed from the two figures in the line above.

**1947 — the losing side tried the same weapon.** "Interest in local politics was stimulated during the week before election by a write-in campaign to reelect W. A. Howe for mayor", and roughly 900 ballots were cast, which the paper put at 75 per cent of the village and "more than double the usual off-year vote". [verified] — same source, 6 November 1947. The result of the mayor's race is not legible on the page that carries it.

**1955 — and a custom stated outright.** David L. Risser (D) was elected mayor over Joseph L. Urich (R) by 354 votes, with council split three and three. "The new president of council and vice mayor will probably be Democrat Francis Reichenbach. According to custom council selects the councilman with the highest number of votes for that position." [verified] — same source, 10 November 1955.

**1957 — "Mayor Risser Only Democrat To Survive Republican Sweep Of Municipal Offices", and the village elected its first councilwoman**, Mrs. Stella Lauriat. [verified] — same source, 7 November 1957.

**1959 — a councilman moved up and the second woman arrived.** Wilbur B. Amstutz (R) defeated Harold F. Klingler (D) 425 to 366, and the Republicans took four of the six council seats. Miss Lois Basinger polled 460 votes to become "the second woman to municipal office in the town's history". [verified] — same source, 5 November 1959. Two women in twenty-one years of this run, and both in the last three of them. [inference] — computed from the two reports.

**Beaverdam is in it too, and it is smaller by an order of magnitude.** Donald E. Barber beat Walter B. Beck for mayor 116 to 43 in 1957, in the village's only contested race that year; in 1959 Robert Snodgrass (R) beat Richard Kizer (D) 119 to 40, with every other office also contested and the whole ticket printed with its vote. [verified] — same source, 7 November 1957 and 5 November 1959. Bluffton's mayoral vote in the same two elections ran in the hundreds on each side.

**The paper reaches further back than its own run, through a nostalgia column.** "From News Grandfather Read" reprints its issue of November 1917 — M. M. Murray (R) elected mayor of Bluffton over A. C. Spangler (D) by 109 votes, the village voting 274 to 203 for woman suffrage and 318 to 166 dry — and "News Our Father's Read" reprints November 1927, where Fred Triblehorn (R) beat A. D. Gratz 450 to 415. [verified] — same source, 7 November 1957, which carries both. Those two are the only Allen County election returns this corpus holds from before 1939. [inference]

**The line does not close, and the paper is why.** W. A. Howe is named as mayor of Bluffton in May 1942, April 1944, May 1946, April 1951 and September 1952 — that is, both before the 1945 election he is reported to have lost and for years after it. [verified] — same source, five further issues.

properties.method: Counted on the ground by the compiler of the 1885 county history as seventy-five mounds, repeated as "some 75" in 1906 by a book that reprints the 1885 text, and reported in 1915 as an estimate against about forty surviving markers. No register exists: the garrison's records were destroyed. [verified]
properties.parameter: graves in the military cemetery at Fort Amanda

blocks.text: **Seventy-five graves.** [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md), which both scans carry identically, with a national cemetery established there in 1812-14 "which has been continued by the settlers". The 1906 history gives some 75 graves and adds that the ground was "formerly cared for by the government as a national cemetery". [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md).

**Forty markers.** By the monument's unveiling in 1915 the same seventy-five is called an estimate and only about forty graves carry a military marker. [verified] — [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md), quoting the souvenir programme, which gives the reason: the identities were lost when the British burned the Capitol and the garrison's records with it.

**Seventy-five flat boats.** [verified] — the same programme, quoted on the facing subject a few pages earlier in the same book. The corpus records the coincidence without explaining it: two counts of two unrelated things, made a century apart from records that no longer exist, agreeing on a number. [inference] — observed here.

**Why this is one node and not four figures on the site.** The 1906 history is not a third witness. Its Fort Amanda chapter reproduces the 1885 text sentence for sentence — the same Harrison date, the same eleven-foot pickets, the same south-east blockhouse, the same Ensign Gray — which is the transmission pattern this corpus found in the war rosters and recorded in [a printed list is a dataset](../../decisions/a-printed-list-is-a-dataset.yml). [verified] — the two books read against each other. So the graves count has two independent sources and not three: an 1885 book and a 1915 programme, and the programme is already calling 1885's figure an estimate.

**The claim nobody will drop.** One of the scows built here is said to have been used by Commodore Perry to buoy his ships over the shallows at Put-in-Bay. The 1885 history offers it "with some degree of authenticity"; the 1921 history calls it "a pleasing story". [verified] — both books. Two historians, thirty-six years apart, both repeat it and neither will stand behind it, which is as close to a source note as either of them comes. [inference]

properties.method: Union of the twenty-three Lima precinct pages of the boards of elections roster — precincts 0005 through 0027 — deduplicated on the office name. `as_of` is the roster's own "last updated" stamp and not the day of retrieval. The seven ward offices are counted as seven, which is how the source names them; a county-wide count that deduplicates differently will not agree on the office total and will agree on the seats. [verified]
properties.parameter: seated holders of the city's elective offices

blocks.text: Every elective seat of the [City of Lima](../jurisdiction/city-of-lima.yml), its holder, and the day the term turns. [verified] — [the elected officials lookup](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md), read across the twenty-three of the county's eighty-eight precincts that lie in the city.
**Eleven seats, eleven offices, none vacant, and one filled by appointment.** [verified] — same source, which marks Jeannine M. Jordan of the fourth ward `*Appointed*` and none of the other ten.

**That is the sharpest contrast in this county's local government.** Twenty-five of the forty-seven seated village officers were appointed to their seats and five village seats stand empty; Lima seats eleven and appointed one. [verified] — [the county's elective seats](allen-county-elected-seats-2026.yml). The city that holds a third of the county's people is the local government whose seats get contested. [inference] See [why the villages are staffed by appointment](../question/why-allen-countys-villages-are-staffed-by-appointment.yml).

**Lima is the only government in Allen County that elects by district.** Its seven council members are chosen one per ward and it elects none at large; every village here elects its council at large, both township boards are elected township-wide, and Delphos elects three at large beside two by ward. [verified] — same source.

**The wards are staggered by parity.** First, third, fifth and seventh began on 5 January 2026; second, fourth and sixth on 1 January 2024. [verified] — same source. Four seats and three alternate every two years, so no single election can turn the council over.

**One city, four term calendars.** The mayor's year runs 1 December to 30 November; the auditor's and the law director's 1 January to 31 December; the president's and the even wards' 1 January to 2 January; the odd wards' 5 January to 6 January. [verified] — same source. The office node called this "what a charter looks like from outside it" when it had three of the four.
**Not one of the eleven carries a party.** The roster prints (R) or (D) beside county and state holders and beside some village ones, and beside none of Lima's. [verified] — same source.
