nodes.label: Crime reported in Lima, 2015–2024

properties.method: Monthly offense and clearance counts summed to calendar years and divided by the agency's own population as the file gives it for June of each year. That population is not the census's — the file puts Lima at 36,452 in 2020 against a census count of 35,579 — so this rate is comparable with the Ohio and United States rates in the same file and not with anything computed from a census denominator. [verified] The department began incident-based reporting on 1 January 2021, so the years before and after that line are not strictly one series. [inference]
properties.parameter: violent crime rate, Lima Police Department jurisdiction

blocks.text: **Lima's violent crime rate has been between two and three times Ohio's in every one of ten years.** [verified] — [the FBI Crime Data Explorer](../../catalog/fbi-crime-data-explorer.md), Lima Police Department.
The agency rates are computed here from counts and the agency's own population; the Ohio and United States rates are the file's, being the sum of its twelve monthly values. [verified] — same source.

**Violent crime here has no trend and property crime fell by forty per cent.** The violent count averaged 280 a year over 2015–2019 and 265 over 2020–2024; the property rate went from 5,672 per hundred thousand to 3,421, a fall of 39.7 per cent. [verified] — same source, computed here. The two measures move independently, which is worth stating because they are usually reported as one number. [inference]

**The clearance rate more than doubled.** 14.6 per cent of violent offenses cleared in 2016 and 12.3 per cent in 2020, against 30.5 per cent in each of 2023 and 2024. [verified] — same source. Whether that is better police work, fewer and different offenses, or the incident-based reporting the department adopted in January 2021 counting differently, this source cannot say. [inference] — see [the agencies](allen-county-law-enforcement-agencies-2026.yml).

**The ratio to Ohio is the stable thing.** 2.38, 2.97, 2.36, 2.07, 2.23, 2.05, 2.02, 2.72, 2.27, 2.47 — no year outside 2.0 to 3.0, across a decade in which Ohio's own rate rose and fell. [verified] — same source, computed here. A city whose absolute rate wanders and whose ratio to its state does not is being moved by whatever moves the state. [inference]

refusals: Whether that is better police work, fewer and different offenses, or the incident-based reporting the department adopted in January 2021 counting differently, this source cannot say.

properties.method: Computed by the Census Bureau from the 2020 TIGER geography, reflecting the corporate boundary as of that geography. [verified]
properties.parameter: land area

blocks.text: Land area of Lima city in the 2020 geography. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), Ohio place file.

This figure is the one in this corpus most exposed to the boundary problem, and it is seeded partly to make that visible. A municipality's land area changes by annexation, so comparing it to a figure from another year without checking the annexations between them compares two different pieces of ground. That check is [boundary-comparability](../../skills/boundary-comparability.md), and the corpus now holds the annexations: fifty-seven of them for the county between 1990 and 2024, eleven of them Lima's, totalling 622 acres. [verified] — [the Boundary and Annexation Survey](../../catalog/census-bas-boundary-changes-ohio.md), as read in [the annexation record](allen-county-annexations-1990-2024.yml). The comparison the caveat was waiting for still cannot be made, for a different reason than the one written here: the land-area column mixes annexation with remeasurement and the county's own land area fell 1,235 acres in a decade it gained ground. See [the control is the figure that cannot move](../../decisions/the-control-is-the-figure-that-cannot-move.yml). This figure describes the **corporation's territory**, not the settlement in the ordinary sense: the Census Bureau tabulates Lima at the corporate boundary of the date, so what the number counts is whatever ground the [City of Lima](../jurisdiction/city-of-lima.yml) had annexed by then. [inference] The node therefore carries a `describes` edge to the jurisdiction as well as to the place. Both are true and they are not the same claim — the place is what the name denotes, and the jurisdiction is what the boundary encloses.

properties.method: Census of Manufactures, taken for the calendar years 1909, 1904 and 1899. Read from rendered images of a 400-dpi scan and checked two ways: the two tables in the volume that report Lima independently agree on 3,607, and the 1909 detail row's components sum to its stated totals both for persons engaged and for wage earners on December 15. Establishments inside the corporate limits only. [verified]
properties.parameter: manufacturing wage earners and value of products, city of Lima

blocks.text: The first measurement of work this corpus has ever held. [verified] — [Abstract of the Thirteenth Census, Supplement for Ohio](../../catalog/census-1910-abstract-supplement-ohio.md), statistics of manufactures.

Written out: **Lima had 85 manufacturing establishments in 1909 employing 3,607 wage earners on average, against 2,733 in 1904 and 1,980 in 1899.** [verified] — same source, the comparative city table and the detail table for cities of 10,000 to 50,000 inhabitants, which agree on 3,607.

**The city's workforce grew 82 per cent in a decade and its output grew 25.** [inference] — computed here. Value per wage earner fell from $3,143 in 1899 to $1,766 in 1904 and recovered only to $2,150 by 1909. Something in Lima's industry became much less productive per head between 1899 and 1904 and had not recovered by 1909.

**Thirty per cent of the wage earners were women** — 1,082 of 3,607 — and 51 were under sixteen. [verified] — same source. The two industries the volume names as Lima's leading ones are **"tobacco manufactures and locomotives"**, which is a workforce of cigar makers and a workforce of machinists in one city. [verified] — same source. See [the locomotive works](../site/lima-locomotive-works-plant.yml).
**Lima was in the group of Ohio cities with products valued between $5,000,000 and $10,000,000**, of thirty-seven cities over 10,000 people. [verified] — same source.

nodes.label: The mayors of Lima, 1842-1886

properties.method: Read from the 1885 county history's chapter on Ottawa Township and Lima City, which narrates the municipal elections year by year from 1842 to 1873 and then prints a list of mayors from 1873 to 1885. Both archive.org digitizations were read and compared line by line; they agree on every name and differ only where scan A substitutes a digit or a letter, each of which is resolved by the sequence rather than by preferring a scan. [verified] Terms are counted as continuous runs under one man, so a re-election is not a new term and the three men who returned after an interval are counted twice. Years are the years of election as the book gives them; the book runs by election year and not by term, so a range like 1851-53 is "elected in 1851, succeeded by the man elected in 1853" and not an assertion about the day either man took office. [inference]
properties.parameter: mayors of Lima, 1842 to 1886

blocks.text: Every mayor of Lima from the town's organization to the printing of the county's first history — **twenty-four men over twenty-seven terms in forty-four years.** [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md), the organic and official history of Ottawa Township, printed pages 476-481, and the list of mayors since 1873 on page 481.

**The corpus's own estimate of this line was wrong in both terms.** It said "about forty holders in forty-three years", written from the shape of the passage rather than from counting it. The count is twenty-four men, twenty-seven terms, and forty-four years from March 1842 to the book's own last entry of 1884-86. [inference] — computed here from the list above.

**Three men served twice**, and none of the three consecutively: Thomas Delzell in 1846 and 1849, Thomas Milligan in 1850 and 1853, and Samuel A. Baxter in 1851 and 1854. [verified] — same source. Richard Metheany served the longest single stretch, four years from 1870.

**Two mayors resigned in office and a third resigned and was reappointed.** Thomas Milligan resigned in January 1854 and Samuel A. Baxter was appointed to the remainder; Thomas M. Robb resigned in September 1869 and the council elected [George W. Overmyer](../person/george-w-overmyer.yml) in his place; and John Melhorn resigned in 1857 and "was appointed in May to fill unexpired term". [verified] — same source. Overmyer is the only mayor in this line the council chose rather than the voters. [inference]

**The book gives the whole council beside the mayor, and the council is where the corpus's other people appear.** [Benjamin C. Faurot](../person/benjamin-faurot.yml) was elected a village trustee in 1867, eighteen years before the well that made him; Matthias H. Nichols was a trustee in 1849, twelve years before he raised the county's first company for the war and after three terms in Congress; Thomas K. Jacobs was a trustee in 1842, marshal in 1846 and treasurer in 1853, and introduced the bill in the Ohio House in April 1861 to tax the county for soldiers' families. [verified] — same source; see [the first company](../event/the-first-lima-company-1861.yml).

**The two digitizations disagree about the date the list starts, and the list settles it.** Scan B prints "The mayors of Lima since 1873" and gives Richard Metheany, 1873; scan A prints 1878 in both places. A list beginning in 1878 cannot open with a man serving 1874-76, so scan B is right and no preference between the scans was needed to say so. [inference] — computed here; see [three witnesses and three dates](../../decisions/three-witnesses-and-three-dates.yml). The same substitution runs through scan A here — 1849 as 1840, 1853 as 1858, Richard as Bichard, Melhorn as Melhom — and every one of them is caught by the sequence it sits in.

**Two later books print this same line, and collating them found the defect in theirs.** The 1906 history's list and the 1921 history's both run from 1842, and the disagreement is confined to four consecutive slots in the 1850s. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md) and [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md).

**The 1906 list has a year with nobody in it, and that is what settles it.** Drop Baxter's second term and the two names after it slide two years earlier, until James A. Newell's April 1858 stops them — leaving **April 1857 to April 1858 with no mayor at all**, the only such hole in thirty-four entries. A list that merely disagreed would not leave a year empty; a list that lost an entry leaves exactly this. [inference] — computed here from the two lists; see [where a list loses a name](../../decisions/where-a-list-loses-a-name.yml).

**The 1921 list lost one more, at the same place.** It gives Milligan once and Baxter once where this line gives each twice, which is what a copyist does reading "Milligan, Baxter, Milligan, Baxter". [inference] — the 1921 history.

**One name in this table is simply wrong, and the book it came from says so three times.** The 1885 mayor list prints "John B. Townsend" in both digitizations. The same volume prints **James B. Townsend** in its election returns, in its index, and in a full biographical sketch — "James B. Townsend, attorney at law, Lima, was born in 1851 ... he was elected mayor of Lima for five years". Both later histories print James. [verified] — the three histories. The table above is left as its source prints it and the reading is James. [inference] — see [James B. Townsend](../person/james-b-townsend.yml), where the same sketch disagrees with the same list about how long he served.

**Two more names are contested and neither is settled.** Both later books print **Dalzell** where this line has Delzell, and **Isaac T. Hickman** where the 1885 book prints J. T. Heckman in both digitizations and in its own index. [verified] — the three histories. The 1885 book prints Delzell seventeen times against Dalzell four, so it is not a slip; and the 1906 and 1921 lists are one lineage rather than two witnesses, since the 1921 book says it is following "the most recent report in Lima". So each of these is one book against one, and the corpus keeps the older reading and records the other. [inference]

**The mayor of 1890 has his name whole in no single book.** The 1885 book prints "I. R. Longsworth", the 1906 list "Ira Longsworth", the 1921 list "Ira R. Longworth". Ira R. Longsworth is the only reading two of the three support in every part. [inference] — the three histories.

refusals: The corpus reads them as two and cannot show it.

properties.method: Read from the 1906 history's dated list of mayors and the 1921 history's undated ordered list, which are very likely one lineage rather than two witnesses: the 1921 book says it is following "the most recent report in Lima", which "enumerates the mayors from the beginning". Dates to 1904 are the 1906 book's. Dates after 1904 are computed here from that book's last dated entry, the 1921 book's statement of the two-year term, and the 1 January 1922 abolition, and are reported as an inference that closes rather than as a source's dating. The count is of entries as printed. It is not a count of terms and not a count of men: the lists give a consecutive re-election its own entry twice and fold three terms into one entry once. [inference]
properties.parameter: entries in the printed lists of Lima's mayors beginning after April 1886

blocks.text: **Everything to 1904 is dated by its source.** [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md), which prints "Mayors of Lima" from April 1842 to "Theo. D. Robb, April, 1904 — " in thirty-four entries.

**Everything after 1904 is dated here, and the dating closes.** The 1921 history gives the succession in order and gives no dates at all, but it states the term — "the mayor and members of City Council have hitherto served two years" — and it dates the end: the commission form of government "comes into effect January 1, 1922, at the end of the term of Mayor Burkhardt". [verified] — [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md). Nine entries follow L. H. Rogers in that list. Nine two-year terms are eighteen years, and April 1904 plus eighteen years is April 1922. [inference] — computed here. The quarter-year residue is the calendar moving: the same 1906 book's list of city solicitors turns on January 1906, where every earlier boundary in it is April.

**The book checks itself once and passes.** Theodore D. Robb appears three times in the list, and a biographical passage elsewhere in the same volume calls him "three times mayor of Lima". [verified] — same source. He died in the third, and the list says the term "was finished by Miles Standish", who is named nowhere else in it.

**The lists cannot be counted as terms, and they say so themselves.** Two men are printed twice running — Theodore D. Robb, and B. H. Simpson — so a consecutive re-election sometimes gets its own entry; but William McComb, Jr.'s six years from 1884 get one entry, and at a two-year term that is three. [verified] — the 1906 and 1921 histories. So the figure below counts entries as printed and not terms served, which are not the same thing anywhere in this line. [inference]
**McComb is the man the city returned to most.** Three separate spells over sixteen years, and H. S. Prophet twice, sixteen years apart. [verified] — the 1906 history.

**The line ends rather than continues.** F. A. Burkhardt was the last mayor of Lima under the aldermanic form, and he was also an advisory editor of the book that records it and the author of a chapter in it. [verified] — [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md); see [the commission government](../event/lima-adopts-commission-government-1922.yml) and [F. A. Burkhardt](../person/frank-a-burkhardt.yml).

nodes.label: Mayors of Lima named inside the gap, 1939–1956

properties.method: Four full-text searches of one newspaper title, and the ALTO OCR of every hit page read in full. "Mayor of Lima" and "Lima mayor" return 22 hits across 21 issues and supply ten of the rows above; "Mayor McClain" supplies two, "Metheany" one, and one more came out of an election-week issue read for another purpose. Nothing here is a term: each row is the date the paper printed the words, not a date the person took or left office, and no row is used to date another. Corbin Shook is counted among the five as a former mayor and is not placed in time. [verified]
properties.parameter: mayors of Lima named in a contemporaneous source, 1939–1956

blocks.text: **[The office](../office/mayor-of-lima.yml) said no source here spanned the ninety-nine years from 1922 to 2021. One did not span them; it sampled them.** A weekly newspaper published in Bluffton, twelve miles up the road, names four different mayors of Lima between 1939 and 1956 and a fifth as a former one. [verified] — [The Bluffton News](../../catalog/chronicling-america.md), `sn87076554`.

**Not one of those fourteen mentions is an election report.** Every name above arrived inside a story about something else — a police appointment, parking meters, a baseball opener, a probate inventory, a symphony, an obituary. [verified] — same source, all fourteen pages read. The one row that reports a Lima election, 20 November 1941, reports it as the *cost* of one: an expense account filed with the county board of elections, printed beside Bluffton's because the comparison was the story. So this table dates people to days and establishes no term, no beginning and no end for any of them. This corpus cannot say who was mayor of Lima on any day but the fourteen printed above. [inference]

**What it does establish is that Lima had a mayor, and a council, and a charter.** The office [the 1921 history said was abolished](../event/lima-adopts-commission-government-1922.yml) effective 1 January 1922 was being held, filled by election and exercising appointment power by November 1939, under "provisions of the City Charter and Ohio civil service laws". [verified] — same source, 8 February 1940. The ninety-nine-year gap is therefore two gaps with a lit stretch between them: 1922 to 1939, and 1956 to 2021. [inference] — computed from the dates above.

**One mayor died in office and the estate is the evidence.** A. L. Metheany was mayor in March 1944; by 31 August the paper called him the late mayor and reported the inventory his administratrix filed in the Allen County probate court — $900 in personal property, $23,019.67 in stocks and bonds, $15,377.84 in accounts and debts receivable, $42,797.51 in all. [verified] — same source. See [Allen L. Metheany](../person/allen-l-metheany.yml), and [Richard Metheany](../person/richard-metheany.yml), mayor of the same town seventy years earlier.

**The mayoralty was non-partisan by 1945 and the county offices were not.** "The results of the light vote in the non-partisan city primary election were tabulated. Only 6,160 voters went to the polls." Three years later the same man who had been mayor ran for county commissioner on a ticket headed REPUBLICAN. [verified] — same source, 9 August 1945 and 28 October 1948.

**A president of council stood in for an absent mayor, and the paper explained it because he was a local boy.** "Emil Kempf, former Bluffton boy is mayor of Lima this week. As president of the Lima council he becomes head of that city's government during the absence of Mayor William Ferguson who is away on a week's vacation." [verified] — same source, 13 September 1945. It is the only account this corpus holds of how Lima's seat is filled when the holder is not in it.

**One of that year's candidates did not live to the primary.** Edward P. Milbaugh, 27, "Lima mayoralty candidate and hotel proprietor", was shot dead on 22 July 1945, and in November a Putnam County Common Pleas jury convicted a sixty-eight-year-old retired carpenter of Ottoville of second-degree murder after three and a half hours; the prosecution said the two had argued over the merits of a fraternal order. [verified] — same source, 8 November 1945. The corpus names the candidate, who was a public one, and not the man convicted, whose name reaches it only through optical character recognition of a neighbouring county's court news. The killing was outside this county and is recorded here because the office it touched is inside it.

refusals: This corpus cannot say who was mayor of Lima on any day but the fourteen printed above.

properties.method: Read from Table 5 of a 300-dpi bitonal scan with no text layer, by rendering the page and reading the block directly rather than by trusting optical character recognition, which misread it. Checked against the eleven differences and eleven percentages the table prints beside the counts, and against two figures the corpus already held from county histories. The `value` above is this series' last and largest term, not the city's peak, which is 1970. [verified]
properties.parameter: total resident population, decennial

blocks.text: Every decennial count for [Lima](../place/lima.yml) from the city's first appearance in the census to 1960. [verified] — [1960 Census, Number of Inhabitants, Ohio](../../catalog/census-1960-number-of-inhabitants-ohio.md), Table 5, *Population of incorporated places of 10,000 or more from earliest census to 1960*.

Written out, because a table is not prose and this corpus publishes prose: **Lima held 7,567 people in 1880, 21,723 in 1900, 41,326 in 1920, 42,287 in 1930, 44,711 in 1940, 50,246 in 1950 and 51,037 in 1960.** [verified] — same source. The four counts before those, 757 in 1850 through 15,981 in 1890, are in the same block of the same table.

**Lima peaked at the 1970 census.** The city rose at every one of the twelve counts above and reached [53,734 in 1970](lima-population-1970-1990.yml), then fell at every count since. The corpus has carried the caveat that 1970 was the earliest federal figure it held and therefore a lower bound rather than a peak, and has said so on the public site and in two tests. It was the peak. [verified] — this source for 1850–1960 and [the 1990 Census volume](../../catalog/census-cph-2-37-ohio.md) for 1970. The claim is about census years: a city can rise and fall inside a decade unobserved, and decennial data cannot speak to that for Lima or anywhere else.

**The last decade before the peak is the flattest.** Lima gained 791 people in the 1950s, 1.6% — its smallest decennial gain in a hundred and ten years, and a tenth of the 1940s' rate. The city did not turn at 1970 so much as arrive there slowing. [inference] — computed from the series above. What happened between 1960 and 1970 to produce a further 2,697 is not established here.

**It corrects the 1920 figure this corpus has published since the oil phase.** The corpus held 41,306, from [Rusler's 1921 history](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md), which prints it twice. The Census gives **41,326**, and both neighbouring rows of Table 5 require that value. Twenty people, and the difference matters less than which of the two sources was believed: the 1921 figure was marked here as [a single witness read once](../../decisions/a-single-witness-read-once.yml), and it is the one that broke. The two figures the same three histories supplied that this table can also test — 7,567 in 1880 and 21,723 in 1900 — match the Census to the person. [verified] — both sources.

properties.method: Three county histories' compilations of published census returns, one figure from each. The 1900 and 1920 figures are for Ottawa Township, which both sources state was coextensive with the city. [verified] The value above is **superseded**: the Census gives 41,326 for the same date and this node keeps 41,306 because its subject is what the histories printed. For Lima's 1920 population, cite [the federal series](lima-population-1850-1960.yml). [verified]
properties.parameter: total resident population, decennial, as three county histories printed it

blocks.text: The city's counts across the oil boom and the forty years after it. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md) for 1880, [History of Allen County, 1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md) for 1900, and [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md) for 1920.

Written out, because a table is not prose and this corpus publishes prose: these three histories put **7,567 people in 1880, 21,723 in 1900 and 41,306 in 1920** in Lima. [verified] — the three sources above, one figure each. **The Census Bureau confirms the first two to the person and contradicts the third**, giving 41,326 for 1920. [verified] — [1960 Census, Number of Inhabitants, Ohio](../../catalog/census-1960-number-of-inhabitants-ohio.md), Table 5; see [the federal series](lima-population-1850-1960.yml), which supersedes this node as a measure and leaves it standing as the record of what the histories printed.

**The corpus believed the wrong one of the two, and had already said which it would be.** The 1920 figure was marked here as [a single witness read once](../../decisions/a-single-witness-read-once.yml) — Rusler's is the only scan of that book the corpus holds, and no second source could be brought against it. The Census table settles it not by being federal but by showing its work: each count is printed beside its increase over the preceding census, and 30,508 + 10,818 = 41,326 while 41,326 + 961 = 42,287. Rusler's 41,306 fails both, and the same passage of Rusler subtracts its own list of incorporated places from the county total and lands a thousand out. [verified] — same sources. No third witness was consulted, and none is needed for arithmetic. [inference]

**These are the corpus's first Lima figures earlier than 2000.** Lima nearly tripled between 1880 and 1900 and nearly doubled again by 1920 — **a fivefold rise in forty years**, which is the demographic shape of [the oil strike](../event/lima-oil-strike.yml). [inference]

**The 1900 and 1920 figures are township figures and that is not an error here.** [Ottawa Township](../question/what-became-of-german-and-ottawa-townships.yml) was coextensive with the city — the 1906 table says so in the row label, twenty-one years before the 1921 volume says it in prose. [verified] — same sources. So the township count is the city count, and the corpus can now date that coextension to 1900 or earlier rather than to 1921.

**All three are compilations, not census publications**, and this node asked for the thing that would test them: "a place-level decennial series from the Census Bureau would replace all three." It arrived, and it replaced one. Two of the three compilations were right to the person across eighty years, which is a better result for county histories than this corpus expected and is worth recording as such. [inference] The 1880 figure comes from a table whose county total the corpus has already found to disagree with the 1906 volume by sixteen people at 1850 — see [the county series](allen-county-population-1830-1900.yml), where the same question is open and no federal series has yet reached it.

properties.method: Read from the places table of the 1990 Ohio CPH-2 volume. The `value` above is the series maximum and also its first term, which made it a lower bound on the city's peak until the 1960 volume supplied the twelve counts before it. It is the peak. [verified]
properties.parameter: total resident population, decennial

blocks.text: **53,734 in 1970, 47,827 in 1980 and 45,549 in 1990.** [verified] — [1990 Census, Population and Housing Unit Counts, Ohio](../../catalog/census-cph-2-37-ohio.md), which marks the 1980 figure `r` for revised. Housing units ran 18,443, 19,096 and 18,666 across the same three counts.

**This locates a peak the corpus said one phase ago it could not see.** Reading only [7,567 in 1880, 21,723 in 1900 and 41,306 in 1920](lima-population-1880-1920.yml) against 40,307 in 2000 — the 1920 figure has since been corrected to 41,326 — the corpus concluded that "eighty years net to roughly nothing" and the peak was somewhere inside them. It is: **the city was 53,734 in 1970**, thirty per cent above its 1920 count and half again what it is today. The rise and the fall were both real and the corpus had a chord across them. [inference]

**And 1970 is the peak, not a lower bound on it.** The four counts this node could not see are 42,287 (1930), 44,711 (1940), 50,246 (1950) and 51,037 (1960), every one of them below 53,734 and each above the one before. [verified] — [1960 Census, Number of Inhabitants, Ohio](../../catalog/census-1960-number-of-inhabitants-ohio.md); see [the federal series](lima-population-1850-1960.yml). The caveat this node wrote against its own figure is answered by evidence rather than dropped.

So Lima's series, at the census years the corpus holds: 7,567 (1880) · 21,723 (1900) · 41,326 (1920) · 51,037 (1960) · **53,734 (1970)** · 47,827 (1980) · 45,549 (1990) · 40,307 (2000) · 35,579 (2020). Between 1970 and 2020 the city lost 18,155 people, **33.8 per cent of itself**, while [the county](allen-county-population-1940-1990.yml) lost 8,927, or 8.0 per cent. Lima's loss is twice the county's, which means the rest of Allen County **gained 9,228** over the same fifty years. [inference] — computed from the two series. That is a different story from the one the corpus has been telling from four years of recent data, where the ring shrinks too: over the long run the ring grew while the city emptied, and only lately have both been falling.

**And the boundary moved underneath these counts.** Between 1980 and 1990 Lima annexed ground from American, Bath and Shawnee townships. [verified] — same source, Geographic Change Notes. So the fall from 47,827 to 45,549 happened while the corporation was getting larger, which makes it an understatement of the decline inside the old boundary. [inference] This is the first annexation event this corpus has ever held, against a [comparability caveat](../../skills/boundary-comparability.md) it has carried since genesis.

properties.method: Decennial enumeration as revised for the intercensal series. [verified]

nodes.label: Lima's railroad traffic, 1905

properties.method: Read from the transportation chapter of the 1906 county history, which dates itself to 1905 by saying the Western Ohio "was completed four years ago, in the spring of 1901". Every sum and product above was computed here from figures the book prints, and each is reported as closing or not closing rather than corrected. [verified]
properties.parameter: passenger trains landing in Lima daily

blocks.text: A page of the 1906 county history prints thirty-odd figures about Lima's railroads. Six are arithmetic, one does not follow, and one settles an argument the book has with itself. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md), whose transportation chapter dates itself to 1905.

**The passenger count closes exactly, twice.** The book lists six steam roads with their daily passenger trains — 14, 10, 12, 6, 6 and 1 — and two interurbans with 20 and 8, then says "there are 49 steam and 28 electric trains landing passengers in Lima daily, making a total of 77 trains". The steam figures sum to **49**, the electric to **28**, and the two to **77**. [verified] — same source, arithmetic performed here on its printed list. Nothing was dropped between the list and the total, which is the only evidence available that the list is complete. [inference]

**The forecast on the same page does not close.** Four additions are promised for 1906: twenty more cars when the Western Ohio reaches Toledo, the Fort Wayne, Van Wert & Lima rising from eight to twenty-five, sixteen on its new Ottawa branch, and twenty on the Lima & Toledo. That is 73 added to 77, or **150**; the book says **145**. [verified] — same source. No reading of the paragraph produces 145: folding the Ottawa branch into the twenty-five gives 134, counting the twenty-five as additional gives 158. [inference]

**Eight figures produce fourteen.** 143 trains × 52 cars = 7,436 cars; × 30 tons = 223,080 tons; 127 car-load cars × 30 = 3,810 tons; 178 × 30 = 5,340; 114 less-than-car-load cars × 5 = 570; 134 × 5 = 670. [verified] — same source, arithmetic performed here. Five counts and three rates yield six more figures, so **six of the fourteen numbers in that block are products of the other eight** and its tonnages carry no information its car counts do not. [inference] — see [arithmetic that closes is about the compiler](../../decisions/arithmetic-that-closes-is-about-the-compiler.yml).

**And 143 is not the same count as the trains on the list.** The six roads' freight trains sum to 90 a day; "in and out" would make 180. Neither is 143, so the freight block was compiled from a different return than the trunk-line table on the facing page. [inference] — same source.

**Most of what moved through Lima had no business there.** 127 + 178 + 114 + 134 is **553** cars handled at the freight offices daily against 7,436 in and out — 7 to 15 per cent, depending on whether a through car is counted twice. [inference] — the same figures.

**The first exact railroad employment count this corpus holds.** 108 men in the railway yards day and night and 74 in the freight offices, **182**, beside 73 miles of yard trackage and 16 shifting engines. [verified] — same source. Every earlier figure was a range or a floor; see [the railroads](allen-county-railroads-1883-1921.yml).

**Forty-four counties, not forty-six.** The book says Lima's trunk lines run "direct to half of the counties in the State — to be exact, 46", then says twice elsewhere that a train may be boarded in **44** counties and reach Lima without a change of cars. [verified] — same source. Ohio has 88 counties, so half is 44 and the sentence contradicts its own adverb. [verified] — [the 2020 Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), 88 Ohio county rows. The corpus reads 44. [inference] — resting on a county count no source here establishes for 1905.

refusals: Six are arithmetic, one does not follow, and one settles an argument the book has with itself.

nodes.label: Lima refinery operator and crude capacity, 1994–2026

properties.method: Thirty-one annual reports, `SITE` LIMA and `STATE_NAME` Ohio, taking the `TOTAL OPERABLE CAPACITY` row for barrels per calendar day. Every report from 1994 to 2026 except 1996 and 1998, which are not archived. Twelve are shown; every figure above is from all thirty-one. [verified]
properties.parameter: Atmospheric Crude Distillation Capacity (barrels per calendar day), Total Operable

blocks.text: Who filed for [the refinery](../site/lima-refinery.yml) and how much crude it could run, as of 1 January of each report year. [verified] — [EIA Refinery Capacity Report](../../catalog/eia-refinery-capacity.md).

**The refinery is larger than it has ever been in this series, and by a quarter.** 145,000 barrels per calendar day in 1994 against 183,000 in 2026 — up 38,000, or 26 per cent — across the decades in which the county's [manufacturing employment](allen-county-manufacturing-employment-1969-2022.yml) fell by more than half. [verified] — [EIA Refinery Capacity Report](../../catalog/eia-refinery-capacity.md). The low is the first year and the high is the last four.

**It is the largest refinery in Ohio.** 183,000 against 172,800 and 150,800 at Toledo and 100,000 at Canton — 30 per cent of the state's 606,600 barrels per calendar day, and 36th of the 124 refineries in the United States. [verified] — [EIA Refinery Capacity Report](../../catalog/eia-refinery-capacity.md), the 2026 report.

**The trough is 146,120 in 2007, the last Premcor year, and the recovery is the Husky years.** Capacity fell 15,380 from the 161,500 it held through 2003, and has risen 36,880 since. [verified] — [EIA Refinery Capacity Report](../../catalog/eia-refinery-capacity.md).

This series dates changes of filing entity and not changes of ownership, and the corporation column does not exist before the 2010 report. [verified] The 1996 and 1998 reports are not published, and the BP-to-Clark change falls in the second gap.

nodes.label: Lima's street railway under four names, 1878–1921

properties.method: Counted from three county histories, each naming the operator of its own day, plus the 1917 federal directory for the absence of the third name. Names, not companies: no source states that any one of these bodies became the next, and the corpus counts what was printed. [verified]
properties.parameter: company names under which Lima's street railway was operated

blocks.text: **The first is described down to the streets it ran on.** "Lima Street Railroad Company. — This company was organized in June, 1878, with George Jameson president and Frederick Agerter secretary. The company's lines run from the Fort Wayne depot west on Wayne to Main, south on Main to Market, and west on Market to the stables beyond the city limits. In winter, sleighs take the place of street cars. The fare is 5 cents, and the trips from 7 A. M. to 10 P. M., regular." [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md).

**[Benjamin Faurot](../person/benjamin-faurot.yml) owned it and lost it.** He "acquired the ownership of the city's first street railway — then a horse-car line", and it is named among the things that slipped through his fingers with the strawboard money: "the Lima street railway system, the Lima Electric Light Company, the Faurot Block and the land about the city." [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md).

**The one dated transfer is a lease, and the book puts it in a biography rather than in its transportation chapter.** "On July 1, 1905, The Lima Electric Railway & Light Company was succeeded by the Lima & Toledo Traction Company, which has leased the property and has powers almost unlimited." [verified] — same source. That chapter, describing the Lima & Toledo as a road still being graded, does not mention that it had by then taken over the city's cars. [inference]

**The system between the horses and the lease was rebuilt from nothing.** The manager who came to Lima in 1902 for the Lima Electric Railway & Light Company "built an entire new system, power house, etc.", having earlier turned a horse-car line into an electric railway in Kansas. [verified] — same source.

**The last name is a company that is not from here.** By 1921 the fifteen miles of electric railway in the city are operated by [the Ohio Electric](../organization/ohio-electric-railway.yml). [verified] — [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md).

**What is not on record is every transfer but one.** No source here states when or how the Lima Street Railroad Company became the Lima Electric Railway & Light Company, nor when the Ohio Electric took over from the Lima & Toledo. The corpus treats the four as one railway because each book describes the same streets, and not because any of them says so. [inference]

properties.method: Computed by the Census Bureau from the 2020 TIGER geography. [verified]
properties.parameter: land area

blocks.text: Land area of [Ohio House District 4](../division/ohio-house-district-4-2020.yml) in the 2020 geography. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), state legislative lower chamber file.

nodes.label: Peak flows on the Ottawa River, 1924–2025

properties.method: Fetched from the USGS peak-streamflow service for site 04187500 and 04187100 and counted here by water year, which runs 1 October to 30 September and is named for the year it ends in. The two gauges are not combined into one series and no figure here is computed across both. The `value` is the largest peak either gauge recorded and the `as_of` is the day it happened, which is not the same as the largest flow the river has ever carried: the record covers 79 of the 102 years between 1924 and 2025, and none before. [inference]
properties.parameter: highest recorded peak flow on the Ottawa River

blocks.text: **The Ottawa River has been gauged for seventy-nine water years and the record is in two halves that cannot be joined.** [verified] — [USGS peak streamflow](../../catalog/usgs-nwis.md).

**They are different places, different periods, and seven water years apart.** Allentown is downstream of Lima and drains a quarter more ground; nothing gauged the river between water year 1982 and water year 1988. [verified] — same source. The median annual peak is 3,240 cubic feet a second at Allentown and 3,210 at Lima — almost identical from a basin a quarter smaller — and the corpus does not read that as a change in the river, because the two figures are from different decades and either urbanisation or the weather of two eras would explain it. [inference]

**Each half has holes and the holes have shapes.** Allentown is missing water years 1936 to 1938 and 1940 to 1942 — the Depression and the war. Lima is missing **2000 to 2009 exactly**, ten consecutive years. [verified] — same source, computed here.

**That ten-year hole swallowed three of the county's four flood declarations.** The federal disaster declarations for severe storms and flooding fall in 2004, 2005 and 2007, and the gauge was not running in any of them. [verified] — same source and [the declarations](allen-county-disaster-declarations-1965-2020.yml). What was in the river in those three years is not recorded anywhere this corpus can reach.

**And the largest measured flood in the modern record brought no federal declaration at all.** 5,700 cubic feet a second on 28 February 2011 is the highest of the Lima gauge's 27 water years, and 2011 is not a declaration year; nor is 2015, the second highest. [verified] — [USGS peak streamflow](../../catalog/usgs-nwis.md) and [OpenFEMA](../../catalog/fema-disaster-declarations.md). This is not evidence that the aid was misdirected. It is evidence that a declaration is an administrative act, which the declarations node had to reason its way to and this measures. [inference]

**The two records overlap on one weather declaration in sixty years.** The gauge covers water years 1989-1999 and 2010-2025; the only non-pandemic declaration inside that window is the storm of June 2012, and that water year's peak — 3,170 cfs on 30 November 2011, sixteenth of twenty-seven — was not in that storm, which the declaration titles as straight-line winds. [verified] — [USGS peak streamflow](../../catalog/usgs-nwis.md) and [OpenFEMA](../../catalog/fema-disaster-declarations.md), computed here; see [the intersection, not the union](../../decisions/the-intersection-not-the-union.yml).

**A third file covers the gauge's ten-year hole and does not fill it.** The county's severe weather record has ninety-five events in the 2000s, including flash floods in 2003, 2004 and 2007. [verified] — [the storm record](allen-county-storm-events-1950-2026.yml). **But a flash flood report is a road under water, not a discharge**, and no arithmetic joins the two: the weather file records that water reached somewhere and the gauge records how much passed a point. The hole in the flow record stays a hole. [inference] — see [the intersection, not the union](../../decisions/the-intersection-not-the-union.yml).

**And the largest flow ever measured here is in none of the three files but this one.** January 1959 brought no federal declaration, and the weather record did not begin counting floods until 1996. [verified] — [the declarations](allen-county-disaster-declarations-1965-2020.yml) and the storm record above.

properties.mouth: 41.2875489, -84.3557802, in Defiance County. Joins the Maumee River. [inference]

blocks.text: The river that collects Allen County's drainage and carries it north to the Maumee at Defiance. [inference] It rises at 40.6669957, -83.8938286 and discharges at 41.2875489, -84.3557802 in Defiance County. [verified] — [USGS GNIS](../../catalog/gnis-domestic-names-ohio.md), feature 1065901. It gives its name to Auglaize Township in the county's south — one of the twelve townships recorded in the [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md). [verified]

Its significance to this corpus is directional. Allen County drains north to Lake Erie rather than south to the Ohio, and the Auglaize is the channel by which it does so. That single fact organizes a great deal: the county's swamp history, its canal, and the basin its water quality is accounted for in are all consequences of being on the Lake Erie side of the divide. [inference]

**It carried freight in 1813 and cannot now.** [Fort Amanda](../site/fort-amanda.yml) stood on its west bank and shipped flour downstream in barrels: Green Clay's letter of 20 June 1813 from Camp Meigs records a consignment received from the fort through Ensign Gray, and the garrison had spent the previous winter building flat boats on this water. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md), both scans. The 1921 history calls that "a thing that would be an utter impossibility on the Auglaize today" and gives the reason — the timber gone and the country drained, so the water runs off instead of standing. [verified] — [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md). A navigable stream became an unnavigable one by clearing and tiling the ground around it. [inference]

**It rises in this county**, at 40.6669957, -83.8938286 in Auglaize township — the township named after it. [verified] — [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md), point-in-polygon. So Allen County is not merely drained by the Auglaize; it is the ground the river starts on. See [where the Auglaize rises](../question/where-the-auglaize-rises.yml). Its whole subbasin, `04100007`, is one of the seven that make up the Maumee's drainage; the four blocks of that township on [the Scioto side](scioto-river-basin.yml) drain the opposite way, so the divide and this river's source are in the same township. [verified] — [USGS Watershed Boundary Dataset](../../catalog/usgs-watershed-boundary.md).

**Twenty-two highway bridges cross it in Allen County, and the oldest bridge in the county is one of them.** The Hay Road structure in [Auglaize Township](../place/auglaize-township.yml) was built in 1909 and is still carrying traffic. [verified] — [what the bridges cross](../measure/allen-county-bridge-crossings-2025.yml) and [the Hay Road bridge](../site/hay-road-bridge.yml).

**It is the larger river and the ungauged one.** The USGS site near Spencerville drains 219 square miles against 160 for the Ottawa at Allentown, and neither it nor the Kossuth site at 201 square miles has an annual peak record; the Ottawa has two. [verified] — [the monitoring sites](../measure/allen-county-water-gauges-2026.yml). Everything this corpus can say about how much water moves through Allen County is about the smaller river, because the smaller river runs through the city. [inference]

**Lima drinks from it, and it is the river with no flow record.** Two of the city's ten surface intakes are on the Auglaize. [verified] — [the water systems](../measure/allen-county-water-systems-2026.yml). So the county's largest water system draws on 219 square miles of drainage for which not one annual peak has ever been recorded, while the smaller Ottawa has two gauges and seventy-nine water years. [inference]

The glacially-formed wetland that covered much of northwest Ohio until it was drained in the second half of the nineteenth century. Allen County lies at its southern margin, and its northern townships were within it. [inference]

It belongs in this corpus because it is the negative space in the county's settlement history: the swamp is why this part of Ohio was settled late relative to the south of the state, why the drainage tile and ditch systems are as extensive as they are, and why the land is as productive as it is now that they exist. [inference] It is also a feature that no longer exists as such, which is a thing this class must be able to hold — a natural-feature node is not required to describe present ground.

**It has no GNIS record.** No feature named "Great Black Swamp" appears anywhere in the 17,921 rows of the Ohio file. [verified] — [USGS GNIS](../../catalog/gnis-domestic-names-ohio.md). That is not because the gazetteer omits vanished features: it carries 56 `Swamp` features in Ohio and marks the drained ones "(historical)" in the name itself. The likelier reason is that GNIS names features with a locatable point, and a wetland that covered much of northwest Ohio across a dozen counties does not have one. [inference] So this node keeps no identifier, and the absence is a fact about how gazetteers work rather than a gap in the retrieval.

nodes.label: Hog Creek

properties.mouth: 40.7708852, -83.9557761 — the head of the Ottawa River.

blocks.text: The stream that, joining Little Hog Creek, forms the Ottawa River. Its mouth is at 40.7708852, -83.9557761 and it rises at 40.7139417, -83.7221552 in the county's east. [verified] — [USGS GNIS](../../catalog/gnis-domestic-names-ohio.md), feature 1066038.

That mouth coordinate is the whole point of this node. It is identical, to seven decimal places, to the source coordinate GNIS gives for [the Ottawa River](ottawa-river.yml) and to the mouth GNIS gives for [Little Hog Creek](little-hog-creek.yml). Three records written by one authority place the same point at the end of two creeks and the head of a river, which is what a confluence looks like in a names file. [verified] — same source. Every `flows-into` edge in this corpus before this one was asserted from general knowledge.

Hog Creek is also the older name of the whole watercourse, and the corpus's [Ottawa River](ottawa-river.yml) node records the name surviving in local usage. GNIS is consistent with that and does not establish it: what the file shows is that the name attaches today to the upper tributary only. [inference]
Ohio has a second Hog Creek, in Champaign County — feature 1041646, and unrelated. [verified] — same source.

refusals: GNIS is consistent with that and does not establish it: what the file shows is that the name attaches today to the upper tributary only.

properties.mouth: 40.7708852, -83.9557761 — the head of the Ottawa River, shared with Hog Creek.

blocks.text: The second of the two creeks that meet to form the Ottawa River. Its mouth is at 40.7708852, -83.9557761 and it rises at 40.722274, -83.8979957. [verified] — [USGS GNIS](../../catalog/gnis-domestic-names-ohio.md), feature 1042627.
Its mouth coordinate is byte-identical to [Hog Creek](hog-creek.yml)'s mouth and to [the Ottawa River](ottawa-river.yml)'s source. [verified] — same source.

nodes.label: Maumee River Basin

blocks.text: The drainage basin that **almost all** of Allen County lies within — the largest watershed draining to the Great Lakes, discharging to Lake Erie at Toledo. 3,548 of the county's 3,552 census blocks and 102,107 of its 102,206 people are in the Great Lakes Region, across three subbasins: Auglaize `04100007` holds 3,200 blocks and Blanchard `04100008` holds 348. [verified] — [USGS Watershed Boundary Dataset](../../catalog/usgs-watershed-boundary.md), by block composition.

**This basin is not a hydrologic unit, which is why no code is recorded here.** The Maumee's drainage is seven subbasins — `04100003` St. Joseph through `04100009` Lower Maumee — and the next unit up that contains them, `041000` Western Lake Erie, also contains six that are nothing to do with the Maumee: Raisin, Sandusky, Huron and three more. [verified] — [USGS Watershed Boundary Dataset](../../catalog/usgs-watershed-boundary.md). So the honest answer to this node's genesis question about its own HUC is that it does not have one, and writing `0410` here would have named a basin four times too large.

**Its other genesis question is answered against it.** Part of Allen County does drain to the Ohio River: four blocks in [Auglaize Township](../place/auglaize-township.yml), 99 people, sit in [the Scioto basin](scioto-river-basin.yml). [verified] — same source. The corpus asserted the Lake Erie side for the whole county from genesis and flagged the southern townships as unchecked; checking them cost one query and moved 99 people to the Gulf of Mexico.

refusals: It is included at genesis for that reason: without it the trace from the Ottawa River runs to the Auglaize and stops in mid-air, and the corpus cannot say where its water goes.

properties.source: 41.0828261, -85.1321928 — the St. Joseph and St. Marys confluence, Fort Wayne.

blocks.text: The river Allen County's water reaches last before Lake Erie. It rises at 41.0828261, -85.1321928 — the confluence of the St. Joseph and St. Marys at Fort Wayne, Indiana — and discharges at 41.6994922, -83.4599325 at Toledo. [verified] — [USGS GNIS](../../catalog/gnis-domestic-names-ohio.md), feature 1084017.

The discharge coordinate is what makes the corpus's Lake Erie claim more than an assertion. Allen County's water leaves the county by the Auglaize, and the river the Auglaize joins ends at Toledo on Lake Erie rather than anywhere on the Ohio. [inference] — the coordinate is verified; that the Auglaize joins *this* river at Defiance is not established by a names file.

nodes.label: Ottawa River

properties.huc_code: 0410000703 Upper Ottawa River, 0410000705 Lower Ottawa River
properties.mouth: 40.9950509, -84.2413355, in Putnam County. Joins the Auglaize River. [inference]
properties.source: 40.7708852, -83.9557761 — the Hog Creek / Little Hog Creek confluence.

blocks.text: The stream that runs through Lima, and the county's principal watercourse. It begins at 40.7708852, -83.9557761 and discharges at 40.9950509, -84.2413355 in Putnam County. [verified] — [USGS GNIS](../../catalog/gnis-domestic-names-ohio.md), feature 1070882. That the discharge point is on the Auglaize remains [inference]: a names file gives a coordinate and never says what is at it.

**It does not begin east of the city; it begins at a confluence.** Its source coordinate is identical to the mouths GNIS records for [Hog Creek](hog-creek.yml) and [Little Hog Creek](little-hog-creek.yml), so the river's head is where those two creeks meet. [verified] — same source. The older name of the whole watercourse was Hog Creek, and the name now attaches to the upper tributary; GNIS is consistent with that and does not establish it. [inference]

**Allen County's own rows do not contain it.** GNIS files a stream under the county of its mouth, so the county's principal river is filed under Putnam and is absent from the 113 features listed for Allen. [verified] — same source.

The present name is shared with a larger, unrelated Ottawa River near Toledo — feature 1066879 in Lucas County against this one's 1070882. [verified] — same source. The collision is now resolvable by identifier rather than by care.

**Where its water goes is now sourced rather than assumed.** The river has two watersheds of its own — `0410000703` Upper Ottawa River and `0410000705` Lower Ottawa River — and both sit inside subbasin `04100007`, which is named for and drains to the [Auglaize](auglaize-river.yml). [verified] — [USGS Watershed Boundary Dataset](../../catalog/usgs-watershed-boundary.md). That settles the basin and not the confluence: the WBD says this water reaches the Auglaize and never says which stream it joins first. Those two Ottawa watersheds hold 47,578 of the county's people between them, 47 per cent, which is what it means to call this the county's principal watercourse.

Being the watercourse Lima grew on, it was also the receiving water for the refinery and the works — the environmental history of this stream and the industrial history of the city are the same subject. [inference]

**Forty-one highway bridges cross it — more than cross any other water in the county, and nearly twice the Auglaize's twenty-two**, though the Auglaize is the larger river. [verified] — [what the bridges cross](../measure/allen-county-bridge-crossings-2025.yml). The difference is [Lima](../place/lima.yml): this river runs through the county seat, and a city is a place where every street has to get over the water. [inference]

**It is the only river in the county with a measured flow, and its record is in two halves.** A gauge at Allentown ran 1924 to 1981 over 160 square miles of drainage; one at Lima has run since 1989 over 128. Seven water years separate them and nothing gauged the river in between. [verified] — [the peak flows](../measure/ottawa-river-peak-flows-1924-2025.yml).

**The largest flow ever measured here is 7,740 cubic feet a second, on 22 January 1959**, more than twice the median annual peak and nineteen per cent above the next largest. [verified] — same source; see [the flood of 1959](../event/the-ottawa-river-flood-of-1959.yml). The largest in the modern half is 5,700, on 28 February 2011.

refusals: The older name of the whole watercourse was Hog Creek, and the name now attaches to the upper tributary; GNIS is consistent with that and does not establish it.

blocks.text: The drainage basin of the Scioto River, which discharges to the Ohio River at Portsmouth and through it to the Gulf of Mexico. **Ninety-nine people in Allen County live in it.** [verified] — [USGS Watershed Boundary Dataset](../../catalog/usgs-watershed-boundary.md).

Four census blocks in [Auglaize Township](../place/auglaize-township.yml), at the county's south-east corner between 40.6487 and 40.7104 north, fall in hydrologic unit `05060001` — the Upper Scioto subbasin of the Ohio Region. Every other block in the county, 3,548 of 3,552, is in the Great Lakes Region and drains to [the Maumee basin](maumee-river-basin.yml). [verified] — same source, by block composition; all 3,552 blocks land in exactly one subbasin and their populations sum to the county's own enumeration of 102,206.

The subwatershed those four blocks sit in is `050600010101`, **Cottonwood Ditch** — a headwater of the Scioto rising in Auglaize Township. [verified] — same source. It is the only named feature on the Ohio River side of the divide in this county.

**No instrument stands on this side of the divide.** All 184 USGS water monitoring sites in Allen County are in Maumee hydrologic units — 168 in the Auglaize, 14 in the Blanchard, two in others — and none in an Ohio River unit. [verified] — [the monitoring sites](../measure/allen-county-water-gauges-2026.yml). That is an absence of gauges and not evidence against the four blocks above: ninety-nine people and a headwater ditch do not get a gauge, and the instrument network was never asked the question this node answers. [inference]

The county's chief fiscal officer and its assessor of real property. The auditor is chosen "quadrennially in each county" and holds office "for four years", and the term begins "on the second Monday in March next after his election". [verified] — [Ohio Revised Code §319.01](../../catalog/ohio-revised-code.md).

**It is the only county office here whose term does not begin in January**, and the roster bears the statute out: the present term runs 13 March 2023 to 7 March 2027, and 13 March 2023 was the second Monday of that month. [verified] — [Ohio county elected officials lookup](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md).

The office keeps the real-property records and financial statements, licenses dogs, regulates weights and measures, administers unclaimed funds and runs the county land bank. It also administers **current agricultural use valuation**, which taxes farmland on what it yields rather than what it would sell for. [verified] — [the county's site](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md). That last function is a live one here: the county was 92.5 per cent farmland in 1910 and the corpus has no later measurement of how much it is now. See [the county's farms](../measure/allen-county-farms-1900-1910.yml).

properties.selection_method: countywide election, terms staggered by statute

blocks.text: The county's governing body, and the first multi-seat office in this corpus. Three commissioners hold it at once, elected countywide to four-year terms. [verified] — [Ohio Revised Code §305.01](../../catalog/ohio-revised-code.md): "The board of county commissioners shall consist of three persons."

**The three seats are distinguished by the day their terms begin, one day apart.** One seat runs from the first day of January after its election; of the two elected together, one begins on "the second day of January next after his election" and the other on "the third day". [verified] — same source. Allen County's roster shows exactly that: 1 January 2023, 2 January 2025 and 3 January 2025. [verified] — [Ohio county elected officials lookup](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md). The dates were read before the statute was, and the statute predicted them.
The board meets in general session every Tuesday and Thursday. [verified] — [the county's site](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md).

nodes.label: Clerk of Courts of Allen County

blocks.text: The custodian of the record for the county's courts. The office handles the "filing, preservation, retrieval and public dissemination of all documents and records" for the Court of Common Pleas, its Domestic Relations Division, and the Third District Court of Appeals. [verified] — [the clerk of courts' site](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md).

**It serves a court that is not the county's own.** The [Third District Court of Appeals](../jurisdiction/third-district-court-of-appeals.yml) hears appeals from seventeen Ohio counties, and its records are kept here — so the office is the point where a county officer does work for a regional court. [verified] — [the court's own site](../../catalog/third-district-court-of-appeals.md), which names the seventeen. That count was an [inference] on this node for one phase and is now read from the source.

The office also runs an Auto Title Division, which is where a motor vehicle title is issued in this county. [verified] — same source. That is the office's highest-volume public function and has nothing to do with courts. [inference]

The present term runs 6 January 2025 to 31 December 2028, four years. [verified] — [Ohio county elected officials lookup](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md). The holder of this office is barred by statute from also being [county engineer](allen-county-engineer.yml). [verified] — [Ohio Revised Code §315.02](../../catalog/ohio-revised-code.md).

The courts this office serves now have nodes: [the Court of Common Pleas](../jurisdiction/allen-county-court-of-common-pleas.yml), [the Lima Municipal Court](../jurisdiction/lima-municipal-court.yml) — whose territory is the whole county despite its name — and [the Third District](../jurisdiction/third-district-court-of-appeals.yml). [verified] — the sources named above.

The office that determines cause of death where a death is violent, suspicious, or otherwise not plainly natural. Ohio requires its holder to be a physician: "a physician who is licensed under Chapter 4731. of the Revised Code to practice medicine and surgery or osteopathic medicine and surgery, and who is in good standing in the person's profession", and to have held that licence for at least two years before election. [verified] — [Ohio Revised Code §313.02](../../catalog/ohio-revised-code.md).

That requirement makes the coroner the only county office here whose candidate pool is fixed by a profession rather than by residence, and in a county of about a hundred thousand people the pool is small. [inference]

The office investigates deaths from crime, violence, suicide or suspicious circumstances, performs autopsies and toxicology, determines blood alcohol in fatal crashes, and testifies as an expert witness. [verified] — [the county's site](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md).
The present term runs 6 January 2025 to 31 December 2028, four years. [verified] — [Ohio county elected officials lookup](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md).

The office responsible for the county's roads and bridges, and the only county office whose holder must be qualified twice over. Ohio requires the county engineer to be "a registered professional engineer and a registered surveyor, licensed to practice in this state". [verified] — [Ohio Revised Code §315.02](../../catalog/ohio-revised-code.md).

**The same section bars four of this county's other elected officers from holding it**: "No person holding the office of clerk of the court of common pleas, sheriff, county treasurer, or county recorder is eligible to hold the office of county engineer." [verified] — same source. Every one of those four offices exists in this corpus, which is what makes the clause readable as a graph constraint rather than a sentence.

**What the office maintains, in its own numbers:** 353 miles of county road, 550 miles of township road, 371 bridges and over 1,400 culverts. [verified] — [the county engineer's site](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md). Nine hundred miles of road is the physical form of a county that is mostly not city; see [the townships](../place/allen-county.yml).

The present term runs 6 January 2025 to 31 December 2028, four years. [verified] — [Ohio county elected officials lookup](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md); the length is arithmetic on those dates and not a statute this corpus has read. [inference]

**A federal inventory now stands beside those figures, and the two counts differ by seven.** The National Bridge Inventory holds **364** bridges in Allen County — 242 owned by the county, 103 by the state, 19 by municipalities and none at all by a township — against this office's 371. [verified] — [the bridges](../measure/allen-county-bridges-2025.yml). The inventory admits only structures spanning more than twenty feet, and its shortest here is 6.4 metres against a threshold of 6.1, so the seven are short rather than absent. [inference]

**The zero is this office's own statute, seen from Washington.** No township in the county owns a bridge, because the county engineer "shall have general charge of the ... maintenance, and repair of all bridges and highways within the engineer's county, under the jurisdiction of the board of county commissioners", while townships build and improve roads. [verified] — [Ohio Revised Code §5543.01](../../catalog/ohio-revised-code.md). §5591.02 puts the bridges inside municipal corporations on the commissioners too, where the road is a county road and not a state highway. [verified] — same source.

**And the condition figures are a ladder by owner.** None of the state's 103 is in poor condition; 29 of this office's 242 are, and 4 of the municipalities' 19. [verified] — [the bridges](../measure/allen-county-bridges-2025.yml). Twelve per cent is the number attached to this office, and it is the number a reader should attach to it rather than the county-wide nine. [inference]

The county's prosecutor, and also its lawyer. The office runs five divisions: Criminal, which prosecutes "hundreds of felony cases annually"; Juvenile; Civil, which "provides legal representation to county officials, townships, and agencies"; Children Services; and Victim Assistance. [verified] — [the county prosecutor's site](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md).

**The civil division is the part that makes this office structural rather than adversarial.** It is counsel to the other eight elected county offices and to all twelve [township governments](../jurisdiction/amanda-township.yml), which means one elected officer advises every other one. [inference]
The present term runs 6 January 2025 to 31 December 2028, four years. [verified] — [Ohio county elected officials lookup](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md).

The office that keeps the county's record of who owns what. It maintains deeds, mortgages and liens, and also records property lines, maps, plats, powers of attorney and military discharges, indexing them so that a chain of ownership and any encumbrance on it can be established. [verified] — [the county recorder's site](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md).

**It is the office that would answer several of this corpus's open questions.** The 151 acres of [the Hover farm](../person/james-a-hover.yml) contracted to [the Solar Refining Company](../organization/solar-refining-company.yml) in 1886, and the ownership chain from Solar to [the refinery's](../site/lima-refinery.yml) present operator, are both recorded here and in no source this corpus holds. [inference]

The present term runs 6 January 2025 to 31 December 2028, four years, and the present holder's service began in January 2005. [verified] — [Ohio county elected officials lookup](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md) and [the recorder's site](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md).
The holder of this office is barred by statute from also being [county engineer](allen-county-engineer.yml). [verified] — [Ohio Revised Code §315.02](../../catalog/ohio-revised-code.md).

The county's elected chief law enforcement officer, one of the separately elected county offices Ohio law establishes for every county. [inference] The sheriff runs the county jail and serves process in addition to policing the unincorporated area.

**Its line of holders is complete.** Thirty-nine tenures run from Henry Lippencott in 1831 to the present holder, with every term's end year equal to the next term's start year and no holder recorded twice in succession. [verified] — [Allen County Sheriff's Office past-sheriffs roster](../../catalog/acso-past-sheriffs.md); the continuity was checked across all thirty-nine entries rather than assumed, and is now checked by [`crates/succession`](../../../crates/succession/) on every test run rather than by hand.

Two features of the line are worth knowing before computing on it. John Keller held the office in 1835–1839 and again in 1843–1845, so the corpus carries one person and two tenures with `term_number` set. [verified] And the roster's ranges are year-only, so consecutive tenures share a boundary year; read as day-precision intervals every adjacent pair overlaps, and none of those overlaps is real.

**A second source now confirms the present holder and dates his term to the day.** Matthew B. Treglia holds a term running 6 January 2025 to 31 December 2028 — four years, which is what fixes `term_length` on this office. [verified] — [Ohio county elected officials lookup](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md). The sheriff's own roster and the elections roster agree on the name and answer different questions: the first gives the start of service in 2017, the second the bounds of the current term.

This office is one of nine elected county offices, and the only one whose line of holders this corpus can trace. For the other eight it holds the present term and nothing before it. [verified] — same source; see [the county government](../jurisdiction/allen-county-government.yml).

**What the office reports now, and the break in the middle of it.** It polices 24,079 people — the unincorporated county outside Lima and outside the three townships with their own forces — and its violent offenses averaged 33.5 a year to 2020 and 89.8 since, while its property offenses fell from 713 to 576. The line between the two is 1 December 2020, when the office began incident-based reporting. [verified] — [the sheriff's offenses](../measure/allen-county-sheriff-offenses-2015-2024.yml). The corpus reads the step as a change in counting and publishes no crime trend across it. [inference]

The office that collects the county's taxes and holds its money. It collects real estate and manufactured home taxes, bills the county's sanitary sewers, administers delinquent accounts, and invests county funds. [verified] — [the county treasurer's site](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md).

**It collects what [the auditor](allen-county-auditor.yml) assesses**, which is why the two offices are separate and separately elected: the body that values property does not receive the money. [inference]

**Its term dates are the only irregular ones on the county roster**, running 1 September 2025 to 2 September 2029 where the other seven single-seat offices run 6 January 2025 to 31 December 2028. [verified] — [Ohio county elected officials lookup](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md).

**The treasurer's own site does not print the holder's name in text**, only in an image. The name in this corpus comes from the elections roster. [verified] — same source. That is worth saying because it is the one county office whose own publication would not have answered the question.
The holder of this office is barred by statute from also being [county engineer](allen-county-engineer.yml). [verified] — [Ohio Revised Code §315.02](../../catalog/ohio-revised-code.md).

nodes.label: Clerk of the Lima Municipal Court

blocks.text: The elected clerk of the [Lima Municipal Court](../jurisdiction/lima-municipal-court.yml), chosen for a six-year term — the longest elective term in this county — and appearing on the ballot of all eighty-eight precincts. [verified] — [the elected officials roster](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md).

**The court has two judges and one clerk, and all three are elected by the same county-wide electorate on the same six-year term.** [verified] — same source; see [the judgeship](judge-of-the-lima-municipal-court.yml). The corpus held the judgeship since its courts phase and not this office, which is the ordinary shape of the omission: a court is remembered by who decides in it.

nodes.label: Judge of the Court of Common Pleas, Domestic Relations Division

blocks.text: The single-seat bench for divorce, dissolution, custody and support in Allen County. [inference] — the division's subject-matter is not established by any source this corpus holds; the name is.

One judge holds it, on a six-year term running 1 January 2023 to 31 December 2028. [verified] — [Ohio county elected officials lookup](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md); the length is arithmetic on those dates. [inference]

The [court's rules](../../catalog/allen-county-common-pleas-local-rules.md) name a Domestic Relations Division among the five divisions they govern, and the county maintains a separate site for it. [verified] — same rules and [the county's court-system page](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md).

nodes.label: Judge of the Court of Common Pleas, General Division

blocks.text: **Two judges hold it at once**, which makes it the second multi-seat office in this corpus after [the board of commissioners](allen-county-board-of-commissioners.yml). [verified] — [Ohio county elected officials lookup](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md), which assigns two of the county's four common pleas judges to the General Division.

**Its terms run six years and the two seats are offset by two.** One runs 1 January 2025 to 31 December 2030 and the other 9 February 2023 to 8 February 2029. [verified] — same source; the length is arithmetic on those dates. [inference] So the two seats never fall vacant together, the same effect the [commissioners'](allen-county-board-of-commissioners.yml) statute achieves by staggering, reached here by a different means. [inference]

The [court's own rules](../../catalog/allen-county-common-pleas-local-rules.md) call this the "General Trial Division" and name a separate Criminal Division beside it, which has no elected judge of its own. [verified]

nodes.label: Judge of the Court of Common Pleas, Probate Division

blocks.text: The single-seat bench for wills, estates, guardianships and — on the county's own arrangement of its courts — juvenile matters, which are administered together here. [verified] — [the county's court-system page](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md), which lists Probate Court and Juvenile Court as separate sites; [inference] that one elected judge covers both follows from the roster naming only a Probate Division seat among the four.
One judge holds it, on a six-year term running 9 February 2021 to 8 February 2027. [verified] — [Ohio county elected officials lookup](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md).

**Its term expires second-soonest of any seat in this corpus**, on 8 February 2027, behind only [the offset commissioner's](allen-county-board-of-commissioners.yml) 31 December 2026. [inference] — computed here across the seventeen seats whose current term dates the corpus holds.

The [court's rules](../../catalog/allen-county-common-pleas-local-rules.md) govern practice in the Probate Division and the Juvenile Division "where applicable", treating them as two divisions where the ballot treats them as one seat. [verified]

nodes.label: Judge of the Lima Municipal Court

blocks.text: Two judges hold this office at once, elected by the whole county rather than by the city the court is named for. [verified] — [Ohio county elected officials lookup](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md), which lists them among Allen County's elected officials; and [Ohio Revised Code §1901.02](../../catalog/ohio-revised-code.md): "The Lima municipal court has jurisdiction within Allen county."

**Its terms run six years and the two seats are offset by two.** One runs 1 January 2022 to 31 December 2027 and the other 1 January 2024 to 31 December 2029. [verified] — same roster; the length is arithmetic on those dates. [inference] Both begin in January, unlike the [common pleas general division](judge-of-the-common-pleas-general-division.yml), whose two seats begin in different months.

A municipal judge here serves six years and an [administrative county officer](allen-county-auditor.yml) four. That holds across every office in this corpus that states a term length — four judicial offices at six years and nine elected administrative ones at four, thirteen offices and seventeen seats. [inference] — computed here. It rests on one county's roster and is a pattern in the data, not a rule this corpus has read anywhere. The [mayor of Lima](mayor-of-lima.yml) is the one office node with no term length at all, and is excluded from the count for that reason.

nodes.label: Judge of the Third District Court of Appeals

blocks.text: The appellate bench that hears Allen County's appeals, and the office this corpus declined to write one phase ago. Four judges hold it, on six-year terms. [verified] — [Ohio county elected officials lookup](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md).

**All four terms begin in February and no two expire in the same year**, running to 8 February 2027, 8 February 2029, 10 February 2029 and 8 February 2031. [verified] — same source. Two expire two days apart in 2029, which is the same device the [board of commissioners](allen-county-board-of-commissioners.yml) uses to keep seats distinguishable. [inference]
