This corpus does not establish that Lima is emptying because it is aging. It carries natural decrease as a component of the county's loss and it carries the concentration in Lima, and those two facts invite that conclusion; the age measure contradicts it. Whatever natural decrease this county has, it is not principally the city's. [verified] — same source.

It does not establish that the county's population decline was caused by its manufacturing decline. The two spans overlap and do not coincide — the city began emptying three years before manufacturing peaked, and manufacturing has risen since 2009 while the population has not. [verified] — [the employment series](../measure/allen-county-manufacturing-employment-1969-2022.yml). A population series cannot establish a cause however many other series sit beside it, and that was true before this corpus had the other series. [inference]

refusals: It does not establish that either mechanism reaches back before 2020.

It does not establish that the decline has ended: fifteen people on 100,851 is far inside what a modelled estimate can resolve, one year is not a direction, and the same programme revises its own earlier years with every vintage.
It does not follow that Lima's mortality is what makes the county smaller.
This corpus does not establish that Lima is emptying because it is aging.
It does not establish that the county's population decline was caused by its manufacturing decline.

properties.character: A local discovery converted into national industry, added on top of a farming county that kept farming. This field said "the county's shift from agriculture to manufacturing" until the agriculture was measured and had not shifted. [inference]

blocks.text: The span opened by [the 1885 strike](../event/lima-oil-strike.yml), in which the Lima–Indiana field made this county a centre of national petroleum production and Lima an industrial city. [inference]

Its character is the attachment of a local agricultural economy to national capital. The refinery, the growth of Lima's population, and much of the built fabric of the city date from it. [inference] *Attachment* is the right word and *replacement* is not: the agriculture was still there at the end of the period, on 92.5 per cent of the county's land. [verified] — [Abstract of the Thirteenth Census, Supplement for Ohio](../../catalog/census-1910-abstract-supplement-ohio.md); see [the county's farms](../measure/allen-county-farms-1900-1910.yml). The field's dominance was relatively brief — it was displaced as new fields opened elsewhere — but the refining capacity it justified is still operating, which is why the period's most durable legacy is [a site](../site/lima-refinery.yml) rather than an industry. [inference]

**The city it attached was already industrial, and this node did not say so.** Six years before the strike Lima stood at the crossing of three railroads, all of which kept repair shops there, and the Dayton & Michigan shops alone covered eight acres and employed 200 to 300 men — the largest establishment in a city of about 7,000. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md), quoting a Lima newspaper of 14 March 1879; see [the network](../measure/allen-county-railroads-1883-1921.yml). The county had about 102 miles of main track in 1883 and its manufactures were already above $2,000,000. [verified] — [the 1885 history](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md).

So *attachment* is still the right word and the thing attached was not only farmland. What the oil did was multiply an industrial base that the railroads had put there thirty years earlier. [inference] Nothing here weighs the two against each other: this corpus has one employment figure from before the boom and it is a range printed in a newspaper.

**The start bound is now supported from the other side.** The 1885 county history, printed as the boom began, treats the county's petroleum as prospective — "a subject for the enterprise of the future" — while cataloguing everything else in Lima to the dollar. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md). A source that would have reported the field and does not is a lower bound on the field. [inference]

**The start bound is now a date: May 9, 1885.** [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md). It is also, on the same source, a slightly later date in substance — the first *persistent* production came from the second well that autumn, the pioneer having broken. [inference]

**The boom is now measurable and the measure is large.** Allen County gained 9,330 people between 1880 and 1890 — **29.7 per cent, the largest decennial gain in its history** — and Lima "doubled her population" in the same decade, going from 7,567 to 21,723 by 1900. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md); see [the county series](../measure/allen-county-population-1830-1900.yml) and [Lima's](../measure/lima-population-1880-1920.yml). The 1906 compilers attribute the increase to the discovery without qualification, and they were living in the town when it happened.

**And the end bound has a shape at last, though not a date.** By 1920 Lima had reached 41,326 — the Census figure; the 1921 history says 41,306 and see [the federal series](../measure/lima-population-1850-1960.yml) — and by 1921 the whole residue of the field was, in the later historian's words, "the Solar refinery and the different companies dealing in oil commodities", with "little oil now being pumped in Allen County". [verified] — [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md). So the *field* was substantially finished before 1921 while the *city* kept growing — which is why this period's legacy is a site rather than an industry, and why 1910 as a placeholder is defensible for production and wrong for consequence. [inference]

nodes.label: The Civil War in Allen County

properties.character: A rural county of nineteen thousand people sustaining a military effort of nineteen hundred men for four years, and organizing itself around that effort — an aid society, a military committee, a relief tax, a board of enrollment, and a camp of rendezvous for eight counties. [inference]

blocks.text: The four years in which a county of 19,185 people put **1,920 men** into United States service — one person in ten, counting women, children and the old. [inference] — computed here against [the 1860 count](../measure/allen-county-population-1830-1900.yml); the 1,920 is [the roster's own total](../measure/allen-county-civil-war-service.yml). It is the first period this corpus has named that is not about what the county produced.

**It begins on a Sunday morning at the courthouse, and the source has the day wrong.** Rusler puts Lima's congregations in church on "a bright Sunday morning, April 12, 1861" when the word came that Fort Sumter had been fired on; a flag went up on a wire between Ashton Hall and the courthouse, the congregations gathered under it when services ended, and a store box was made into a platform. [verified] — [the 1921 history](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md).

April 12, 1861 was a **Friday**. The Sunday was the 14th, the day Sumter's garrison marched out, which is when the news would have reached a town in northwestern Ohio. [inference] — computed here. The scene is not in doubt; its date is off by two days, and the book supplies the correction four sentences later by dating everything that follows.

[verified] — [the 1885 history](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md) for the first, second and fourth; the 1921 history for the third, which attributes it to an official report it does not name. See [what the county sent](../measure/allen-county-civil-war-service.yml), where the transmission of the first of them is traced through three books and found to have been corrupted on the way.

**What it cost is not in any of the three books as a number.** The 1885 roster records the fate of each man and never adds them up. Counted, at least **165** of the 1,920 died in service, and only about one in four of those was killed. More Allen County men died at Nashville, a hospital town, than in any battle. [inference] — [the dead](../measure/allen-county-civil-war-dead.yml).

**It ends without an ending in the record.** The rosters stop at muster-out and the county histories move to the Grand Army posts, Memorial Hall and the Woman's Relief Corps — organized within three years of the close, and the oldest women's society in the county. [verified] — the 1921 history. The character of the span is set by the going out and not the coming home, because that is what the sources chose to record.

nodes.label: The World War in Allen County

properties.character: A county with no camp, no battle and no invasion, organising a war out of committees: a draft board, a council of defense, a Red Cross chapter, a war savings drive, a truck factory and a hall where men were sworn in and fed lunch. [inference]

blocks.text: The nineteen months in which a county of sixty-eight thousand put **at least 4,158 men** into United States service — one person in sixteen — and organised itself around a war it never saw. [inference] — computed here against the 1920 census; the roster count is [the list's own](../measure/allen-county-world-war-service.yml).

**It has no local beginning the sources will give.** The Civil War period in this corpus opens on a named Sunday at the courthouse with a flag on a wire. This one opens with committees. The 1921 history describes the county before the war as "resting secure in their remoteness, the farmer continued to till his fields", and dates nothing between that and the draft board. [verified] — [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md).

**What the county built for it was a truck.** "Lima industry was represented on the war front by the Liberty truck", built by [Gramm-Bernstein](../organization/gramm-bernstein-motor-truck-company.yml), and the book's own caption calls it the first truck used in the war. [verified] — same source. Three of the volume's photographs are of it, one a convoy in Lima's Public Square before leaving for Washington.

**What it built for itself was an administration.** A draft board serving without pay — F. M. Watt and Clarence Breese for the county outside Lima, with James J. Weadock, George H. Quail, Dr. T. R. Thomas and J. L. Van Pelt; a Council of Defense chaired by B. A. Gramm, whose woman's branch passed from Mrs. Kent W. Hughes to Mrs. Lena B. Davis to avoid overlapping the Red Cross; a War Savings committee under H. E. Simonton. [verified] — same source.

**And it met its money quota and then stopped.** Allen County's War Savings quota was $1,297,000 and it subscribed $1,367,000, $70,000 over. In 1919, with the war finished, Ohio as a whole took 25 per cent of its quota and Allen County 30 — "a good relative showing", and the book adds that "the people did not incline to make a sacrifice again". [verified] — same source.

**Its induction hall is a building this corpus already holds.** [Memorial Hall](../site/lima-memorial-hall.yml) was where men were sworn in, "from a radius many miles in every direction from Lima", and luncheons were served to everybody entering the service. [verified] — same source.

**The war reached the county's map.** German Township became American on 16 August 1918, on a petition of its own citizens. [verified] — [the renaming](../event/renaming-of-german-township-1918.yml). And it reached the state hospital: 244 cases of influenza that autumn, of which 8 per cent died. [verified] — [the hospital](../site/lima-state-hospital.yml).
Sheriff of Allen County, 1893–1898. [verified] — [Allen County Sheriff's Office past-sheriffs roster](../../catalog/acso-past-sheriffs.md).

The roster gives a name and a year range and nothing else, so this node carries no dates of birth or death and no biography. Ohio requires an elected county officer to be an elector of the county, so a `resided-in` edge to Allen County is a legal inference rather than a fact the roster states. [inference]

Mayor of Lima in March 1944, and dead before the end of that August. [verified] — [The Bluffton News](../../catalog/chronicling-america.md); see [the mayors named inside the gap](../measure/lima-mayors-1939-1956.yml).

**The one act of his mayoralty this corpus holds is a fire budget.** "Two 20-year-old pieces of fire apparatus will be replaced as soon as new equipment can be obtained, Mayor A. L. Metheany of Lima announced after City Council appropriated $10,000 for that purpose. One fire station has been closed." [verified] — same source, 2 March 1944.

**The evidence that he died in office is a probate inventory.** "Allen L. Metheany, late mayor of Lima, left an estate worth $42,797.51, according to the inventory and appraisement filed in the Allen county probate court by Mrs. Emma H. Metheany, administratrix" — $900 in personal property, $23,019.67 in stocks and bonds, $15,377.84 in accounts and debts receivable. [verified] — same source, 31 August 1944. The three parts sum to $39,297.51, which is $3,500 short of the total the paper prints, so one component of the inventory is not in the story. [inference] — computed here.
Member of lima city council, seated in 2026. [verified] — [the elected officials lookup](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md).
He sits for the second ward, one of the three even-numbered wards whose terms began in January 2024 and run to January 2028. [verified]
Ohio requires an elected municipal officer to be an elector of the municipality, so the `resided-in` edge below is a legal inference rather than a fact any source read here states. [inference]
Director of law of lima, seated in 2026. [verified] — [the elected officials lookup](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md).

He holds the city's legal office where the county's is held by an elected prosecuting attorney; the two are separate offices with separate electorates and this corpus has not established which prosecutes what. [inference]

**Admitted to the practice of law in Ohio by examination on 1 November 1983, registration number 6150.** [verified] — [the attorney directory](../../catalog/ohio-attorney-directory.md), which returns exactly one Anthony Layton Geiger, with an Allen County address of record and an active status.

The Lima businessman whose drilling produced the 1885 strike that opened the Lima oil field. [inference] He was drilling for natural gas, on the pattern of the Findlay gas boom to the north, and struck oil instead. [inference]

**His other business interests are now on record, and they are most of industrial Lima.** [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md), printed the year of the strike and therefore describing him entirely as he was before it:

**The paper mill matters to the received account.** A straw-board works is a fuel-hungry industry; his daughter Carrie married the secretary of the Lima Gaslight Company on January 7, 1885; and the same volume records gas shows across the county as an undeveloped prospect. [verified] — same source. That is the setting the drilling story requires, established independently of the story.

**The well is now on record and so is why he drilled it.** It was completed May 9, 1885 on the grounds of his own Lima Straw Board Works, by the contractors Brownyear and Martin, for a double purpose: better process water, and the natural gas that Findlay and Bowling Green had just found. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md). The corpus's `[inference]` that he was drilling for gas is verified, and gains a first motive nobody retells — he wanted water.

A second historian adds that he had "acquired the ownership of the city's first street railway — then a horse-car line — and secured the exclusive control of the Lima Strawboard Company", and was president of the Strawboard Association of the United States. [verified] — same source. And of the strike itself: "It was not a great success in itself but it was the pioneer stake in an industry that has produced millions for Allen County." [verified] — same source. The well that carries his name broke; [the second one](../event/lima-oil-strike.yml) made the field.

**He was building a railroad two years after the well.** The Columbus, Lima & Milwaukee Railway was commenced in 1887 by Faurot; by 1906, after "various stages of litigation and contest", it was operating as the Columbus & Lake Michigan between Lima and Defiance, through Ottawa, German and Sugar Creek townships, with its main offices in Lima. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md); see [the network](../measure/allen-county-railroads-1883-1921.yml). The 1906 book calls him "the late" and the road unfinished, so both the man and the line outran their own beginnings. [inference]

**He held office in Lima eighteen years before the well.** Benjamin C. Faurot was elected a village trustee in 1867, alongside James H. Corns, Uriah Pangle, J. R. Hughes and C. D. Robbins, under Mayor John Collett. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md); see [the line of mayors](../measure/lima-mayors-1842-1886.yml), which prints the council beside the mayor for every year from 1842. It is the earliest dated fact this corpus holds about him. [inference]

**He was leasing ground in the county four months after the strike.** An oil lease over part of the north-west quarter of section 17 in Bath Township ran to "B. C. Faurot et al", dated 29 September 1885 and recorded 30 April 1886; it was later released. [verified] — [Section Ground book list](../../catalog/allen-county-recorder-section-ground.md), volume 0028A page 164. It is the only record this corpus holds of him acting outside the city, and the only one of his dealings it has from a land record rather than from a county history.

**He owned the street railway too, and it is on the list of what he lost.** He "acquired the ownership of the city's first street railway — then a horse-car line", and among the wealth that slipped through his fingers the 1906 history names "the Lima street railway system, the Lima Electric Light Company, the Faurot Block and the land about the city". [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md); see [the street railway under four names](../measure/lima-street-railway-1878-1921.yml). His 1883 electric light plant beside the opera house and the horse cars he bought met in [the first electric car](../event/the-first-electric-car-in-lima-1886.yml), three years later.

nodes.label: Frank A. Burkhardt

blocks.text: **His term ended the office.** The commission form of government came into effect on 1 January 1922, "at the end of the term of Mayor Burkhardt", after eighty years in which Lima had been "ruled by a mayor". [verified] — [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md); see [the commission government](../event/lima-adopts-commission-government-1922.yml) and [the mayors of 1886 to 1922](../measure/lima-mayors-1886-1922.yml).

**He is inside the source as well as in it.** He sits on the 1921 history's advisory board of editors, listed as "Mayor Frank Burkhardt" beside Senator Stephen D. Crites of [Elida](../place/elida.yml); and he wrote a paper for it, "Trails, Traces and ...", which the book quotes and folds into its chapters on the county's roads. [verified] — same source.

**That is a thing to hold onto when reading the book's account of the charter.** The volume's pages on the commission government are enthusiastic about a change that ended the office its own advisory editor held, and they were written while he held it. The corpus records the enthusiasm as the book's and not as the county's. [inference] — see [read a word in its source register](../../decisions/read-a-word-in-its-source-register.yml).

refusals: The corpus does not know when he was born, what he did before 1920, or what he did after the office stopped existing.

blocks.text: Mayor of Lima, in office from November 1939 and still in office in November 1943. [verified] — [The Bluffton News](../../catalog/chronicling-america.md); see [the mayors named inside the gap](../measure/lima-mayors-1939-1956.yml). He is the first holder of [that office](../office/mayor-of-lima.yml) this corpus can name between 1922 and 2021.

**He arrived cutting.** "Mayor Frank McClain of Lima last week swung the economy ax 48 hours after taking office, when he chopped 12 street department workers from the city pay roll." [verified] — same source, 23 November 1939.

**His re-election in 1941 is the only Lima election this corpus can price.** He filed election expenses of $306.40 with the Allen County board of elections; Bluffton's mayor filed $6.39 for his. [verified] — same source, 20 November 1941. The paper printed the two side by side because the difference was the story.

**He left the office and stayed in politics.** By October 1948 he was advertising in this same paper as "Former Mayor of Lima, Ohio, Republican Candidate For County Commissioner". [verified] — same source. Lima's mayoralty was non-partisan by 1945 and the county commission was not.

The only man in Lima's first forty-four years to become mayor without an election, and later a probate judge who helped decide what the county's courthouse would look like. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md).

**The council made him mayor in September 1869**, in place of Thomas M. Robb, who had resigned. Every other mayor in [the line](../measure/lima-mayors-1842-1886.yml) was chosen at an election. [verified] — same source.

**He organized the county's war relief before that and captained a company during it.** He was secretary of the Auxiliary Aid Society organized at Lima on 23 April 1862, and the roster of commissioned officers gives "Overmyer, Geo. W., 81st O. V. I., Aug. 9, 1862, Nov. 23, 1864" among the captains. [verified] — same source, Chapter IX; see [what the county sent](../measure/allen-county-civil-war-service.yml).

That roster entry is in one digitization only — the other recovers 90.9 per cent of the roster and not this line — so the dates rest on a single reading of a single book. [inference] — see [a printed list is a dataset](../../decisions/a-printed-list-is-a-dataset.yml).

**He was Probate Judge of Allen County in 1881**, and in that office sat with the sheriff, the clerk of courts and the county commissioners on the committee that chose the plans for [the present courthouse](../site/allen-county-courthouse.yml). [verified] — same source. The corpus already held that committee and knew one of its members by name.
He also stood for county office as a Democrat, and the 1885 book prints his votes in the county's election returns. [verified] — same source.

nodes.label: H. S. Prophet

blocks.text: Mayor of Lima from 1882 to 1884, and the only holder of that office in [the line](../measure/lima-mayors-1842-1886.yml) whom a later history describes as a soldier. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md) for the office and [the 1921 history](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md) for the rest.

**The 1921 book calls him a colonel and says why.** "Col. H. S. Prophett, a Civil war veteran, wounded in battle, and honorably mentioned by his commanding general for 'conspicuous gallantry and efficiency in battle,'" and it spells the surname with two t's where the 1885 book uses one. [verified] — the 1921 history.

**The 1885 roster carries two Prophets among the captains, and they are probably one man.** "Prophet, H. S., 15th O. V. I., April, 1861, Aug., 1861" — a three-month enlistment in the first call — and "Prophet, Hinchman, 43d O. V. I., Sept. 1, 1861, resigned June, 1863". [verified] — the 1885 history, both digitizations, which agree on both entries and disagree only on the second resignation year, where the cleaner scan reads 1803 and the other 1863.

Three months in a ninety-day regiment followed by a commission in a three-year one is the ordinary sequence for an Ohio officer of 1861, the initials fit a man christened Hinchman S., and the roster prints the two entries adjacent because it is alphabetical. [inference] — computed here. It is a reading and not a finding: the book names them separately and this corpus cannot show they are the same.

**He was mayor twice, sixteen years apart, and the corpus knew only the first.** April 1882 to April 1884, and again April 1898 to April 1900. [verified] — [the 1906 history](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md); see [the mayors of 1886 to 1922](../measure/lima-mayors-1886-1922.yml).

**A third list confirms the 1921 book's prose about him exactly.** That book says he "served as city solicitor for four years"; the 1906 history's separate list of city solicitors gives "H. S. Prophet, April, 1874, to April, 1878" — four years, from a table the 1921 book was not reading. [verified] — the 1906 and 1921 histories. It is a small check and it is the only one in this line that two independent lineages both pass. [inference]

refusals: It is a reading and not a finding: the book names them separately and this corpus cannot show they are the same.

blocks.text: The Shawnee Township farmer who paid $5,000 of his own money so that the refinery would be built in Allen County. [verified] — [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md).

He settled with the leaseholders for $5,000. Months later Rockefeller sent him a personal cheque for $2,500 — "you are the squarest farmer I ever did business with... I will take one-half your loss while you are standing the other half". [verified] — same source.

**He is in the corpus because of what he explains.** This corpus established by coordinate, two phases before it had any history, that [the refinery](../site/lima-refinery.yml) stands on unincorporated ground in [Shawnee Township](../place/shawnee-township.yml) with a Lima postal address — and recorded that as a fact about tax base and authority without being able to say why. This is why: it was a farm, chosen in 1886 for its position between two railroads, and nothing has annexed it since. [inference]

**His own book gets his name wrong once and right three times.** The 1885 history's list of mayors prints "John B. Townsend" in both digitizations; the same volume prints James B. Townsend in its election returns, in its index, and in a biographical sketch of him. Both later county histories print James. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md), [1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md) and [1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md); see [the line of mayors](../measure/lima-mayors-1842-1886.yml).

**He paid for his legal education by touring with a company of singers.** Born in Allen County in 1851, son of a commission merchant who came from New York in 1850, went back, and returned in 1859 by way of Bluffton; educated in the Lima schools; and from 1868 to 1874 he studied law "while traveling through the country with a first-class company of vocalists, giving concerts and lecturing in the interest of the Townsend medicines" — his father's patent remedies, "so extensively advertised throughout the world". [verified] — the 1885 history. He was admitted to the bar by the Supreme Court at Columbus in 1874, elected justice of the peace in Lima, and then mayor. [verified] — same source.

**At twenty-five he is the youngest mayor in the line the corpus holds**, taking the office in 1876 two years after admission to the bar. [inference] — computed here against [the line](../measure/lima-mayors-1842-1886.yml).

**The same book cannot agree with itself about how long he served.** Its list gives 1876 to 1880, four years; its sketch of him says "he was elected mayor of Lima for five years", and puts three years as justice of the peace after an 1874 admission, which would begin the mayoralty in 1877. [verified] — same source. Neither reading is preferred here: the list is the record of an office and the sketch is a life told once, and the corpus has no third witness for either the length or the start.

**What the office was for, in his telling.** "It was during his administration and through his personal diligence that the fair city was purged of the tramp nuisance, and other evils." [verified] — same source. Lima in those four years was a town of about seven thousand with three railroads crossing it, which is what produces a tramp nuisance and what a mayor of that decade was expected to answer for. [inference] — see [the railroads](../measure/allen-county-railroads-1883-1921.yml).

The county itself, as ground rather than as government: 402.545 square miles of land and 4.306 square miles of water in the northwest quarter of Ohio, with an internal point at 40.771627, -84.106103. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md).

The land is glacial till plain, flat and poorly drained, and its northern reach lay within the Great Black Swamp until nineteenth-century drainage. [inference] That flatness is the reason the county's transport history runs through a canal and then a railway junction rather than through a river port: its streams drain north and west to the Auglaize and the Maumee and were never navigable here.

**It is three places.** Lima holds 35,531 people; the three townships wrapped around it — [American](american-township.yml) 14,571, [Shawnee](shawnee-township.yml) 12,509 and [Bath](bath-township.yml) 9,399 — hold 36,479 between them, more than the city; and the other nine townships hold about thirty thousand across roughly five hundred square miles. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md), sub-county file. That suburban middle is largely outside any municipality: Shawnee Township contains no incorporated place at all. [verified] — same source.

**Its whole population history, with no gaps.** The county has a count at every decennial census from 1830 to 2020 and an estimate for 2024: **578 (1830), 9,079 (1840), 12,100 (1850), 19,185 (1860), 23,623 (1870), 31,314 (1880), 40,644 (1890), 47,976 (1900), 56,580 (1910), 68,203 (1920), 69,419 (1930), 73,303 (1940), 88,183 (1950), 103,691 (1960), 111,144 (1970), 112,241 (1980), 109,755 (1990), 108,464 (2000), 106,331 (2010), 102,217 (2020) and 100,866 (2024).** [verified] — assembled from [1830–1900](../measure/allen-county-population-1830-1900.yml), [1890–1910](../measure/allen-county-townships-1890-1910.yml), [1940–1990](../measure/allen-county-population-1940-1990.yml) and the four modern measures — which rest between them on [Leeson 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md), [the 1910 Ohio supplement](../../catalog/census-1910-abstract-supplement-ohio.md), [the 1950 volume](../../catalog/census-1950-number-of-inhabitants-ohio.md), [CPH-2-37](../../catalog/census-cph-2-37-ohio.md), [the 1970s county estimates](../../catalog/census-county-estimates-1970s.md), [the intercensals](../../catalog/census-intercensal-2000-2010.md) and [Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md). Every figure is from a published table. Twenty-one observations, and until this phase two of them were missing.

**Once, nine-tenths of it was farms.** In 1910 the county held 2,939 farms covering 240,472 of its 259,840 acres — 92.5 per cent of the land area — with 203,222 acres improved and $25,992,184 of farm property standing on them. [verified] — [Abstract of the Thirteenth Census, Supplement for Ohio](../../catalog/census-1910-abstract-supplement-ohio.md); see [the county's farms](../measure/allen-county-farms-1900-1910.yml), [what they produced](../measure/allen-county-farm-output-1909.yml) and [its animals](../measure/allen-county-domestic-animals-1910.yml). That is the same census that counts 30,508 people in Lima, so the county was already more than half city by population while still being nine-tenths farm by ground. [inference]

**It is two-thirds farms now, and it is a hog county.** 178,921 acres in 2022 — 69.4 per cent of the land area — on 897 operations, of which 268 part-owners farm 78.4 per cent of the ground and more than half of all farmland is rented from somebody else. [verified] — [the Census of Agriculture](../../catalog/usda-census-of-agriculture.md); see [the modern farms](../measure/allen-county-farms-2002-2022.yml), [the livestock](../measure/allen-county-livestock-2002-2022.yml) and [the crops](../measure/allen-county-crops-2022.yml). The county held 31,741 hogs on 59 places in 2002 and 235,800 on 28 in 2022, and sells more of them than of anything else it raises.

So the county's other nine-tenths has an answer at both ends and none in the middle: 52,322 of the 61,551 acres that left the farms went in the ninety-two years no census in this catalog covers. [inference] — computed here from the two censuses. See [when the farmland went](../question/when-the-farmland-went.yml). The 1910 and 2022 farm counts are not subtracted anywhere in this corpus, because the two censuses define a farm differently; see [a farm count is a definition](../../decisions/a-farm-count-is-a-definition.yml).

**Half the jobs in it are held by people who live somewhere else.** 48,730 jobs are located in Allen County and 24,461 of them are held by residents; 24,269 people commute in and 18,374 residents commute out, so 42,643 cross the county line on a working day and the county draws 5,895 more workers than it sends. [verified] — [who comes and goes](../measure/allen-county-commuting-2022.yml). The in-commuters come mostly from the ring of rural counties — Auglaize, Putnam, Van Wert, Hardin, Hancock.

**And it pays about four fifths of what the country pays.** An average weekly wage of $1,131 in 2024 against $1,267 for Ohio and $1,454 nationally, across 49,690 covered jobs. [inference] — [what work pays](../measure/allen-county-wages-2024.yml). Health care is the largest employer at 9,767 jobs and manufacturing the largest payer, at 8,779 jobs and 28.0 per cent of all wages.

**Who represents it, and under which map.** The county sends one member to the Ohio House from [the 78th District](../division/ohio-house-district-78-2023.yml) and one to the Ohio Senate from [the 12th](../division/ohio-senate-district-12-2023.yml), both under the legislative map adopted 29 September 2023; and it is not split between districts in either chamber. [verified] — [Ohio county elected officials lookup](../../catalog/ohio-boe-elected-officials-allen.md); [inference] for the not-split, reasoned from the roster naming one of each. Its sitting member of Congress sits for the 4th District. [verified] — same source.

**Six colleges stand in it and they have lost a third of their students since 2010.** 8,615 in the autumn of 2023 and 10,789 across the twelve months, against 16,702 in 2010 — a fall of 35.4 per cent while the county itself fell 3.9. [verified] — [the enrolment series](../measure/allen-county-college-enrollment-2010-2023.yml). Together they award 2,918 credentials a year, of which 85 per cent are below a bachelor's degree. [verified] — [higher education](../measure/allen-county-higher-education-2023.yml).

**Three and a half thousand of its people do not live in a household.** 3,522 of 102,206 — 1,513 in correctional facilities, 966 in nursing homes, 788 in student housing and 255 in shelters, group homes and residential treatment centres — leaving 98,684 in 40,935 occupied units, an average household of 2.411. Another 3,628 units stood empty. [verified] — [the group quarters](../measure/allen-county-group-quarters-2020.yml) and [the occupancy](../measure/allen-county-occupancy-2020.yml).

**It sent one person in ten to the Civil War.** A county of 19,185 in 1860 put 1,920 men into United States service over the four years, and at least 164 of them did not come home. [inference] — [what the county sent](../measure/allen-county-civil-war-service.yml) and [the dead](../measure/allen-county-civil-war-dead.yml). It was also, for a few weeks in August 1862, the rendezvous of the whole Eighth Military District: about 1,600 men camped across the Ottawa from a town of fewer than two thousand. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md); see [Camp Lima](../site/camp-lima.yml).

**It rose for a hundred and fifty years and has fallen for forty-four.** The peak is 1980 and the county is now smaller than it was in 1960. [inference] The first two figures count different ground — the [reorganization of 1848](../event/reorganization-of-1848.yml) moved 138 square miles — so the series is continuous only from 1850.

**The outline is not fixed either, and this corpus had assumed it was.** Between the 1990 and 2000 censuses Allen County gained territory from Putnam County, by way of [Marion Township](marion-township.yml) taking ground from Jennings Township across the line. [verified] — [Census 2000, Population and Housing Unit Counts, Ohio](../../catalog/census-phc-3-37-ohio.md), geographic change notes. It is the only movement of the county line on record here since 1848.

**It is small enough to be invisible in the county's own total area**, which is 406.88 square miles in the 2000 volume, 406.85 in the 2010 one and 406.851 in the 2020 gazetteer — three hundredths of a square mile across twenty years and a boundary change. The *land* figure in the same three sources reads 404.43, 402.50 and 402.545, a fall of more than twelve hundred acres in a county that gained ground. [verified] — the same volumes and [the 2020 gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md). What moved was the line between land and water on a map, not the line around the county; see [the control is the figure that cannot move](../../decisions/the-control-is-the-figure-that-cannot-move.yml).

**It has been named in ten federal disaster declarations since 1965**, for eight distinct incidents — tornadoes, a blizzard, four rounds of severe storms and flooding, an evacuation from a hurricane nine hundred miles away, and a pandemic. Two of the ten brought money to households. [verified] — [the declarations](../measure/allen-county-disaster-declarations-1965-2020.yml).

A township of 33.315 square miles about 9 miles west of the county's centre, internal point 40.734865, -84.272548. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), Ohio county subdivisions.

Its population was 2,070 at the 2020 estimates base and 2,049 in 2024. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md), sub-county file. Its population fell by 21 over those four years, as all but two of the county's subdivisions did.
It contains no incorporated place; all of it is unincorporated. [verified] — same source, which lists no place within this township.

**No school district is named for it and three divide it**: 1,072 of its people are in [Spencerville Local](../jurisdiction/spencerville-local-school-district.yml), 665 in [Shawnee Local](../jurisdiction/shawnee-local-school-district.yml) and 324 in [Elida Local](../jurisdiction/elida-local-school-district.yml). [verified] — [2020 Census Block Assignment Files](../../catalog/census-block-assignment-2020.md) crossed with [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md) block geography. A township with no village and no district of its own has no institution that takes its name as a whole, which is worth knowing before reading anything into how little is written about it.

**Erected in 1830 by the commissioners of Mercer County** — the earliest township organization recorded in this county, and it happened two years before Allen County had a board of its own, while Allen was attached to Mercer for judicial purposes. Thirteen electors lived in it and twelve of them came to the organizing meeting; Samuel Baxter was chosen clerk and Daniel Hoak justice of the peace. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md).
**It is named for [Fort Amanda](../site/fort-amanda.yml)**, built in 1812 by Col. Poague's command and named for the colonel's wife. [verified] — same source.

**The fort is not in this township and has not been in this county since 1848.** The federal gazetteer puts it in Auglaize County at 40.6830556, -84.27, and the county's own map service returns no township, no survey section and no parcel for that point — 0.188 miles, about nine hundred and ninety feet, south of the line. [verified] — [USGS Geographic Names](../../catalog/gnis-domestic-names-ohio.md) and [Allen County GIS](../../catalog/allen-county-gis-rest.md). The 1848 act kept "the north half of Amanda" and the south half went to Auglaize County with the fort in it, so this township carries a name whose referent it lost. [inference] — the act text is [the 1885 history's](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md); see [of here is not located here](../../decisions/of-here-is-not-located-here.yml).

In the [reorganization of 1848](../event/reorganization-of-1848.yml) it lost sections 7 and 18 to [Spencer](spencer-township.yml) and was recomposed from the south half of Marion and its own north half. [verified] — same source.

**Earlier still, it was falling: 1,425 people in 1890, 1,384 in 1900 and 1,263 in 1910.** [verified] — [Abstract of the Thirteenth Census, Supplement for Ohio](../../catalog/census-1910-abstract-supplement-ohio.md); see [the 1890–1910 divisions](../measure/allen-county-townships-1890-1910.yml). So its low point is 975 in 1940 and its high point before the war is 1890, and the doubling below is measured from near the bottom of a fifty-year decline. [inference]

**It held 1,008 people in 1930, 975 in 1940 and 980 in 1950**, and 2,070 at the 2020 estimates base. [verified] — [1950 Census, Number of Inhabitants, Ohio](../../catalog/census-1950-number-of-inhabitants-ohio.md), Table 6; see [the township series](../measure/allen-county-townships-1930-1950.yml). So it doubled, and all of it happened after 1950 — through the 1930s and 1940s the township was flat and slightly falling. [inference] It has no incorporated place, so every one of those people was and is counted in unincorporated territory.
A township of 24.017 square miles wrapping the west and north of Lima, internal point 40.769378, -84.17822. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md).

It is the most populous township in the county outside Lima itself, and the Census Bureau's "balance of American township" figure — the township minus the incorporated villages inside it — is the larger part of that. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md), sub-county file. Its population was 14,571 at the 2020 estimates base and 14,445 in 2024 — **the most populous civil subdivision in the county after Lima**, and 12,541 of the 2024 figure is the balance outside [Elida](elida.yml), the one village in it. [verified] — same source.

**Neither the refinery nor the tank plant is here.** This node claimed both stand on or near its boundary with Lima, and therefore that this township holds most of the county's heavy industry. Both are in [Shawnee Township](shawnee-township.yml), south of Lima; this township wraps Lima's west and north. [verified] — [Allen County GIS](../../catalog/allen-county-gis-downloads.md) and [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md), agreeing independently on both points. The claim is withdrawn entire rather than narrowed: it named two sites and was wrong about both.
It does hold a fifth of [census tract 39003010300](../division/census-tract-39003010300.yml) — 13,403,443 square metres and 408 people. [verified] — same source, block composition.

**This township was called German until some time after 1885.** The commissioners' act of December 6, 1831 established it "under the name German", over the territory running west from Section 3, Town 3, Range 6 to the old Amanda line. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md). That book's German Township "forms the geographical centre of the county", takes the Ottawa River in from [Shawnee](shawnee-township.yml) at Section 33, and passes it by Allentown and [Elida](elida.yml) into [Sugar Creek](sugar-creek-township.yml) — which is this township and no other, since Elida is in it and in nothing else. [inference] Its erection date therefore belongs here, and it makes this the third township the county had.

In 1848 it lost its north tier of sections to Sugar Creek and kept its name; in 1857 it gave 1,040 acres to Ottawa Township. [verified] — same source, and [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md) independently, giving the same acreage thirty-six years later.

**The name changed on August 16, 1918, and the reason was the war.** The citizens of German Township petitioned, and the Allen County commissioners acted — the same instrument that erected the county's townships and incorporated its villages. Article II of the petition says only "that good cause is shown"; the 1921 historian reads it plainly — "'good cause' means patriotism" — and sets it in its moment: "The name German had come into disfavor when the German nation changed its attitude toward the rest of the world. School books were undergoing changes at the time, and business concerns bearing the name German were eliminating the offensive designation, and the people of German Township were caught in the wave of popular sentiment." [verified] — [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md), which is a single witness read once for this date.

**The same page records the dissent**, three years after the fact: "there are residents of the township who a little later on would not have voted for the change, because of sacred associations in early history. They do not hold the German people responsible for the conduct of some of their leaders." [verified] — same source. The corpus had declined to assert the obvious motive; the motive is confirmed, and so is that it was contested at the time. **As German Township its line with Lima moved twice, and once each way.** Part of German was annexed to Lima city in 1902, and part of Lima city was annexed back to German in 1906. [verified] — [Abstract of the Thirteenth Census, Supplement for Ohio](../../catalog/census-1910-abstract-supplement-ohio.md), Allen County footnote. This is the earliest dated boundary event the corpus holds anywhere in the county, and the pattern it belongs to — four events into the city and two out of it, each outward one a year after an inward one — is set out at [Lima](lima.yml).

**As German Township it held 1,615 people in 1890, 1,951 in 1900 and 2,172 in 1910**, the Census using the old name at all three censuses. [verified] — [Abstract of the Thirteenth Census, Supplement for Ohio](../../catalog/census-1910-abstract-supplement-ohio.md); see [the 1890–1910 divisions](../measure/allen-county-townships-1890-1910.yml). It is one of only four of the county's twelve whose lowest recorded count is 1890 — it has grown at every observation the corpus holds, and ninefold since. [inference]

**It held 2,560 people in 1930 and 2,957 in 1940**, before Lima crossed into it: the 1950 return is 25,151 of which 19,270 is Lima city, leaving 5,881 outside the city. [verified] — [1950 Census, Number of Inhabitants, Ohio](../../catalog/census-1950-number-of-inhabitants-ohio.md), Table 6; see [the township series](../measure/allen-county-townships-1930-1950.yml). At 14,571 in 2020 it is **more than five and a half times its 1930 size outside the city**, the second fastest growth of the county's twelve townships. [inference] [Elida](elida.yml) ran 542, 551 and 607 across the same three censuses, so almost none of that growth is the village.

The Census returns it as American at all three of those censuses, the earliest being 1930. That is consistent with, and no more than consistent with, the [renaming of August 16, 1918](../question/what-became-of-german-and-ottawa-townships.yml): the first federal count after the change already carries the new name. [inference]

A township of 35.99 square miles about 11 miles south-east of the county's centre, internal point 40.695518, -83.928053. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), Ohio county subdivisions.

Its population was 2,764 at the 2020 estimates base and 2,819 in 2024. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md), sub-county file. It is one of only two subdivisions in the county that grew over those four years, by 55.

It contains [Harrod](harrod.yml) [verified] — same source, which reports it as a place within this township — and also [Westminster](westminster.yml), a census designated place of 406 that the sub-county file does not list because it has no government. [verified] — [2020 Census Block Assignment Files](../../catalog/census-block-assignment-2020.md).

Its schools are split: 2,740 of its people are in [Allen East Local](../jurisdiction/allen-east-local-school-district.yml) and 17, on two blocks at the south-east corner, in Auglaize County's [Waynesfield-Goshen](../jurisdiction/waynesfield-goshen-local-school-district.yml). [verified] — same source, crossed with [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md) block geography.

**The continental divide runs through it.** Four of its census blocks — 99 people and 43 housing units, along the county's eastern edge between 40.6487 and 40.7104 north — are in [the Scioto basin](../natural-feature/scioto-river-basin.yml) and drain to the Ohio River and the Gulf of Mexico. They are the only ground in Allen County that does. [verified] — [USGS Watershed Boundary Dataset](../../catalog/usgs-watershed-boundary.md), by block composition.

**Established March 5, 1832 by order of the commissioners of Allen County** — the first township the county's own board created from nothing rather than inherited. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md).

**A township named Scioto was disestablished into it in December 1832** and attached to Auglaize "for judicial purposes"; until [Perry](perry-township.yml) was established in December 1833 its twelve eastern sections were part of this township. [verified] — same source. The county has carried no Scioto township since, and this township is still where [its Gulf-side ground](../natural-feature/scioto-river-basin.yml) lies — the only part of Allen County that drains to the Ohio.

**The later history says Scioto is unexplained; the earlier one explains it.** In 1921 Rusler writes that "when Allen County was organized in 1831, its four townships were Amanda, Bath, Jackson and Scioto; in 1832 there was a German but no Scioto and no explanation is offered about it." [verified] — [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md). The explanation is in the book on the shelf beside it: the commissioners disestablished Scioto in December 1832 and attached its district to this township for judicial purposes. The corpus's older source answers its newer source's stated gap — which is the argument for holding both.

**Its 1,929 people in 1890 stood as its highest count for the next sixty years**, against 1,909 in 1900 and 1,883 in 1910. [verified] — [Abstract of the Thirteenth Census, Supplement for Ohio](../../catalog/census-1910-abstract-supplement-ohio.md); see [the 1890–1910 divisions](../measure/allen-county-townships-1890-1910.yml). [Harrod](harrod.yml) ran 269, 370 and 474 across the same three censuses, so the village nearly doubled while the township slipped — the growth below is a recovery before it is an expansion. [inference]

**It held 1,675 people in 1930, 1,719 in 1940 and 1,912 in 1950**, and 2,764 at the 2020 estimates base. [verified] — [1950 Census, Number of Inhabitants, Ohio](../../catalog/census-1950-number-of-inhabitants-ohio.md), Table 6; see [the township series](../measure/allen-county-townships-1930-1950.yml). It has grown at every observation the corpus holds, which no other township here has done, and it is also one of only two subdivisions in the county that gained population between 2020 and 2024. [inference] [Harrod](harrod.yml) ran 421, 422 and 482, so the village has been about a quarter of the township throughout and is now a sixth.

A township of 30.698 square miles about 3 miles east of the county's centre, internal point 40.781965, -84.042618. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), Ohio county subdivisions.

Its population was 9,399 at the 2020 estimates base and 9,263 in 2024. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md), sub-county file. Its population fell by 136 over those four years, as all but two of the county's subdivisions did. That makes it the third most populous of the county's thirteen civil subdivisions.
It contains no incorporated place; all of it is unincorporated. [verified] — same source, which lists no place within this township.

**It is older than the county's own government and no record of its erection survives.** The 1885 compiler, working from the commissioners' books, found the name and organization of Bath in use before Allen County was organized and "no record of its establishment either in the records of Allen or Mercer County"; he concedes that by 1831 it was a regularly organized township with Lima at its centre, with Chris. Wood, John Schrouf and James Daniels as justices. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md). This is the one township in the county whose erection is not on record anywhere the corpus has looked.

**Its boundary with Lima moved twice in four years, and once each way.** Part of Bath was annexed to Lima city in 1905, and part of Lima city was annexed back to Bath in 1903. [verified] — [Abstract of the Thirteenth Census, Supplement for Ohio](../../catalog/census-1910-abstract-supplement-ohio.md), Allen County footnote. Together with the annexation from Bath between 1980 and 1990, that is three dated boundary changes on this township's line with the city, spread across eighty-five years.

**It has moved twice more since, and one of them is measured to the square metre.** Lima annexed from Bath again between 2000 and 2010, and between the 2021 and 2022 gazetteer files this township lost 4,484 square metres while Lima gained 4,483 — 1.11 acres, from two rows computed independently. [verified] — [the 2010 volume](../../catalog/census-cph-2-37-ohio-2010.md), geographic change notes, and [the gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), Ohio county-subdivision and place files for 2021 and 2022.

**Its own area figures cannot be differenced across censuses.** Bath shows 30.98 square miles of land in the 2000 volume and 30.70 in the 2010 one, a fall of 179 acres — but so does every township in the county except Spencer, including seven that gave ground to nobody, and the county itself lost 1,235 acres of land it did not lose. [verified] — the two volumes; see [the control is the figure that cannot move](../../decisions/the-control-is-the-figure-that-cannot-move.yml).

**It held 1,448 people in 1890, 1,517 in 1900 and 1,501 in 1910**, before the city arrived. [verified] — [Abstract of the Thirteenth Census, Supplement for Ohio](../../catalog/census-1910-abstract-supplement-ohio.md); see [the 1890–1910 divisions](../measure/allen-county-townships-1890-1910.yml). Its lowest recorded count is 1890 and it has grown six and a half times since, which is the third largest growth of the county's twelve townships. [inference]

**It held 2,875 people in 1930 and 3,438 in 1940**, before Lima crossed into it: the 1950 return is 22,919 of which 17,469 is Lima city, leaving 5,450 outside the city. [verified] — [1950 Census, Number of Inhabitants, Ohio](../../catalog/census-1950-number-of-inhabitants-ohio.md), Table 6; see [the township series](../measure/allen-county-townships-1930-1950.yml). At 9,399 in 2020 it is more than three times its 1930 size outside the city. [inference] The [refinery](../site/lima-refinery.yml) sits in [Shawnee](shawnee-township.yml) rather than here, but the annexations that took Lima's corporation into Bath are the same process, and one of them is dated: the city annexed from Bath between 1980 and 1990.

**Two of the county's six colleges stand in it, and both give Lima as their post town.** [Rhodes State College](../organization/james-a-rhodes-state-college.yml) and [Ohio State's Lima campus](../organization/ohio-state-university-at-lima.yml) share 4240 Campus Drive, which the Census Bureau places in this township and in no incorporated place. [verified] — [IPEDS](../../catalog/ipeds.md) and [the Census geocoder](../../catalog/census-tiger-landmarks.md). Between them they enrol 4,708 students, more than half the county's total. [inference] — computed here against [higher education](../measure/allen-county-higher-education-2023.yml).

A village of 0.63 square miles in [Richland Township](richland-township.yml), about 8 miles north-east of the county's centre, internal point 40.832487, -83.973383. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), Ohio places.

Its population was 321 at the 2020 estimates base and 314 in 2024. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md), sub-county file. It lost 7 people over those four years.

**All of it is in Allen County.** The same file marks a place that crosses a county line with `(pt.)` and marks this one plainly, which is what separates it from [Bluffton](bluffton.yml) and [Delphos](delphos.yml). [verified] — same source.

**The village is one voting precinct, exactly.** Precinct `BEAVERDAM` holds 319 people and 151 housing units, and every block in it is in the village and every block of the village is in it. [verified] — [2020 Census Block Assignment Files](../../catalog/census-block-assignment-2020.md) crossed with [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md) block geography. Four of the county's nine municipalities are single precincts on these terms; the other five are split, and [Lima](lima.yml) is cut into 23. [verified] — [the county's voting districts](../measure/allen-county-voting-districts-2020.yml).

**The Census spelt it as two words until at least 1940.** "Beaverdam village returned in 1940 as Beaver Dam." [verified] — [1950 Census, Number of Inhabitants, Ohio](../../catalog/census-1950-number-of-inhabitants-ohio.md), Table 6, Allen County footnote. So the one-word form is the later one and the change is datable to between 1940 and 1950 in federal usage. [inference] The 1885 history agrees: it spells the place "Beaver Dam" throughout — scores of times in each of the two scans the corpus holds — and never as one word in either. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md), both scans. The two disagree on the tally, because they break lines differently; they do not disagree on the form. Which is what the etymology below would lead one to expect, and is the kind of agreement that makes the etymology likelier rather than merely repeated.

**Established in 1853, and named for the beaver dams** that were abundant near the original town site. [verified] — [Allen County](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md), cities and villages page. The [Village of Beaverdam](../jurisdiction/village-of-beaverdam.yml) was incorporated twenty-five years later, in 1878.

**Frederick Shull established it**, laying it out on Sections 29, 30, 31 and 32 of [Richland Township](richland-township.yml) — the original town bounded by North Street, Lima Street and Church Street. He was the village's postmaster when the office moved here about 1849, four years before the plat. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md). The county's page gives 1853 and no name; this source gives the name, and the two agree on the year against an OCR reading of 1858 in the other scan — see [two scans of one book](../../decisions/two-scans-of-one-book.yml), where an unrelated source settling a scanning dispute is the case the rule was written for.

**Its ground is the one piece of this county the survey grid cannot name.** Beaverdam's internal point falls inside the county's polygon for T3S R8E §5, and that polygon is 1,282 acres on a footprint 1.04 by 2.01 miles — one section's number drawn over two sections' ground. No parcel contains the point either, so there is no second witness. [verified] — [the survey sections](../measure/allen-county-survey-sections.yml).

**Two railways ran through it and one of them was electric.** "The Lake Erie & Western Railroad and the Lima & Findlay traction line pass through the village." [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md). The Lima & Findlay is named in that book's township chapters and in none of its transportation chapter; see [the interurban](../measure/allen-county-interurban-1901-1921.yml).

**Two tornadoes have been recorded at this village, fifty-six years apart.** The F3 of 19 July 1950 ended two-tenths of a mile from it after 9.7 miles from the south-east side of Lima, and an F1 touched down here at 14:18 on 22 June 2006 in the middle of the windstorm that crossed the county. [verified] — [the tornado of 1950](../event/the-tornado-of-19-july-1950.yml) and [the tornadoes](../measure/allen-county-tornadoes-1950-2026.yml).

nodes.label: Bluffton

properties.area_sq_mi: 3.652 land, 0.069 water (2020) — whole village, both counties

blocks.text: A village of 3.652 square miles in the county's north, internal point 40.892048, -83.887793. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md).

Like [Delphos](delphos.yml), Bluffton straddles a county line — here the Allen–Hancock line — and appears in Allen County tables as `Bluffton village (pt.)`, with 3,762 in the 2020 estimates base against a village total that is larger. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md). So its edge to the county is `partially-within`, not `within`.

It is the seat of Bluffton University and has a Swiss Mennonite settlement history that distinguishes it from the rest of the county. [inference] **It was originally known as Shannon.** [verified] — [Allen County](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md), cities and villages page, which also names [Bluffton University](../organization/bluffton-university.yml) here and its Mennonite affiliation.

**Platted in 1837 as Shannon, by Joseph Deford**, on Sections 1 and 12 of [Richland Township](richland-township.yml) — four blocks bounded by Jackson, Monroe, Jefferson and Riley streets. **The name was changed to Bluffton in 1872-73**, "although long prior to this the latter name was bestowed upon it". [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md), both scans agreeing. At 1837 it is the county's second-oldest platted town after [Lima](lima.yml).

**"Long prior to this" is now dated, and it is eleven years prior.** On 17 August 1861 the town voted to incorporate and to be called Bluffton. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md) and [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md); see [the ballot](../event/the-naming-and-incorporation-of-bluffton-1861.yml). **The corporation and the post office changed names twelve years apart**: the 1885 book's 1872–73 is the post office, which had been Croghan, then Shannon, and "again in 1873 named Bluffton". [inference] — the three books read together. So the ground was called Shannon for twenty-four years and its post office for thirty-six.

**Its bank is why John Dillinger was in the Allen County jail.** He was brought up from Dayton in the autumn of 1933 charged with robbing "the Bluffton, O., Commercial Bank of $2200", and was awaiting trial at Lima when three men shot the sheriff and took him out of the cell. [verified] — [Chronicling America](../../catalog/chronicling-america.md), *The Washington Daily News*, 13 October 1933; see [the raid on the Allen County jail](../event/allen-county-jail-raid-1933.yml).

**Its two witnesses to its own ground disagree, and the county line is why.** The section grid puts Bluffton's internal point in T2S R8E §1; the parcel containing the same point is numbered into §12, directly south. [verified] — [the survey sections](../measure/allen-county-survey-sections.yml). The point is the *whole* village's, Hancock County included, so it sits near that section line rather than inside either section with a margin — which is the same straddle that makes this village `Bluffton village (pt.)` in every census table. [inference]

**An interurban ran down its main street, and the through route it belonged to crossed the whole state.** "An electric railway passes directly through Main street, starting from Toledo and ending in Cincinnati, thus making Bluffton a railroad center." [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md). The same book's transportation chapter, counting trains that landed passengers in Lima, does not name this line; see [the interurban](../measure/allen-county-interurban-1901-1921.yml).

**Its water crosses a county line and its records show why that matters.** The village owns eight wells and buys surface water from Ottawa Village in Putnam County, which is why the federal file codes it a surface-water system though it owns no intake. [verified] — [the water systems](../measure/allen-county-water-systems-2026.yml). It was over a drinking-water standard for ten consecutive quarters from October 2013, the longest such run in the county's record, and cleared all ten on 7 April 2016. [verified] — [the violations](../measure/allen-county-water-violations-1984-2026.yml).

**The county's deadliest tornado ended near here.** The F4 of 11 April 1965 is recorded ending at 40.87, −83.87, 1.8 miles from the village, after 17.8 miles from Elida. [verified] — [the tornado](../event/the-tornado-of-11-april-1965.yml).

**And three-quarters of the county's 2007 flood damage was in this ZIP code.** 45817 holds 109 of Allen County's 227 owner registrations for the flood of August 2007, 91 of its 195 inspections and $481,404 of the $663,302 of inspected damage — 72.6 per cent, at an average of $4,416.55 a property. [verified] — [the household aid](../measure/allen-county-household-disaster-aid-2007-2020.yml). The village, its university and its school district were all paid public assistance for it. [verified] — [who was paid](../measure/allen-county-disaster-aid-applicants-2005-2025.yml).

**A third witness to the county line, and it is a mailing list.** The eight Ohio attorneys with a Bluffton address of record divide six to Allen County and two to Hancock, with none left unassigned — the same clean split [Delphos](delphos.yml) shows on its own line. [verified] — [the attorney directory](../../catalog/ohio-attorney-directory.md). That register's county is self-reported and is incomplete where no county line runs through a city, so its completeness here is the straddle appearing in a source with no reason to care about it. [inference]

refusals: The corpus does not assert its section.

blocks.text: A village of 0.277 square miles in [Monroe Township](monroe-township.yml), about 4 miles north of the county's centre, internal point 40.830753, -84.084489. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), Ohio places.

Its population was 519 at the 2020 estimates base and 508 in 2024. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md), sub-county file. It lost 11 people over those four years.

**All of it is in Allen County.** The same file marks a place that crosses a county line with `(pt.)` and marks this one plainly, which is what separates it from [Bluffton](bluffton.yml) and [Delphos](delphos.yml). [verified] — same source.

**The village is one voting precinct, exactly.** Precinct `CAIRO` holds 517 people and 216 housing units, and every block in it is in the village and every block of the village is in it. [verified] — [2020 Census Block Assignment Files](../../catalog/census-block-assignment-2020.md) crossed with [TIGERweb](../../catalog/tigerweb-census2020.md) block geography. Four of the county's nine municipalities are single precincts on these terms; the other five are split, and [Lima](lima.yml) is cut into 23. [verified] — [the county's voting districts](../measure/allen-county-voting-districts-2020.yml).

**Established in 1848 as West Cairo**, and renamed Cairo in 1922. [verified] — [Allen County](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md), cities and villages page. Main Street here was part of the Lincoln Highway, the country's first coast-to-coast road. [verified] — same source.

**It was platted in 1848 by Jacob Miller**, on Sections 29, 30, 31 and 32 of [Monroe Township](monroe-township.yml), running east from the Brenneman farm and lying mainly west of the Perrysburg Road at its crossing with the Bucyrus Road. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md). The county's own page gives 1848 without a founder; this is a second source arriving at the same year by a different route, seventy years earlier.

**The corporation dates from April 12, 1875**, twenty-seven years after the plat: "the village lay dormant awaiting developments until April 12, 1875, when it was organized and it still maintains a corporate existence." [verified] — [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md).

**Two more witnesses, with the mechanism and the first mayor.** The 1885 and 1906 histories give the same day and add that the village "was organized under authority of the commissioners, given April 12, 1875, on petition of" forty-one named citizens, with Dr. J. S. Clippinger elected mayor that year. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md) and [History of Allen County, 1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md); see [the organization](../event/the-organization-of-cairo-1875.yml). Three books, one date, and the corpus had read all three before it asked them this.

**A third witness for the older name, and the first federal one.** The 1910 census returns it as *West Cairo village*, at 386 in 1910, 338 in 1900 and 325 in 1890. [verified] — [Abstract of the Thirteenth Census, Supplement for Ohio](../../catalog/census-1910-abstract-supplement-ohio.md). So the name was in federal use as West Cairo as late as 1913, which sits inside the window the two county histories already gave and narrows nothing — but it does mean the 1922 renaming changed a name the Census Bureau was using, not only a local one. [inference]

properties.area_sq_mi: 3.322 land, 0.045 water (2020) — whole city, both counties

blocks.text: A city of 3.322 square miles on the county's western edge, internal point 40.846581, -84.336474. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md).

Delphos straddles the Allen–Van Wert county line, and the Census Bureau's Allen County rows record it as `Delphos city (pt.)` for exactly that reason: the 3,941 counted there in the 2020 estimates base is the Allen County portion, not the city. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md). Any figure for Delphos taken from an Allen County table and reported as the city's population understates it. Its edge to the county is `partially-within` for the same reason, matching the qualification [the Village of Bluffton](../jurisdiction/village-of-bluffton.yml) already carries.

The city grew as a port on the Miami and Erie Canal, which is why it sits on the county edge rather than on any natural centre. [inference] See [the Miami and Erie Canal](../site/miami-and-erie-canal.yml).

**It is the only place in this county besides Lima with anything on the National Register.** Two listings, both on the Allen County side: St. John Catholic Church, listed 3 January 1980, and the Marks Family House, 1 April 1982. Every other village in the county has none. [verified] — [the NPS spatial dataset](../../catalog/nrhp-national-register.md); see [the county's list](../measure/allen-county-national-register.yml). **It was four towns before it was one.** The county records Delphos as originally Howard, Section Ten, West Bredeick and East Bredeick, merged into a single town in 1851. [verified] — [Allen County](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md), cities and villages page. That is the only municipality in the county the source describes as made rather than founded, and it is a different kind of origin from a platted town site: four settlements with four names, none of which survives on the map.

**The merged town was incorporated by an act of February 7, 1851**, and held its first election on March 3, returning Lester Bliss as mayor and Smith Talbott as recorder. The corporation spent $80.67 in its first year. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md), both scans agreeing on the act's date. That puts a day on the year [the county's own page](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md) gives for the merger, from a source that had never seen it.

**Section Ten was a place before it was a name.** The tract was the Ten-Mile Woods: in 1834 William Brady and William Scott cut a road from the Auglaize River through it to Van Wert and "not even one cabin was to be seen in all that distance". [verified] — same source. The town's first newspaper, in 1848, was still called the *Section Ten Budget*.

**It was an interurban town as well as a steam one.** The 1906 history lists it on four steam railways "besides being on one of the best traction lines in the country — The Fort Wayne, Van Wert & Lima". [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md). By 1921 it still had interurban service to Lima and Fort Wayne; see [the interurban](../measure/allen-county-interurban-1901-1921.yml).

**A third witness to the county line, and it is a mailing list.** The twenty Ohio attorneys with a Delphos address of record divide thirteen to Allen County and seven to Van Wert, with none left unassigned. [verified] — [the attorney directory](../../catalog/ohio-attorney-directory.md). The county on that register is self-reported and is demonstrably incomplete elsewhere — seven Lima addresses carry no county at all, and Lima lies wholly in one — so its completeness here is the straddle appearing in a source with no reason to care about it. [inference]

nodes.label: Elida

blocks.text: A village of 1.102 square miles in [American Township](american-township.yml), about 5 miles west of the county's centre, internal point 40.78699, -84.199651. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), Ohio places.

Its population was 1,924 at the 2020 estimates base and 1,904 in 2024. [verified] — [Census Population Estimates](../../catalog/census-popest-2024.md), sub-county file. It lost 20 people over those four years.

**All of it is in Allen County.** The same file marks a place that crosses a county line with `(pt.)` and marks this one plainly, which is what separates it from [Bluffton](bluffton.yml) and [Delphos](delphos.yml). [verified] — same source.

**Established in 1852**, and the [Village of Elida](../jurisdiction/village-of-elida.yml) incorporated in 1878. [verified] — [Allen County](../../catalog/allen-county-official-site.md), cities and villages page.

**It has reported more annexation than it is.** Five annexations between May 1990 and May 2021 totalling 912.9 acres, against a village that occupied 703.6 acres in the 2012 geography and 745.6 in the 2024 one. [verified] — [the Boundary and Annexation Survey](../../catalog/census-bas-boundary-changes-ohio.md) against [the gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), Ohio place files. One of the five, ordinance 622-92 of 11 March 1992, claims 640.0 acres — exactly one square mile, which is the size of a survey section and not of a parcel. What the excess is, this corpus does not know: reported acreage is what a village put on a form, and a form is not a survey. [inference] — see [the annexation record](../measure/allen-county-annexations-1990-2024.yml).

**It was platted in 1852 by Griffith John**, on Sections 7, 8, 17 and 18 of what was then German Township — now [American](american-township.yml). [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1885](../../catalog/leeson-allen-county-1885.md). Griffith John is the same man who petitioned the commissioners in March 1833 to enlarge German Township and who assessed its district in 1846: the village was laid out by the township's own long-standing figure, on ground he had spent twenty years enlarging. [verified] — same source.

**It is named for the founder's brother.** "Griffith John was its founder, and it bears the name of his brother Elida John who never lived in the community." [verified] — [A Standard History of Allen County, 1921](../../catalog/rusler-allen-county-1921.md), which also confirms 1852 and the 1878 incorporation. That is a single witness read once, and it is the only etymology the corpus has for this village; the commonly repeated alternative — that Elida is a contraction of two women's names — appears in no source held here.

**An interurban ran through it, parallel to the steam road.** "It is situated on the Pittsburg, Fort Wayne & Chicago Railway and the Fort Wayne, Van Wert & Lima traction line", and in 1905 the Pennsylvania handled 484 car-loads of freight at this station, principally grain and live-stock. [verified] — [History of Allen County, 1906](../../catalog/miller-allen-county-1906.md). It is the only village in the county the sources place on [the interurban Lima financed](../organization/fort-wayne-van-wert-and-lima-traction-company.yml) by name and by station rather than by compass.

**Its water is Lima's.** The village owns no source of its own: its one supply facility is a permanent consecutive connection from the Lima City system, and it serves 4,109 people on 1,684 connections — more than twice the village's own population, so most of its customers are in [American Township](american-township.yml) around it. [verified] — [the water systems](../measure/allen-county-water-systems-2026.yml). [inference]

refusals: What the excess is, this corpus does not know: reported acreage is what a village put on a form, and a form is not a survey.

properties.former_names: Listed as "Fort Shawnee village" in Census files through the 2010 census, and as "Fort Shawnee CDP" in the 2020 geography. [verified]

blocks.text: A community of 9.51 square miles south of Lima, internal point 40.681287, -84.149835. [verified] — [2020 Census Gazetteer](../../catalog/census-gazetteer-2020.md), where it is listed as `Fort Shawnee CDP`.

It was an incorporated village through at least 2010: the intercensal file lists `Fort Shawnee village` with 3,866 at the 2000 base and 3,726 at the 2010 census.
